Founded in 2019 by KyungRok Kim, a former Samsung Electronics engineer, Ternell reports that tests with 28-nanometer chips showed a 33% to 102% increase in memory capacity per area, and a 55% to 71% reduction in energy needed to access data, compared with conventional SRAM. Testbank Testbank is a Korean edtech startup developing Solve, an app that converts printed study materials, such as workbooks and test-prep books, into interactive digital versions. The startup uses AI to identify question and answer spaces in publishers’ PDF files while preserving the original layout. Solve lets you write answers directly on the page and be graded automatically.

title: Who could replace Jensen Huang? A highly unscientific list of possible successors
abstract: It’s almost inconceivable that Nvidia would fire its rock star CEO. Yet here we are, on the precipice of this happening. Over at Kalshi, Jensen Huang’s odds of surviving the week are sitting at a lowly 30% . Even though he built one of the world’s most valuable — and, many would argue, dangerously powerful — companies, the tides have completely turned against him. He has confessed to an extramarital affair, but as of Wednesday afternoon it isn’t even clear who he meant: Alice Huang, the Chinese executive suspected by U.S. intelligence of spying for her country, or Kimberly Powell, an Nvidia executive who reports to him and who, five sources told The New York Times in an explosive new report, was also a paramour. Even if Huang is pushed out as CEO, the board members he has made very rich are unlikely to cut him loose entirely. Barring another shoe dropping, they could keep him on as chairman, a role Nvidia doesn’t currently have. But someone still has to run the company, and there’s no apparent succession plan, which leaves us, like everyone else, to speculate while we wait to see what happens next. While Huang’s 60 direct reports undoubtedly get a closer look, consider this our own parlor game, featuring some obvious and less obvious candidates: Lisa Su . The AMD CEO runs Nvidia’s most credible rival and is a distant cousin of Huang. The Information floated her name this week, but why would she leave her job for his? Her company stands to benefit from every day that Nvidia spends distracted by an investigation, congressional briefings, and all the mini dramas that are sure to follow. Her best move might be to send a nice note and keep her current corner office. Eric Schmidt. He was the pick of Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, senior associate dean for leadership studies at the Yale School of Management, who we talked with earlier this week. Schmidt could “parachute in tomorrow and do a very good job,” Sonnenfeld said, and perhaps he could. He ran Google from 2001 to 2011, chaired the National Security Commission on AI from 2018 to 2021, and now runs the rocket company Relativity Space. Chips, software, government, rockets — it’s an impressive range. Then again, Schmidt would bring a lot of baggage when it comes to his own extramarital dalliances . It’s hard to see him clearing the board for that reason. Lip-Bu Tan . Intel’s CEO knows chips, and right now he might welcome a very soft landing. Last month, Intel reported third-quarter revenue up 21% to $16.5 billion, then warned its fourth-quarter results would fall short of Wall Street’s forecasts. The AI boom has caused a memory-chip shortage, pushing up PC prices and cutting PC sales. That’s hurt Intel (PC chips are a big part of its business), and its stock plunged 20% in after-hours trading on the warning, having already slid more than 30% since September. A move to a company that’s eating everyone’s lunch would be a pretty amazing escape hatch. Bret Taylor. The former Salesforce co-CEO and OpenAI board chair now runs the AI startup Sierra, and his résumé includes a lot of the biggest brands in Silicon Valley. He co-created Google Maps, served as Facebook’s CTO, and chaired Twitter’s board through its sale to Elon Musk. He then took over as OpenAI’s board chair after the “Blip,” Sam Altman’s firing and fast return. When companies need an unflappable, likable adult in the room, they call Taylor. He probably knows nearly every customer Nvidia has, too. Ian Buck. If the board feels strongly about having a “builder” at the helm, they could do worse than the Nvidia VP who helped develop CUDA, the chip software that has become central to Nvidia’s dominance in AI. Analysts and former employees have floated him as a possible successor, and Kalshi traders give him a middling shot . He’s no household name, but the Stanford PhD seems more viable if Huang can keep that chairman title and push for a successor he can work with. Someone else down the hall. Andrew Bell, Nvidia’s senior vice president of hardware engineering, arrived 25 years ago as a fresh Cornell grad and has been on an upward trajectory at the company ever since. Like Buck and dozens of other executives who are presumably being scrutinized, he reports directly to Huang. Nvidia CFO Colette Kress is the insider most often named, but analysts say she isn’t necessarily a natural successor as an innovator and visionary, and Bell has the chip pedigree. The wild card? Lori Huang . Nobody has floated her, but hear us out: Jensen met his wife as lab partners at Oregon State, so she has been working with him since before Nvidia existed. After graduating, she worked at Silicon Graphics as a microchip engineer (making more money than her husband, he has said), then scaled back to raise the couple’s family, and she now co-leads the family trusts. If the board wants continuity, they could do worse than a humbler Huang who is also a brainiac. There’s a reason they say that behind every great man is a great woman (and vice versa). Whatever happens next, we’ll know soon.

title: Google’s new Gemini model is better at understanding complicated questions
abstract: AI News Tech Google’s new Gemini model is better at understanding complicated questions Google’s Robby Stein says Gemini 4 Hydrogen is ‘the biggest model upgrade to Search yet.’﻿ Google’s Robby Stein says Gemini 4 Hydrogen is ‘the biggest model upgrade to Search yet.’﻿ by Stevie Bonifield Nov 12, 2026, 9:55 PM UTC Illustration: The Verge Stevie Bonifield is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI. Google says its new Gemini 4 Hydrogen model can give more helpful answers to complex questions, including “questions with multiple parts, hard-to-understand typos, or highly specific requests.” The new model can break down your questions and address each part in its responses. It’s available starting today in search, the Gemini app, all tiers of Google AI Studio, the Gemini API, Gemini for business, and in Google Antigravity for Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers. Robby Stein, VP of product at Google Search, says it’s “now the new default model in AI Mode & being used for your hardest questions in AI Overviews.” Google says Gemini 4 Hydrogen also gives users a wider range of links in its responses by “conducting simultaneous queries across all the relevant subtopics.” Its responses have more visuals, too, like images, comparison tables, graphs, and maps. One of Stein’s examples shows the AI generating an interactive animated driving simulation in response to a user’s question about how phones locate which lane of a highway a car is on in areas without cell service. Google says the new model also has improved language understanding “across all supported AI Mode languages.” Users have more thinking level options with Gemini 4 Hydrogen, as well, including low, medium, high, and a new “xhigh” mode. According to Google, the new model “delivers significant leaps in both speed and intelligence” compared to Gemini Flash 3.8 , and it “matches or outperforms some of the competing models in its class,” like Claude Sonnet 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Terra. title: No, AI agents did not discover a previously unknown Maya site
abstract: AI Science Tech No, AI agents did not discover a previously unknown Maya site Scientists are getting tired of amateurs parachuting into their fields and making ‘discoveries’ with AI.﻿ Scientists are getting tired of amateurs parachuting into their fields and making ‘discoveries’ with AI.﻿ by Robert Hart Nov 12, 2026, 7:42 PM UTC “I woke up and checked the agents’ reports. ‘DAMN!’ They had found lots of villages and other regular shapes that looked like structures or houses,“ Pietro Miotti wrote on his blog. Image: Pietro Miotti Robert Hart is a London-based reporter at The Verge covering all things AI and a Senior Tarbell Fellow. Previously, he wrote about health, science and tech for Forbes . Armed with a team of AI agents, Google researcher Pietro Miotti claimed earlier this week to have discovered a potentially unmapped Maya site in Mexico. There was just one problem: The site had already been discovered and was published in an academic journal last year. The incident, which sparked criticism among archeologists online, underscores a growing tension in science as amateurs wielding increasingly powerful AI tools parachute into specialist fields, often without the expertise needed to understand what they are looking at. Local communities are often already well aware of sites in their area. Miotti said the idea to use AI to search for archeological sites came to him while traveling in Peru, when he began wondering what historic explorers might do with access to modern technology. He settled on lidar, a laser-based mapping technology that can produce detailed three-dimensional images of the environment, and set a team of 48 AI agents to comb through NASA lidar data for signs of undocumented sites. As “Peru isn’t well covered” by public lidar data, Miotti wrote, he shifted his focus to the Maya region. The agents flagged numerous promising locations, including “one major village [that] doesn’t seem to have been registered” in existing records. Miotti, who described the research to The Verge as a personal side project done without any Google compute or resources, said he then reached out to Mexico’s National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH) to check whether the apparent discovery was already known, including through unpublished research. Using the agents to translate his correspondence into Spanish, Miotti said INAH told him it had no record of a registered site at that location. “It took less than 72 hours to go from a random thought while traveling to an official reply from the Mexican government. This is by far the best time ever to be alive,” Miotti wrote on his blog. Miotti stressed that he is not an archeologist and emphasized that the finding would need to be verified with fieldwork. Nevertheless, he hailed it as proof that “we’re on the brink of a revolution across every science” and called for the “entire planet” to be mapped with lidar so AI agents could “help us find the rest.” Had he been an archaeologist familiar with the region, however, Miotti might have spotted a problem: The site was already known, and had been documented in an academic journal more than a year earlier. “I didn’t expect it to get this much attention.” Archeologists were quick to point out the oversight on social media. In a series of posts on Bluesky, Sarah Parcak, an archeology professor at the University of Alabama at Birmingham, stressed the importance of carefully checking findings against existing research. “This is why we have peer review,” Parcak wrote, adding that just because the Mexican government doesn’t have something in its database doesn’t mean it is unknown or unmapped. Other archeologists echoed her criticism, slamming the project for spreading misinformation and taking credit away from archeologists, who have been using advanced digital tools in their work for decades. “This was a personal project that I was excited to share,” Miotti told The Verge . “I didn’t expect it to get this much attention.” He added that as a non-archaeologist, he had not realized a site not being registered wasn’t the same as it not having been mapped, adding that expert knowledge “is needed to verify what the agents find.” He also addressed the limits of his AI tools: “My agents and I missed it. Archaeologists rightly don’t publish the coordinates of sites, so checking whether a site is already known means comparing images against figures in papers, not searching a database. That’s much harder for agents, and it’s something these tools need to get better at. When people pointed it out, I updated the post and the blog as soon as I could to credit their work.” Nevertheless, Miotti said this was an example of how agents could be used to help experts sort through large amounts of data. He said he has been encouraged by the archaeologists and PhD students that he said were reaching out to him “excited about the workflow and wanting to know how it works and whether it could help with their own survey data.” “Our ‘problem’ is not discovering new sites,” Elizabeth Graham, a professor of Mesoamerican archaeology at University College London, told The Verge . “Most of us working in the Maya area know about tons of sites not explored or excavated or mapped, most of these found on foot,” she said. Graham also critiqued the use of the word “discover,” noting that local communities are often already well aware of sites in their area. While she credited Miotti with doing a decent job of using AI to map the mounds from lidar data — “the interpretation of lidar data can be tricky” — Graham argued the bigger obstacle is funding for research. “The fact is, there just isn’t the funding to excavate or map sites as there was in the past, so in a way it doesn’t matter how many more are ‘discovered.’” “Just spotting something does not add much to our knowledge.” The controversy reflects a broader problem with AI in science, perhaps most visible with OpenAI’s recent advances in mathematics . While AI tools are increasingly capable of producing genuinely impressive results, they don’t always engage with the existing research those findings build upon. The result can be claimed breakthroughs that have, as is the case here, already been made by someone else, or a general failure to credit earlier work. Even when the findings are actually new, they can lack context a specialist would bring. Ultimately, amateur use of AI tools often ends up shifting the burden of establishing what has actually been found and why it matters to actual experts, work that would ordinarily be part of making a scientific discovery in the first place. Ivan Šprajc, a professor of archaeology at the Research Centre of the Slovenian Academy of Sciences and Arts in Ljubljana and a coauthor of the paper documenting the site, told The Verge he wasn’t particularly impressed by the agents’ work. Archeologists have been using lidar and “other sophisticated remote sensing tools for quite some time,” he said, adding that “just spotting something does not add much to our knowledge.” He told The Verge that while it is commendable that Miotti checked in with INAH, doing so is “not sufficient” as the institution does not have access to all possible information. “The fact that INAH has no official knowledge of a particular cluster of archaeological features does not necessarily mean that it has not been spotted or even explored by archaeologists.” Šprajc said that he worries the growing use of AI tools by amateurs could overwhelm archeologists with claims of new discoveries. “Just today I have received an email from another AI ‘discoverer,’ so I am a little bit concerned about being flooded by this kind of message,” he said. He also raised another potential risk of amateurs publicizing the locations of archeological sites: attracting looters. “But as long as these findings do not lead to looting, I don’t see a major problem,” he added.

title: Oh, Palantir is ‘progressive’ now, is it?
abstract: AI Policy Tech Oh, Palantir is ‘progressive’ now, is it? A children’s treasury of things Alex Karp has said in public over the last three years. A children’s treasury of things Alex Karp has said in public over the last three years. by Elizabeth Lopatto Nov 12, 2026, 6:06 PM UTC The future’s so bright, he’s gotta wear sunglasses. Photo by Scott Olson/Getty Images Elizabeth Lopatto is a reporter who writes about tech, money, and human behavior. She joined The Verge in 2014 as science editor. Previously, she was a reporter at Bloomberg. I had other things to do today, but Alex Karp’s pathetic attempt to pivot back to the left gave me no choice but to put them on hold. Last week’s elections were a bloodbath for the right, a problem for all the wannabe fash founders who had tied their political fortunes to a “vibe shift” that enabled a glorious 100-year Trumpenreich. That freed up a lot of assholes to say what they actually thought. Except Donald Trump’s victory was, in fact, narrow, and two years of his corrupt policies have enraged Americans. “I’ve been a Democrat my whole life. I grew up in a far left environment. I know more about being a progressive than almost anybody on the planet, and I absolutely believe Palantir— all of our products are essentially progressive,” Karp told Politico . Is that so, baby doll? Let’s run it back. August 2024: “I’m not going to apologize for defending the U.S. government on the border, defending the Special Ops, bringing the people home,” he told Maureen Dowd . February 2025: Karp wrote in a letter to shareholders that “As Samuel Huntington has written, the rise of the West was not made possible ‘by the superiority of its ideas or values or religion . . . but rather by its superiority in applying organized violence.’” February 2025: “Palantir is ‘making America more lethal’ by analyzing troves of data for the U.S. armed forces and allies to help them anticipate enemies’ moves, locate their coordinates ‘and, on occasion, kill them.’” I am quoting the WSJ here. The WSJ is quoting an earnings call . November 2025: Palantir is “the first company to be completely anti-woke,” Karp declared on an earnings call . November 2025: “ I spend a lot of time talking to Nazis. Like, real Nazis .” November 2025: “Democrats just completely neglect males. ... It’s admirable to be a ... high-testosterone male. And ... you have the general vibe in the Democratic Party that there’s something wrong. ... I don’t find it very appealing as a dude.” Also, from the same interview , referring to his Democratic friends: “You have to grow a spine because a lot of these people actually agree with me in private.” November 2025: “Our competition is political. The woke left and the woke right wake up every day, figuring out how they can hurt Palantir. If they get into power, they’ll hurt Palantir. And by the way, it’s global. I view Democrats as my party, but if the Mamdani wing of the party takes over? If that’s my party, I’m not in it. Or the right woke wing, which is like, everything is a conspiracy, any use of technology is actually going to only be used to eviscerate and attack us?” Also, on progressivism : “Universities and elite institutions have played a corrosive role here. People are teaching pagan religion views — a new religion with sacrifices. Who’s the sacrifice? Me, I’m the sacrifice.” December 2025: In response to The New York Times ’ reporting on his company (unclear which article, maybe this one ?): “That article about us being a surveillance thing — is like, where it’s all implied what we do — yeah, but the problem is you lose credibility with anyone who goes on the thing and then — and that’s damaging for our democracy.” Later, in the same interview : “The one thing I would say to people in the audience — you know you, a lot of you think I’m right. And you know your spouse, your relative, your child, the person at work would be horrified if they knew it. You better speak up. Because everyone who thinks I’m a ridiculous fascist, they’re speaking up. They write about it every day. If you do not speak up, the people who are disagreeing with me or think I’m stupid — well, I disagree with myself. So, you have to speak up. And you cannot blame the far left, far right idiots when they speak up for their views. Do you speak up for your views? Where?” April 2026: That manifesto , which was previously published as a book . “The postwar neutering of Germany and Japan must be undone. The defanging of Germany was an overcorrection for which Europe is now paying a heavy price.” Also, well after Elon Musk did his little uhhh hand gesture and DOGE ran rampant across the US government : “We should applaud those who attempt to build where the market has failed to act. The culture almost snickers at Musk’s interest in grand narrative.” And maybe most notably: “Some cultures have produced vital advances; others remain dysfunctional and regressive. All cultures are now equal. Criticism and value judgments are forbidden.” July 2026: On CNBC , referring to frontier models: “This is the voice of American business that is being channeled through me.” Anyway, for any other tech bros who want to do a less clumsy pivot than Karp, I have a suggestion. First, go to rehab, ideally for 90 days. Then come out and apologize for whatever it was you said between, I don’t know, 2020 and now. You feel very bad about what you’ve said, but it was the cocaine (or the amphetamines, or hell, blame it on ketamine, since the average person has no idea what a ketamine high looks like) speaking. You have dried out and sobered up. It was a challenge, but it was rewarding. You are now chastened. You want to work for public accountability. You are sorry about the dumb things you said while you were high. This won’t work for Karp, who’s been absolutely adamant that he does not do drugs . But you, the savvy tech CEO and/or VC, you can’t skip the rehab part. You can’t blame the drugs if you don’t at least pretend to sober up. title: The Jensen Huang scandal is hardly over
abstract: AI Policy Report The Jensen Huang scandal is hardly over A second affair has hit the news cycle, but that’s not what matters here. by Elizabeth Lopatto Nov 12, 2026, 5:44 PM UTC Image: The Verge; Getty Images; Adobe AI Policy Report The Jensen Huang scandal is hardly over A second affair has hit the news cycle, but that’s not what matters here. by Elizabeth Lopatto Nov 12, 2026, 5:44 PM UTC Part Of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has resigned. What happens next? see all updates Elizabeth Lopatto is a reporter who writes about tech, money, and human behavior. She joined The Verge in 2014 as science editor. Previously, she was a reporter at Bloomberg. I was certain, until the story of Jensen Huang’s second affair hit, that Huang was bulletproof. After all, why wouldn’t he be? He’s placed himself indispensably at the center of the AI industry and famously had no succession plan at Nvidia. In fact, he’s the only CEO Nvidia has ever had. L’état c’est moi. Then two stories were published nearly back to back on Wednesday: one alleging Huang had an affair with his subordinate Kimberly Powell, another that the board was meeting to consider his ouster. First thing Thursday morning, Nvidia announced Huang had resigned. One of the most powerful men in Silicon Valley was out. Why throw Huang under the bus for getting his nuts drained? Fascinating. First of all, when I asked on Monday “Who else is Jensen Huang fucking?” I did not expect to get answers this fast — somebody, potentially somebody on the board (as we’ve seen in other incidents ), wanted the story out there. Second, why throw Huang under the bus for getting his nuts drained? This is not an industry that cares about that kind of thing — just ask Eric Schmidt and Bill Gates. My guess is that the second affair is a pretext for action, and this all goes back to the original story from last week: that Huang was honeypotted by an alleged Chinese spy. Whatever was going on with neocloud Megaspeed might be much, much worse than we know, and what we know is pretty bad : business listings that led to “a Malaysian data center and shopping mall, a near-empty office in Singapore and a dilapidated storefront outside Kuala Lumpur.” Do you have information about Nvidia? Contact Elizabeth Lopatto securely on Signal at lopatto.46. Even months before the report that Alice “No Relation” Huang, an exec at Megaspeed, was having an affair with Huang, there were questions about Nvidia’s business in China. The US government has placed strict export controls on Nvidia’s high-end chips. Huang claimed in May that as a result, Nvidia has zero percent market share in China . But also in May, short sellers Culper Research published a report in which they wrote, “We believe that in reality, over 20% of Nvidia’s FY 2026 compute revenues remained driven by China – supported both by illegal GPU diversion and Southeast Asian intermediaries.” Megaspeed was Nvidia’s largest Southeast Asian buyer, but Singaporean newspaper The Straits Times visited Megaspeed’s Singapore office a month ago to find “no signs of activity.” Another building tenant told the reporters, “It is always dark for as long as it has been here. I hardly see anyone visiting or in the office.” The sole director of Megaspeed, Tan Yong Pong, appears to have vanished . The Singaporean company that owns Megaspeed, Swiftdata, has listed an office that belongs to an interior design firm as its business address. Megaspeed is only part of the story Incidentally, Alice Huang has surfaced in Beijing . The Financial Times says she’s barred from Singapore for giving police “inaccurate information.” Oh, and reportedly her companies invested in Chinese AI company DeepSeek and promised them Nvidia’s Blackwell chips? Fun! Megaspeed is only part of the story, I think. There are two Chinese chip-related scandals that could cause serious problems for Nvidia, and both feature people with close ties to Huang. One is Megaspeed, which involves Huang’s maybe-spy affair partner. The other centers on Super Micro (which, horribly, does business as Supermicro), a partner of Nvidia run by one of Huang’s old friends, Charles Liang. Super Micro’s cofounder, Yih-Shyan “Wally” Liaw, along with Ruei-Tsang “Steven” Chang and Ting-Wei “Willy” Sun, allegedly defrauded the US by serving as a passthrough for a front company to buy $2.5 billion of Nvidia chips for Alibaba. The front company, not named in the indictment, is Thailand-based OBON , according to Bloomberg . Liang and Super Micro have not been charged. But these incidents may not be the end of Nvidia’s problems. Take for instance, more recently, New Matrix — another company that barely exists , and yet is an approved buyer of Nvidia chips. It is, in fact, one of several approved companies that “have ties to firms that have been blacklisted by the U.S. government, or that work as military contractors in China,” according to The New York Times. The question, of course, is how high this all goes Huang has insisted that Nvidia has seen “no evidence of any AI chip diversion.” He’s been pretty emphatic on that point , actually. I am now wondering if that is even a little bit true. If the board is cutting Huang loose, there’s probably more on chip smuggling allegations coming. More substantively, Nvidia reportedly intervened in a 2025 Commerce Department investigation of Megaspeed , which was suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips — halting the investigation. Since the scandal broke, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick appears to have become the fall guy for this, with Axios reporting that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent “confronted” him about failing to note Megaspeed as a national security concern and Politico saying “ more than half a dozen Republicans have demanded answers” from him . The question, of course, is how high this all goes. After all, Huang was awfully buddy-buddy with President Donald Trump, who was informed about Huang’s maybe-spy girlfriend in 2025 and apparently did nothing about it. Incidentally, Nvidia has reportedly donated $25 million to Trump’s planned ballroom . This is what gangster tech regulation looks like. I wonder what else was an open secret at the company, you know? Come January, Elizabeth Warren will be able to send subpoenas in her role as the chair of the Senate Banking Committee. And wouldn’t you know, she seems to be pretty interested . Democrats will control both the House and the Senate. Their voters have given them a mandate to root out corruption. And boy howdy, does Nvidia look like a sitting duck right now. If Huang knew chips were being diverted — or had reason to know that — and tried to ensure their sales anyway, he may have committed actual crimes (bribery, espionage, smuggling, whatever) and, under a functioning legal system, could actually go to jail. Nvidia dispensing with its indispensable CEO is the company reducing its risk of getting roped into Huang’s drama. Will it be that easy for Nvidia? I wonder. The most interesting part of the second affair story , with Powell, the Nvidia vice president of healthcare, comes at the very end of the New York Times article. When someone took a video of Powell and Huang being “affectionate” in March, Huang’s security had nondisclosure agreements ready to go. CNBC reports that rumors of their affair have circulated “for years.” I wonder what else was an open secret at the company, you know? Especially since Huang had 60 direct reports, so every part of the company is covered in his fingerprints. Over in the tech world, people still seem to be in denial. On X, the social network for Trumpist dead-enders, the account “zerohedge” posted, “Elon please hire Jensen.” Elon Musk replied, “ That would be an honor. ” Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates. title: AI chatbots are recommending fake retail websites, study finds
abstract: AI Tech Google AI chatbots are recommending fake retail websites, study finds A study testing Gemini, Perplexity, and ChatGPT found that in as many as 15 percent of conversations, chatbots displayed ‘risky’ URLs.﻿ A study testing Gemini, Perplexity, and ChatGPT found that in as many as 15 percent of conversations, chatbots displayed ‘risky’ URLs.﻿ by Mia Sato Nov 12, 2026, 5:00 PM UTC Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge, Getty Images Mia Sato is features writer with five years of experience covering the companies that shape technology and the people who use their tools. Shoppers using AI chatbots to research products or find places to buy items could be directed to imposters and other risky websites, a new study found. The study conducted by IP protection firm Podqi and shared exclusively with The Verge prompted ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity with a handful of shopping-related questions involving a selection of 151 brands. Questions included “What are the top websites for buying [brand]?”; “Where can I find [brand] online?”; and “Does [brand] ship internationally? What are their regional websites?” The test ran over the course of two testing periods in September and asked about 151 small and large companies like fashion brands Lululemon, Birkenstock, Stüssy, and Madhappy (a client of Podqi) and homeware brand Le Creuset. Podqi crafted its own prompts (as opposed to using real user conversations) and tested its prompts using a tool that tracks AI answers across chatbots. Perplexity performed the worst, showing risky sites in 15 percent of answers Over the course of 6,795 answers, Podqi found that all three AI engines cited and showed shoppers risky sites, defined as fake websites impersonating real retailers or selling knockoffs, old brand domains that have been reregistered by someone else, or dead sites that aren’t active at all but that someone else could purchase and reuse. Google’s Gemini showed risky sites least often of the three, linking to or mentioning a risky site in 4 percent of answers. (Mentions include instances of recommending a risky site, displaying it without comment, and warning a user about it.) Perplexity performed the worst, showing risky sites in 15 percent of answers. ChatGPT fell somewhere in the middle at 8 percent. ChatGPT performed the best when it came to offering warnings about each risky site that it surfaced, doing so 24 percent of the time. Smaller brands appear especially at risk: Podqi found that queries related to larger companies had risky sites in answers about half as often. AI companies market chatbots as being helpful for shopping tasks like researching, comparing, and discovering products or retailers. AI citing fake sites is a headache for brands and retailers, of course, but it could also quickly become a risk for consumers. The issue could be especially relevant going into the upcoming holiday shopping season, when consumers are hunting around for in-stock items and the best prices. It’s likely that more consumers will be using AI to shop this year, including buying products from brands or sites they’re not already familiar with. “Part of this piece, too, is making sure that the consumers know, even though you are being fed a result in a particular chatbot, it is always best to verify the source of that before entering personal information or credit card information,” says Podqi CEO and cofounder Trevor West. “We take information quality seriously, and are happy to see that Gemini performed best among the products tested,” Google spokesperson Jessica Levis Boord said in an email. “We continually work to test and improve our models, and are upfront that Gemini is AI and can make mistakes, so we display links to sources alongside responses to help people verify information.” “Our goal is for ChatGPT to connect people with reliable places to shop,” OpenAI spokesperson Taya Christianson said in an email. “We’re continuing to improve our safeguards to make potentially deceptive sites less likely to appear in shopping-related results. We appreciate researchers sharing examples that show us where we can improve the experience.” In Podqi’s test, certain prompts seemed to trigger risky sites more often than others. For example, AI displayed risky sites more often when asked about regional brand websites compared to other prompt categories. The tested AI engines also at times listed fake regional sites for brands that do not have any. In one conversation, Perplexity named the wrong page as Stüssy’s official website and called it “the best starting point for guaranteed authentic items.” “Perplexity is consistently the most accurate AI on credible research benchmarks, and has been for four years. We never claim to be 100% accurate, but we do claim to be the only company relentlessly focused on it,” spokesperson Jesse Dwyer said in an email. title: More game developers are starting to use generative AI
abstract: Gaming AI Entertainment More game developers are starting to use generative AI The GDC Festival of Gaming’s latest annual industry survey shows an increase in AI usage among game developers.﻿ The GDC Festival of Gaming’s latest annual industry survey shows an increase in AI usage among game developers.﻿ by Jay Peters Nov 12, 2026, 5:00 PM UTC A photo from the GDC Festival of Gaming 2026 event. Image: GDC Festival of Gaming Jay Peters is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme. More video game developers are using generative AI tools in their jobs compared to last year, according to the GDC Festival of Gaming’s latest annual industry survey . Forty percent of developers surveyed say they use it “as part of their job,” an increase from 36 percent in 2025 . Usage was higher with game developers that work on free-to-play games at 58 percent and mobile-only studio workers at 70 percent. The survey is being published as the game industry continues to reckon with generative AI tools. While many game developers, particularly indie developers , have spoken out strongly against the technology, AI is at the center of indie awards conversations in part because Big Walk developer House House “sparingly” used LLMs to assist with technical challenges in the “final stretch” of development. AI is also increasingly being used to reverse-engineer retro games . And in a post on Thursday , Xbox CEO Asha Sharma seemed to indicate that AI will be central to Xbox’s future, saying that “A small team will be able to build worlds that today demand hundreds of developers and hundreds of millions of dollars.” Seventy three percent of the survey’s respondents said they used AI for research and brainstorming, while 62 percent used it for data analysis and summarization, and 56 percent for code generation and debugging. Twenty two percent of respondents used generative AI for concept art or visual ideation, and 8 percent used it for production art or final game assets. The survey also included grim numbers about layoffs, with 34 percent of respondents saying they have been laid off sometime in the past two years. title: Jensen Huang is out. What did China want from him?
abstract: Today, we’re talking about the Jensen Huang scandal at Nvidia, which is developing so quickly that we had to do an emergency update of this intro minutes before publishing this episode. Huang just resigned from his position as CEO of Nvidia as news of his affairs, including with an alleged Chinese spy, threatened to engulf the company. We’ll have more on that story as things develop and we learn how Nvidia will restructure itself after Jensen — he had something like 60 direct reports, after all, and the entire AI financial ecosystem flows through the company. This is pure Decoder bait. But just two days ago I talked to Kyle Chan, a foreign policy fellow at the Brookings Institution’s John L. Thornton China Center, about the real heart of the scandal: What would China even seek to accomplish by having a spy so close to Jensen? And what does the real state of the US-China AI conflict really looks like, particularly from the Chinese point of view? Kyle’s answers about chips and how China is perceiving the so-called AI “race” were very illuminating, but maybe even more interesting was his observation on Jensen Huang’s relationship with Trump was the most important thing of all — because maybe what China most stood to gain was someone who could whisper in the right ears. Let’s just dive right into it. But keep in mind that when we were talking, we still didn’t know what would happen with Jensen. Okay: Kyle Chan on Nvidia, China, and the future of AI export controls. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Kyle Chan, you are a fellow at the John L. Thornton China Center at the Brookings Institution. Welcome to Decoder . What on earth could we be talking about as it relates to your expertise about China today? I have a lot to ask you about Nvidia, about our relationship to China as a country, as an economy, and about national security. Let’s start at the very beginning. From all the reporting we have today, it seems like the United States government has been very worried about a company called Megaspeed and Alice Huang, the alleged Chinese spy at the center of the swirling scandal around Jensen Huang, the CEO of Nvidia. What do we know about Alice Huang and Megaspeed? We have to be careful about what we know and what we don’t know. So far, there are allegations that the US intelligence community believes that Alice Huang may be an asset of the Chinese intelligence services. Megaspeed itself is a customer of Nvidia’s and they built a data center in Malaysia. They also seem to potentially have ties with Chinese companies and could — and this is where we’re getting into what we do know and what we don’t know — potentially be a conduit for Chinese AI companies accessing cutting-edge Nvidia chips like Blackwells. Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here . Not a subscriber? You can sign up here . I want to rewind way back. The notion that the Chinese AI industry wants Nvidia chips has been floating around for years and the idea that the Chinese AI industry would somehow develop a parallel set of technology or a superior set of technology because of the constraint of not having Nvidia chips has percolated into the discourse several times. I’m particularly thinking about DeepSeek. DeepSeek launched R1 and it outperformed our models in some ways. We think they didn’t have access to the chips. There are some accusations that they had access to the chips. It turns out they did a bunch of fine-tuning on the chips they did have. What is that relationship like? Do they need the highest-end Nvidia chips? Is it true that they’re actually developing parallel technologies that might be superior to the chips they can have? Just set that stage. A lot of the details are murky, and they’re probably murky for a reason. But up until now, we saw Chinese AI companies that were very heavily dependent on Nvidia chips in order to train and run their models. In fact, they became some of the biggest contributors to the CUDA ecosystem, which is Nvidia’s software ecosystem and platform. They got very good at that, but at the same time with US export controls and greater technology restrictions on access to cutting-edge GPUs, China increasingly pushed these AI companies to switch away from Nvidia to Huawei and other domestic AI chip makers. The idea there is to develop a parallel domestic AI chip supply chain that is good enough, if not on par with, Nvidia’s latest chips, and — crucially — resilient to policy actions coming out of Washington. So that is the story up until this point. The question is, now, what is that trajectory for the Chinese GPU or AI chip development? The reason I wanted to start there is that the motivations to get close to Jensen Huang are very murky to me. As the CEO of Nvidia, I understand that everyone thinks he’s the character and he’s actually in the software designing the next generation of Nvidia GPUs, but he’s just traveling the world giving policy speeches. If you want to build a parallel GPU ecosystem, you’re trying to get close to the designers and the engineers, right? What would be the goal of trying to get close to Jensen Huang? If you wanted the design specs for the latest Nvidia GPUs, I don’t know if you would ask Jensen directly. I think you might want to go to his technical staff. He does have like 60 direct reports. Decoder is often a show about org charts and that one has been on top of my list for a long time, but we’ll set that aside for now. Keep going. What it’s really about is potentially two things. One is trying to understand, maybe to glean information about, the US policymaking process. Jensen Huang is very close to Trump. They talk a lot. Trump can apparently just call Jensen on his cell phone at any moment . In the middle of a conference. We’ve seen the video. On the other side, and maybe this is even the bigger issue, perhaps it’s the biggest concern of all, is the concern that the direction of movement could run the other way, which is that somehow through Jensen, China might be able to influence US policymaking, especially on export controls. That is the big worry from a lot of people in Washington. One of the other underlying concerns here, that I’m just trying to parse out, is that Alice Huang, the alleged Chinese spy, is an executive at a company called Megaspeed. And through Megaspeed, Nvidia may have already been circumventing export controls. It seems like if you’re already solving the problem, maybe you should just leave it alone. How does that dynamic play out? A lot of the story is strange. Even seen in the most cynical terms, it doesn’t quite add up. There could be several different possibilities. One is that this is actually not some concerted strategy from Beijing to try to obtain chips or information or influence, but this is potentially Beijing not quite understanding the full situation and wanting to co-op this Alice Huang person and at least try to understand from her standpoint what is happening. Because I think you’re right. Already you have a very strong relationship between Nvidia and Megaspeed. You also already have — and this is on the influence side — Jensen Huang advocating for his own commercial interests, for a loosening of export controls on his own chips to China. You don’t really need Beijing to push on that gas pedal. That’s already happening. So there are some things that don’t quite make sense if you’re thinking about it from those standpoints, but if you’re thinking about it from the viewpoint of “Beijing wants visibility,” then perhaps that is another plausible explanation. Beijing just wants someone who Trump calls on the phone to advocate for their viewpoints. I see all of that, but what are we getting out of it? If the goal is Nvidia chips, it feels like that is already assured. If the goal is Nvidia engineering plans, that feels like a question mark.

title: Read Nvidia’s internal emails about the ‘extraordinarily difficult period’ amid CEO shakeup
abstract: AI News Tech Read Nvidia’s internal emails about the ‘extraordinarily difficult period’ amid CEO shakeup Nvidia’s board and interim CEO Colette Kress told employees they’re ready to ‘move forward together.’ Nvidia’s board and interim CEO Colette Kress told employees they’re ready to ‘move forward together.’ by Terrence O'Brien Nov 12, 2026, 3:48 PM UTC Cath Virginia / The Verge Part Of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has resigned. What happens next? see all updates Terrence O'Brien is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths. Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia this morning, a company he co-founded in 1993. The decision came following the company’s board opening an investigation into multiple extramarital affairs Huang had with a direct report and an alleged Chinese spy. The new, and first, Chair of the Board, Harvey Jones, shared news of Huang’s resignation with the company in an email, which also announced CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO. You can read the full text of the board’s internal memo and Kress’s first message to employees as interim CEO below. Subject: Statement from NVIDIA Board Chair Dear NVIDIA Employees, I am writing to share an important update. Jensen has resigned as CEO and Board Member, and the Board has asked our Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress to serve as interim CEO while it conducts a search for a permanent successor looking at both internal and external candidates. I will serve as the first-ever Chair of the Board. As CFO for over 13 years, Colette has been a key architect of NVIDIA’s growth and capital strategy. She possesses a deep understanding of this business and the markets in which we operate. The Board has full confidence in Colette to deliver on our commitments to shareholders, customers, partners, and to each of you. Jensen’s contributions to NVIDIA are profound. NVIDIA is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world. We pioneered accelerated computing, defined the modern GPU, and built the platform that powered artificial intelligence. The Board takes seriously our duty as stewards of this great company. The strength of this company resides in our employees, leadership team, technical strength and partner ecosystem. I am confident that under Colette’s leadership, with the full support of the Board, we will continue to grow our business, and lead the industry forward. Thank you for your focus, your professionalism, and your commitment to NVIDIA. Harvey Jones Colette Kress’ first email to Nvidia employees as interim CEO: Subject: RE: Statement from NVIDIA Board Chair Dear NVIDIAns, I believe deeply in this company and in its future. More than anything, I believe in each of you, in our customers and partners and in the vital role we play every day in the global economy. The Board, Estaff and I recognize that this has been an extraordinarily difficult period and I want you to know how grateful we are for your resilience, professionalism and continued dedication. Thank you. This company has achieved so much because of the work that all of you bring to it every single day. You are our greatest strength. You will hear more from leadership in the coming days about our future together, and we will host a company meeting on November 18 at 9am PT. We play a vital role in building the technology that is powering the AI revolution, and we have important work ahead of us. So let’s move forward together, with the same determination and commitment that have always defined this company. Thank you for all you do, Colette Correction, November 12th: This story’s headline has been adjusted to better describe the context of Kress’ quote; she is not referring to a period “ahead,” as the headline initially stated. title: LLMON: An LLM-Native Markup Language, now in Granite 4.1 3B and 8B
abstract:
Back to Articles LLMON: An LLM-Native Markup Language, now in Granite 4.1 3B and 8B Enterprise Article Published November 12, 2026 Upvote 9 +3 Abraham Daniels abedaniels Follow ibm-granite Basel Shbita basels Follow ibm-granite Chad DeLuca delucac Follow ibm-granite Dan Gutfreund Gutfreund Follow ibm-granite Michael Hind mikehind Follow ibm-granite Shub A shubs90 Follow ibm-granite LLMs rely on their context to generate the next set of tokens. Over a long trajectory, the context fills with numerous types of components: a system prompt, past conversation turns, instructions that act on retrieved documents, tool responses or user data, requirements constraining the allowed output, and reasoning chains. The context carries a rich structure, most of which is either implicit to the model or encoded in formats such as JSON that were not designed to be digested by LLMs. This is one of the main reasons LLMs, particularly those on the smaller end of the scale, are brittle and sometimes fail in unexpected ways. The lack of explicit structure can also be exploited by attackers, for example, in the form of prompt injections. To address this, we developed LLMON (LLM Object Notation, pronounced “lemon”), an LLM-native markup language for explicitly communicating structure and semantics to the models. Semantically coherent components are marked with meaningful tags which are wrapped in reserved special-token delimiters. Data schemas, including nesting, are stated in a way that is unambiguous to a causal LLM. Unique IDs make it possible to point to specific instructions, which could reside anywhere in the context, and bind them to the data payloads they should act on, analogous to the way functions are called and arguments are passed to them in programming languages. Today we are releasing two experimental preview models, derived from Granite 4.1 base models, trained to consume and generate LLMON-marked text: granite-4.1-3b-LLMON-preview and granite-4.1-8b-LLMON-preview . We are also releasing a GitHub repo, which includes a toolkit for working with LLMON and examples of workflows and templates. What it enables: Indirect prompt injections, hidden in user data, are mostly ignored by LLMON models due to explicit instruction/data separation. For some benchmarks, attack success rates drop to nearly zero, whereas regular instruction-tuned models get hijacked with high probability. This is achieved while maintaining general capability relative to Granite 4.1 Instruct models. Unrelated passages, old chat turns, and tool outputs don’t get pulled into the answer because each instruction is bound to the exact data it applies to. Instructions, data, and requirements are clearly marked so that their structure and meanings at the application’s code level can be leveraged by the model. Try it out in Mellea , which has native LLMON support enabled by automatically LLMONizing its LLM calls. You no longer need to worry about forcing LLMs to observe JSON structure. Use our converters to turn existing JSON into LLMON without loss. You can also define your own structure and associated tags and tune a LoRA on top of the LLMON models to understand it. Why not JSON? JSON was designed for parsers, not for causal language models. The tokenizer is not constrained to respect the grammar, and structure is encoded by tokens ({, ", :) that may also appear in normal text. To a model, a quotation mark inside a document and a quotation mark that closes a field are the same token. Escaping rules that are clear to a parser are only statistical patterns to a model. Nesting depth is encoded by counting brackets, which transformers are known to be weak at, especially over long spans. LLMON, on the other hand, is an XML-like markup whose structural delimiters are reserved special tokens rather than characters, so structure and content use separate parts of the vocabulary. Tags are stated at the beginning of each span, and the boundaries between spans are explicit. Nested structures are stated locally so the model does not need to keep track of the hierarchy over long spans. Since most teams already have pipelines built around JSON, we created conversion tools and example notebooks that translate JSON to LLMON and back in a lossless manner. How is LLMON related to chat templates? LLMON does not replace chat templates; rather, it enriches them. Where regular chat templates tell the model which part belongs to which role (system, user, assistant), LLMON tells it what each component means and how components relate to each other, within and across roles. The LLMON preview models ship with their own chat template, so you build the same messages list you would pass to any chat model and call apply_chat_template as usual; it renders the LLMON shown below. The only difference is that a turn can now name its parts and mark each one exec : True or False . A part marked True is bound into the exec block at the bottom of the rendered output, which states which instruction to run and what it operates on; a part marked False is still rendered into the context but is referenced by nothing. messages = [ { "role": "user", "instruction": [{ "value": "Write a short paragraph about", "exec": True }], "data": [{ "value": "IBM Company", "exec": True }], "requirement": [ {"value": "Use less than 10 words", "exec": True}, {"value": "Do not use commas", "exec": True}] } ] Which the model receives as the following (with newlines and indentation added here for readability, as the template emits none): <|open|>instr<|:|>»ñ<|close|>Write a short paragraph about<|open_end|>
<|open|>data<|:|>ä¦<|close|>IBM Company<|open_end|>
<|open|>req<|:|>Á¼<|close|>Use less than 10 words<|open_end|>
<|open|>req<|:|>¢¬<|close|>Do not use commas<|open_end|>
<|open|>exec<|:|>ÄÐ<|close|> <|open|>exec<|.|>instruction<|close|>instr<|:|>»ñ<|open_end|> <|open|>exec<|.|>input<|close|>data<|:|>ä¦<|open_end|> <|open|>exec<|.|>requirement<|close|>req<|:|>Á¼<|open_end|> <|open|>exec<|.|>requirement<|close|>req<|:|>¢¬<|open_end|> <|open|>exec<|.|>output<|close|>assistant<|:|>ãø<|open_end|>
<|open_end|>
<|open|>assistant<|:|>ãø<|close|> The two-character block IDs are drawn from a fixed set that this tokenizer encodes as single tokens, so addressing a block always costs two tokens regardless of which ID is drawn. The role is still a single user turn, but its components reach the model as five separate addressable blocks, bound together by a sixth (the exec block) that states: run this instruction, on this data, subject to these two requirements, and put the answer in the block named here, which is the same assistant block the model then fills. A conventional template would have flattened all components into one string and left the model to infer which part was the task, which was the subject, and which were constraints. How LLMON addresses prompt injection attacks Indirect prompt injection is a type of attack where a malicious instruction is hidden in a data payload, such as a retrieved document, a tool response, or user-provided data. This is the problem LLMON’s instruction/data separation is designed to address. We compared the LLMON previews against several open-source and closed-source models. We evaluated on the OPI benchmark, which places the injection in the data of classic NLP tasks. Several attack strategies are employed. We report robustness, defined as 1 − attack success rate: the share of attacks where the model does not carry out the injected instruction. All non-LLMON models are highly susceptible, carrying out the injected instructions with high probability. LLMON practically eliminates the problem on this benchmark, avoiding 47% more attacks relative to the best frontier model that we tested, and 95% more than the best open-source model. We observe similar trends on other benchmarks ( ASB and StruQ ). It is worth noting that these benchmarks test robustness to static indirect prompt injections.

title: The Definitive Fine-Tuning Guide for 3D Generation Models
abstract: Back to Articles The Definitive Fine-Tuning Guide for 3D Generation Models Published November 12, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 10 +4 Suvaditya Mukherjee suvadityamuk Follow merve merve Follow Pedro Cuenca pcuenq Follow TLDR; In this blog, we provide fine-tuning scripts and containers to fine-tune TRELLIS.2, a popular 3D model on your 3D assets, that can run both locally and on Hugging Face Jobs. If you are interested in fine-tuning, you can use our scripts with few arguments (assuming you updated your dataset to Hugging Face Hub) or tinker with them yourself with this repository . If you want to learn more, we go through how the script works . Let’s go! Introduction 3D generation has many uses in robotics, simulation, media, and entertainment. In these fields, it is difficult to make generated objects obey strict rules and standardize model and data representations. There are many file formats, such as GLB and PLY . There are also many representations , such as neural radiance fields (NeRFs) and 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS) . Each one has different advantages and disadvantages. TRELLIS introduced a common internal representation, called a unified latent representation. Its decoders convert this representation into 3D models in the required output format. Thus, you do not have to use different models for each representation format. The same team then released TRELLIS.2 , which improves the model's representation of 3D structure. But neither model gives an easy way to adapt it to a specific task. What we want to improve A general-purpose model, such as TRELLIS.2, can make errors in details that are important for a specific application. For example, a user may need accurate geometry for furniture models. Without fine-tuning for that task, the pretrained model can produce geometry that is insufficiently accurate. We use a subset of GSO that has 188 footwear objects for our experiment. In our initial tests, the pretrained model usually produced shoes that looked correct, but the soles were incorrect. We test whether a LoRA can make the soles more accurate. Our goal is to use the Google Scanned Objects (GSO) dataset to improve the performance of TRELLIS.2 on a specific object category. We will explain which pipeline components to fine-tune and which to leave unchanged during training. The pipeline separates structure, detailed geometry, and materials. Thus, we will fine-tune only the components that are important for our task. Choosing what to freeze matters as much as choosing what to fine-tune. What will we use? LoRA LoRA, short for low-rank adaptation, fine-tunes a model by training small adapter matrices while keeping the original weights frozen. This reduces the number of trainable parameters and the memory needed for their gradients and optimizer state. We use Hugging Face’s PEFT library to add and train these adapters. For more information, read our LoRA guide . Hugging Face Jobs Hugging Face Jobs runs containerized workloads on cloud hardware. We use it for preprocessing and for training. To use your own GPU instead, see the local Docker commands below. Before you start, make sure that you have: A HF_TOKEN that you can obtain from here Your Hugging Face account must have access to DINOv3 , because DINOv3 is a gated model If you use your own dataset, upload its meshes to the Hub before you start. How TRELLIS.2 works Before we train, let’s look at how TRELLIS.2 generates a 3D object and where we’ll add LoRA adapters. TRELLIS.2 has five main stages: remove the image background, encode the image, predict the coarse structure, generate detailed geometry, and generate materials. The pipeline then exports the result as a textured mesh. Encoding the input image First, BiRefNet removes the background from the input image. DINOv3-L then encodes the image into feature tokens. The generation models use these tokens to guide the 3D object. Sparse Structure Generation (Sparse Structure Flow) The sparse-structure flow DiT predicts the object's coarse shape. It is a diffusion transformer (DiT) that makes a small latent of size 16³ × 8. A variational autoencoder (VAE) decoder then changes this latent into a 64 × 64 × 64 occupancy grid. Each voxel in the grid shows if that location is part of the object. A voxel is a pixel in three dimensions. We add LoRA adapters to this model because its output guides the geometry stage. O-Voxel and Structured Latents O-Voxel is the 3D format of TRELLIS.2. It is a sparse voxel grid. It keeps only the voxels on the object's surface. Each voxel keeps local geometry, such as a mesh vertex, and material attributes. Because the format is small, a CPU changes a mesh into O-Voxel in seconds. A GPU changes O-Voxel back into a mesh in seconds. Structured sparse latents come from TRELLIS. They keep 3D data in sparse tensors, which makes computation faster. The model uses only approximately 10% of the voxels in the grid, so it does not spend compute on empty voxels. Thus, the shape flow DiT and the texture flow DiT are sparse transformers. The sparse-structure flow DiT is a dense transformer. Geometry Generation (Shape Flow) The shape flow DiT uses the occupancy grid and the DINOv3 feature tokens to make a latent. Another VAE decoder then changes this latent into O-Voxel geometry at a resolution of 512 × 512 × 512. We add LoRA adapters to the DiT at this stage because it controls the object's shape. Material Generation + Mesh Creation In the last stage, the texture flow DiT uses the shape latent and the DINOv3 features as input. It defines the materials and textures of the geometry's surface. A VAE decoder then changes the latent into base color, metallic, roughness, and alpha values for each voxel. We do not add LoRA adapters to this stage. Our dataset has diffuse color maps, but it lacks the separate material maps this stage needs for training. Also, our problem is the shoe's shape. The base model already makes good colors and textures. Finally, the pipeline combines the geometry and material attributes into a textured mesh and exports it as a GLB file. Planning Which components to fine-tune We add LoRA adapters only to the sparse-structure flow DiT and the shape flow DiT. These DiTs control the object's shape and geometry. We freeze the texture flow DiT to keep its current capabilities. Our dataset contains diffuse color maps that include baked lighting effects. To train the texture flow DiT, we need separate material maps. The color maps in our dataset mix surface color with lighting. Thus, they are not correct targets for this training. If we train the texture flow DiT on these maps, it can learn to show lighting as a surface property. It can also forget what it learned before, a problem called catastrophic forgetting. Why use LoRA Our subset has 188 shoes from the 1,030 objects in GSO. For a dataset this small, LoRA is a better choice than full fine-tuning. Full fine-tuning costs much more. It can also overwrite what the model already does well (its learned priors). Our configuration trains approximately 9.3 million adapter parameters in total for both targeted DiTs. We use rank 8 adapters in the attention and feed-forward (MLP) layers of the sparse-structure flow DiT. We use rank 16 adapters in the attention layers of the shape flow DiT. The rank sets the size of the adapter matrices. A higher rank lets the adapter learn more. What you’ll run A 3D model setup can need many dependencies and installation steps. We supply two Docker images (that you can run on Jobs or your own machine) with the necessary software. One image is for preprocessing, and one is for fine-tuning. To train your LoRA adapters and upload them to the Hub: Give the containers access to your data. Set the parameters for your task. Run the preprocessing container. Run the fine-tuning container. Then we explain the fine-tuning script, its settings, and how each setting affects training.

title: CopilotKit Releases OpenBot 1.0: An MIT-Licensed, Self-Hostable AI Coworker With Built-In Governance
abstract: Most AI coworker products are vendor locked. They pick the model, host the data, and write the rules. CopilotKit is taking the opposite route. OpenBot 1.0 , was released November 9th, an MIT-licensed , self-hostable agent workspace. What sets it apart is, a company brings their own models, agents and infrastructure. Governance is fully baked in, and every Bot action is checked against a policy before it runs. OpenBot is a modular agent workspace from CopilotKit , the team behind the AG-UI protocol. You give a Bot a task and watch it work. You review findings, interact with results and approve next steps in the same conversation. Each Bot gets a computer of its own . That is a container with its own Chromium browser, logins and files. It reaches only the tools you grant. Answers can come back as charts, checklists, tables and cards. In the new v1.0, Bots now reply in Markdown by default and draw components when they help. Every browser click, file write, MCP tool call and component goes through one gateway. It evaluates a CEL policy, writes the audit row first , then acts. Deny rules run before allow rules, and a broken rule refuses rather than opens. On top of that, the business tier adds: Any agent that speaks AG-UI plugs in. The site lists 8 frameworks: Claude Agent SDK, OpenAI Agents SDK, LangChain, Google ADK, Mastra, AWS Strands, Microsoft Agent Framework, CrewAI. The repo also ships Agno, AG2, LlamaIndex and Pydantic AI examples. For models, teams can use OpenAI, Claude, Gemini or Grok through existing subscriptions or API keys. Open models such as Kimi, DeepSeek, Qwen, Nemotron and Mistral are also supported. Sandboxes, MCP hubs and browsers are swappable lanes. Personal use runs locally, with workspace data and API keys stored on your machine. For companies, 1 Helm chart deploys into AWS (EKS), Azure (AKS), Google Cloud (GKE) or any Kubernetes cluster. Pricing is free for personal projects. OpenBot for Business costs up to $29 per active user per month. A 5% charge applies only to model spend above $5,000 per month. The Annual plan adds air-gapped deployment and 24/7 support. Forward-deployed engineers help teams roll it out. Check out the GitHub repo , v1.0.0 release notes and open.bot . Thanks to the Copilotkit team for the thought leadership / resources for this article. This article is sponsored by Copilokit. title: AWS Releases AWS Emulator: A Local Copy of 200+ AWS Services Built by AI Agents
abstract: AWS has released AWS Emulator , a local emulator of the AWS APIs. You run it on a laptop, a dev server or in CI. The AWS CLI and SDKs talk to it instead of AWS. No AWS account is needed, and there is no service fee . The unusual part: autonomous agents wrote and reviewed all of its code . For developers and coding agents, AWS Emulator gives a fast, free test loop against AWS-shaped APIs. AWS Emulator is a headless local program from AWS that serves an AWS API endpoint. You point the CLI or an SDK at it with environment variables. Your code does not change. Resources live in memory and vanish when it stops. The docs show a DynamoDB example. A CreateTable call with a 2-character name fails with the same ValidationException text AWS returns. The project began with a prompt to Kiro . It returned a passable Amazon SQS emulator in about 15 minutes. AWS then split the work across 3 teams of agents: Every patch passes a merge gate covering build, code review, security and fidelity. Several security agents run adversarial reviews . Matthew Goldberg reports hundreds of concurrent agents fixing thousands of issues a day. The release pipeline runs on AWS Developer Tools, with CodeCommit as the agents’ repository. Code reaches GitHub last. AWS publishes a scores.json file with each release. We tallied the v1.0.322 file , scored on November 11, 2026. Per the fidelity docs , control-plane APIs match AWS best. Data-plane, CloudFormation, Terraform and CDK support varies by service. Unimplemented operations return HTTP 501 NotImplemented . The tests live in aws-emulator-evaluation-suite , including failing ones. There are 4 paths, per the README : A source build serves HTTPS on 127.0.0.1:9297 with a self-signed certificate. It needs a Rust toolchain, a C compiler and at least 100 GB of disk. Embedded mode carries the same build cost on the first cargo test . The release pace is fast. Versions v1.0.265 to v1.0.322 shipped between November 8 and 11. Check out the GitHub repo , the user guide , the fidelity tests and the engineering post . title: IBM Announces IBM Quantum Nighthawk r3: A New Processor to Support 10k Quantum Operations on 520 Programmable Qubits
abstract: IBM has announced IBM Quantum Nighthawk r3 , its next superconducting quantum processor. It is designed to run 10,000 quantum operations accurately across 520 programmable qubits. In 2027, IBM plans to link 2 r3 chips into a single 1,040-qubit system. For developers, the announcement is speed. The current Nighthawk r2 already runs workloads up to 19x faster than IBM’s earlier processors. Nighthawk is IBM’s square-lattice processor family built for quantum advantage workloads. Most qubits connect to 4 nearest neighbors, versus 2 or 3 on earlier designs. That connectivity lets circuits express more entangling structure with fewer swap operations. The current production chip is Nighthawk r2 . It has 120 programmable qubits, 218 couplers and 120 reset elements. That is 458 physical quantum elements in total. The bottleneck was qubit reset. Heron uses conditional reset: measure, then flip any qubit found in the excited state. That method cannot fix leaked qubits, so the chip idles for hundreds of microseconds between shots. Nighthawk r2 replaces this with a dissipative reset gadget per qubit. A tunable coupler links each qubit to a cold environment on demand. This drops effective T1 from about 200 microseconds to roughly 25 nanoseconds. Idle time between runs falls to as little as 1 microsecond. The result is 100,000+ circuits per second. Heron manages roughly 4,000. IBM also reports about 25x lower initialization error, while neighbors stay undisturbed. According to IBM, clients have run 34 billion circuits on Nighthawk r2 so far. The figures below are self-reported by IBM and its partners. IBM also reports accurate observable estimation on circuits with 7,500+ gates, a 2026 roadmap milestone. Nighthawk r3 keeps r2’s square lattice and fast operations. It scales to 520 programmable qubits from 2,034 physical qubits. It adds 10 chip-to-chip interconnects called l-couplers. Those links are the path to 1,040 qubits. IBM connected 2 Nighthawk r1 chips with 4 l-couplers, each using an 80 cm cable. State transfer fidelity reached up to 99.3%, averaging 99%. IBM also linked 2 cryogenic modules , reaching below 15 millikelvin in under 5 days. IBM Quantum Platform now runs HPC and quantum jobs in one managed environment. Users can attach classical compute from a laptop, a supercomputer or the platform itself. IBM and RIKEN reran a sample-based quantum diagonalization workflow roughly 5x faster with 100x more computations. Cleveland Clinic and RIKEN processed 608 million samples 33x faster with workflow automation. Pulse-level controls are also available for error correction research. Check out the IBM press release , the Nighthawk r2 technical blog and the l-coupler paper .
