title: Building Graph-Enhanced GenAI Applications with graphrag-toolkit
abstract: Building Graph-Enhanced GenAI Applications with graphrag-toolkit Learn how graph-enhanced RAG connects related facts that plain vector search misses, then build a multi-hop research assistant with AWS Labs' open-source graphrag-toolkit, Neo4j, and pgvector. By Shittu Olumide , Technical Content Specialist on November 12, 2026 in Language Models A standard retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) chatbot handles "what does the return policy say" without any trouble: it finds the chunk, hands it to the model, and it's done. Ask it something like "how does the return policy interact with the warranty terms for international orders," and it starts to wobble. That answer isn't sitting in any single chunk. It requires connecting two separate pieces of the document that were never near each other in the source text, and a vector search that only measures how similar each chunk sounds to the question has no way to make that connection on its own. That specific gap — a system that finds relevant text but can't follow relationships between pieces of it — is exactly what graph-enhanced retrieval exists to close. This article walks through what that actually means, introduces AWS Labs' open-source graphrag-toolkit , and then builds a real, working graph-enhanced research assistant from scratch, with every piece of code checked directly against the toolkit's own documentation rather than assumed from memory. What Graph-Enhanced Generative AI Applications Actually Are Graph-enhanced RAG, usually shortened to GraphRAG, is retrieval that queries a knowledge graph rather than a plain vector index, so an application can follow actual relationships between pieces of information instead of only finding text that sounds similar to the question. Neo4j's own explainer frames this as combining the retrieval strengths of a knowledge graph — explicit entities and the relationships between them — with the generative fluency of a large language model (LLM), so the model reasons over connected facts rather than isolated fragments of text. This isn't a single vendor's marketing framing. Oracle's own write-up on the same idea makes essentially the same case from a completely different part of the database industry: standard RAG treats every chunk as an independent island, while a graph captures how those islands actually connect, which entities appear in multiple places, and how concepts relate across an entire document collection rather than within one paragraph at a time. Two major database companies converging independently on the same core argument is a reasonable signal that the underlying problem is real, not a talking point invented to sell graph databases. Where Plain Vector RAG Actually Falls Short It's worth being precise about the mechanism here rather than just gesturing at "vector search isn't perfect." A standard vector store retrieves chunks purely based on semantic similarity between the embedded question and the embedded chunks, and it does that retrieval for each chunk in isolation. There's no representation anywhere in that process of how one chunk relates to another: whether they discuss the same entity, whether one provides context the other depends on, or whether they sit in a cause-and-effect relationship. Multi-hop questions — ones that require two or three separate, connected facts assembled together before an answer makes sense — are exactly where this breaks down. And it's a structural limitation of the retrieval mechanism itself, not something better prompting or a larger context window can reliably fix. The problem isn't that the model can't reason once it has the right information; it's that plain vector search often never surfaces all the right pieces in the first place. Introducing graphrag-toolkit The graphrag-toolkit is an open-source, Apache 2.0-licensed Python toolkit built by AWS Labs specifically to close that gap. It's made up of two components. The first, and the focus of this article, is lexical-graph , a framework for automatically building a hierarchical knowledge graph from unstructured documents and querying it. The second, BYOKG-RAG (Bring Your Own Knowledge Graph), is a separate approach for teams that already have a knowledge graph and want a multi-strategy question-answering layer over it, without re-extracting anything from scratch. AWS introduced the toolkit publicly in its own launch blog post , and the design behind the hierarchical lexical graph model is documented in a dedicated research paper , "Hierarchical Lexical Graph for Enhanced Multi-Hop Retrieval." It's also not purely theoretical: Deloitte uses the lexical-graph inside its Amazon Neptune-based GenAI Security Intelligence Center, a real production deployment covered in a re:Invent 2025 technical session . How It Actually Works This is the technical core worth understanding before writing any code. Per the toolkit's own graph model documentation , a lexical graph organizes extracted content into six connected levels: source, chunk, topic, statement, fact, and entity. Retrieval can hop between any of these levels rather than being stuck retrieving only at the chunk level the way a plain vector store is, which is the structural feature that makes multi-hop questions actually answerable. Building that graph happens in two distinct stages, extract and build, and they're deliberately kept separate. The extract stage ingests raw source documents, chunks them, and uses an LLM to pull out topics, statements, facts, and entities. The build stage takes those extracted elements and populates the actual graph and vector indexes from them. Running these as two genuinely separate, micro-batched, resumable pipeline stages, rather than one monolithic process, means a large ingestion job can be paused, inspected, or filtered partway through without losing progress. One detail is worth knowing specifically, because it explains why extraction quality holds up as well as it does: the process makes two separate LLM calls per chunk rather than one. The first call cleans up the raw chunked text into a set of well-formed, self-contained propositions. The second call then extracts topics, statements, facts, and entities from those cleaned propositions rather than from the messier raw text directly. That extra step is optional (the second call can run directly against raw content), but per the toolkit's own documentation, extraction quality measurably improves when the proposition-cleanup pass runs first. Querying: Traversal-Based Search Here's the actual query mechanism, sourced directly from the toolkit's querying documentation . A user's question first gets embedded, and that embedding runs a top-K similarity search against the vector store to find anchor points: statements or chunks that look relevant on the surface. Those anchors then seed one or more graph traversal queries, which pull in thematically connected content from across the graph, not just the chunks that scored highest on similarity alone. The retrieved content, grouped by topic and source, is then supplied to an LLM alongside the original question to generate the actual answer. One genuinely current fact is easy to miss: the toolkit also ships an older semantic-guided search strategy, but the documentation states directly that it's likely to be retired in a future release. Traversal-based search is both the current default and the one worth building against today, which is exactly the approach used in the hands-on build below. Before writing any code, it's worth knowing what's actually swappable in this toolkit and what isn't, since the choice affects both cost and setup complexity.

title: 7 FREE Books to Learn About Building AI Systems
abstract: 7 FREE Books to Learn About Building AI Systems Building an AI agent is easy. Building one that actually works in production is not. These 7 free books cover the engineering knowledge you need to make that jump. By Kanwal Mehreen , KDnuggets Technical Editor & Content Specialist on November 12, 2026 in Artificial Intelligence When someone asks me, "Can you build an AI application just by vibe coding?" my answer is yes, you probably can. But building an application that works is one thing. Building an AI system that can handle a million requests without becoming too slow or too expensive is a different challenge. There is a lot more to AI engineering than making sure your model gives the right answer or completes the task. You need to think about inference latency, GPU memory, deployment, context management, and what happens when your application starts getting more traffic than you expected. If you're building AI agents, things get even more complicated. There are some good courses that cover these concepts too, but I'd recommend reading books in depth if you really want to build your fundamentals. You don't necessarily have to pay for them either. I've gathered 7 FREE books that I feel are worth reading. Some are older and you may have already heard of them, while others are newer. So, let's get started. 1. Machine Learning Systems Design by Chip Huyen This book is one of the classics and is good for beginners, so I'd start with this one. It treats machine learning as an end-to-end problem and covers its four main stages: 1) project setup, 2) preparing data pipelines, 3) modeling (selecting, training, and debugging), and 4) serving (testing, deploying, and maintaining). Each stage includes links to practical resources and case studies from machine learning engineers at large tech companies. Another good thing is that it has 27 system design questions at the end for practice. A lot has changed since 2019, so it doesn't go deep into large language model (LLM) infrastructure, but it's still useful for understanding how machine learning systems fit together. 2. Machine Learning Engineering Open Book by Stas Bekman This is more of a reference than a book you read from start to finish. It's based on Stas Bekman's experience with large model projects like BLOOM-176B and IDEFICS-80B, and it covers GPU hardware, networking, storage, SLURM orchestration, training, inference, and debugging. I'd keep it bookmarked for when you run into problems like GPU out-of-memory errors or slow multi-node training. The GitHub repository has nearly 20,000 stars, and it's distributed under a CC BY-SA 4.0 license, so it's free to read and share. 3. AI Agents in Depth: Design Principles and Engineering Practice by Bojie Li If you're building AI agents, I'd definitely recommend checking this one out. It starts with a simple idea: an agent is an LLM, context, and tools. From there, it covers context engineering, memory, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), tool integration, and multi-agent systems, and it explains the engineering decisions behind agents that handle longer, more complicated tasks. It also comes with lots of practical experiments. Bojie Li has another book, Understanding AI Infra , which I really like, so I'm sharing it here too. 4. The Architecture of AI Agents and LLM Systems by Aleksandr Drobiazkin This is a much newer book that focuses specifically on building LLM applications. It covers how language models work, context engineering, RAG, structured outputs, tool calling, and different agent architectures. It also goes into the engineering side, like evaluation, observability, security, inference costs, and latency. Instead of just showing you how to use a framework, it also explains the trade-offs between approaches. It also has a companion course. 5. Inference Engineering by Philip Kiely This is probably one of the most relevant books on this list if you're interested in deploying LLMs and making them faster and cheaper. It walks through the whole inference stack, from GPUs and model architectures to serving software and production deployments. You'll learn about batching, quantization, memory usage, and latency, and how to choose the right hardware or serving setup. I'd recommend it if you're experimenting with local LLMs or engines like vLLM . It also explains why a model can run fine for one user but start struggling when hundreds of requests hit it at once. 6. LLM Inference Illustrated by Ted Kyi This book is really good if you want to understand what happens when an LLM generates a response. It's also full of detailed diagrams, so it works well if you learn better visually. It walks through how tokens get generated one at a time, then covers how inference systems make that faster, lighter on memory, and able to scale. Instead of treating model serving as a black box, you'll get a clearer understanding of the engineering techniques that make it possible to serve LLMs efficiently. 7. How to Scale Your Model by Jacob Austin et al. This book comes from researchers at Google DeepMind, and I'd highly recommend it if you want to understand how LLMs are trained and served across thousands of accelerators. It starts with how TPUs work and then goes into their architecture, memory bandwidth, model sharding, distributed training, and inference optimization. One thing I really like is that it uses LLaMA 3 as a practical example to explain how much memory, computing power, and money you need to train or serve a large model. Some of the math can get quite technical, but it's a great resource nonetheless. Final Thoughts You don't have to read all seven books from beginning to end. Pick the ones that match what you're working on, and come back to the rest when you need them. I think we're reaching a point where almost anyone can build an AI application with the help of coding agents. But knowing how to make that application reliable, fast, secure, and affordable is what separates a working demo from a production system. And that's exactly why I think learning AI systems engineering is becoming more important, not less. Kanwal Mehreen is a machine learning engineer and a technical writer with a profound passion for data science and the intersection of AI with medicine. She co-authored the ebook "Maximizing Productivity with ChatGPT". As a Google Generation Scholar 2022 for APAC, she champions diversity and academic excellence. She's also recognized as a Teradata Diversity in Tech Scholar, Mitacs Globalink Research Scholar, and Harvard WeCode Scholar. Kanwal is an ardent advocate for change, having founded FEMCodes to empower women in STEM fields. <= Previous post Next post =>

title: Using Claude Opus 5.5 as your daily driver for knowledge work
abstract: Claude Opus 5.5 is now the default model in Claude on Pro, Max, Ultra, and Team plans. We recommend it as your daily driver for knowledge work, meaning the model you leave selected when you work with Claude on research, analysis, and writing or producing memos, reports, spreadsheets, and decks. If you or your team have been using Sonnet for daily work and saving Opus for heavy analysis or complex projects, it’s worth reconsidering because a more capable model can finish a task by doing less work, which can then offset much of its higher price per token . Here's how the current models compare: How our models compare for knowledge work Model Use it for Price per million tokens (input / output)* Relative speed Claude Haiku 5.5 Quick lookups and high-volume work where speed matters most $0.10 / $0.50 Fastest Claude Sonnet 5.5 Quick, well-scoped tasks, and polished documents, slides, and spreadsheets from a clear brief $2 / $10 Fast Claude Opus 5.5 Most knowledge work: research, analysis, and finished docs, decks, and spreadsheets that need judgment $4 / $20 Moderate Claude Fable 5.2 The most ambitious, open-ended technical work, in fields like coding, finance, and the sciences $8 / $40 Moderate *Prices are for usage billed by the token ( model comparison ). Haiku 5.5's prices apply to prompts up to 100k tokens, and longer prompts cost $0.50 / $2.50. On Pro, Max, Ultra, and Team plans, higher-priced models use your limits faster. Pro plans and standard seats on Team and seat-based Enterprise plans don’t include Fable 5.2 in their limits outside limited-time launch offers, so it runs on usage credits. Haiku 5.5 is our fastest and least expensive model, built for quick lookups and high-volume work like writing summaries and sorting data. This is our first Haiku model with effort controls, so you can ask for a more careful pass before switching to a larger model. It’s best suited to short, narrowly scoped tasks. For longer analysis, switch to Opus 5.5. Sonnet 5.5 is faster and cheaper than Opus 5.5 for well-scoped tasks that have a clear brief. This could be asking Claude to turn finished notes into a polished document, or to build a deck using a slide template. At higher-effort settings, however, cost per task with Sonnet 5.5 gets close to Opus 5.5, so if you find yourself pushing Sonnet to Extra high or Max effort, consider switching to Opus 5.5. Opus 5.5 is built for complex work that needs careful judgment, like research, financial analysis, and producing finished docs, decks, and spreadsheets. We share details on why we recommend Opus 5.5 for daily knowledge work later. Fable 5.2 is best for your most demanding reasoning and long-running work, like deep multi-step research or coding that you can hand off to a large team of subagents that run for hours. For most knowledge work, start with Opus 5.5 and move to Fable 5.2 when a project’s scope and complexity calls for it. Fable 5.2 is available on all paid plans, though how it draws on your usage depends on your plan. Whichever model you're on, if Claude didn’t do as well as you expected, try a higher effort first before moving up a model. If it had the context, clearly tried, and still got it wrong, move up a model. Opus 5.5 does its best work on documents, research, finance, and charts Opus 5.5 follows instructions precisely and stays in scope, so the spreadsheets, slides, and documents it produces often need little editing. It's careful with figures and sources, too. In one internal research test, Opus 5.5 wrote reports on a company's quarterly performance using only a saved snapshot of the web, in which the company’s earnings release was hard to locate. An automated grader checked every figure and quote against the pages in that snapshot, under a condition that the report would fail if even a single figure or quote was invented. Across effort settings, 16 of its 18 reports passed. Its writing is clearer than that of earlier models, too. Opus 5.5 puts the most important information first, uses less jargon, and follows the writing rules you give it, and on longer tasks it says plainly what it did, what it found, and what it needs from you. That also makes its work easier to check, which we count as a safety benefit as well as a practical one. John Ruelas, a staff software engineer at Ramp, said : “It writes like a good colleague, and follows our writing rules. A design spec came out usable with very minimal edits, and when it rewrote one of our prompts I preferred its version to my own.” Financial analysis is another strength. Opus 5.5 reads dense filings, financial models, and charts accurately and keeps track of context across a whole project or deal. In another internal test, it analyzed a proposed merger between two fictional HR software companies, building a financial model in Excel and then turning it into an executive presentation on whether the deal made sense at its price. It finished in 63 minutes, compared with 93 for Opus 5 on the same task, at half the cost, with a more thorough model, and an easier-to-read presentation. Frank Corrao, who leads central equity quant research engineering at investment firm Walleye Capital, said that at higher effort settings, Opus 5.5 “detected that the minute indexing in our own instructions was off by one and corrected for it, noting that this would cost it points with the grader. It was right, and no model we’ve tested had caught and acted on that before.” Opus 5.5 is our best Opus model for vision. It reads dense documents, charts, screenshots, and diagrams accurately, which makes it reliable for pulling data out of documents. Even at its lowest effort setting, it read values off dense charts more accurately than Opus 5 did at its highest. Getting more out of Opus 5.5 Each new model is a reason to retest what you hand to Claude and to drop prompting habits built for older models. Try these tasks first Ask for a finished file. If you want a spreadsheet or a document, ask for the spreadsheet or document rather than an outline to build from. More often than not, Opus 5.5 can get from your request to the finished file in one pass. Have it check long documents. Give it a long plan, report, or deck and ask it to find mistakes and inconsistencies. Opus 5.5 catches details that are easy to miss in long documents, such as a chart in a deck that doesn’t match its source data. Hand it a research question. Ask a question without a set answer and have it pull sources together, work through long documents, and write up what it finds as a memo, report, or deck. Try visual work. Its vision gains carry over to design, so try it for prototyping an interface, building a website, or illustrating a concept. Change these prompting habits Connect Claude to your work files and systems. This is one of the most useful steps for getting output that fits your work, because when Claude can reach your files and systems through connectors, it can go get what a task needs instead of working only from what you paste in. On Team and Enterprise plans, an owner has to turn a connector on before members can use it. Say what done looks like in your first message. Instead of prompting Claude with instructions one at a time, describe your goal, the finished output, and when you want it to stop and ask. Opus 5.5 carries long, multipart work through to the end better than Opus 5 did. Delete “think hard” and “think carefully.” Thinking is always on for Opus 5.5, and it decides how much to think based on your request and the effort level. In our testing, removing those lines made replies start sooner, with no clear drop in quality. Start at Medium effort. Medium is the default for Opus 5.5, and on our coding and knowledge-work evaluations, Opus 5.5 at Medium matched or beat Opus 5 at High. Higher settings think longer and cost more without always producing better work, so move up to High when Medium stalls. To change the setting, click the model name next to the send button and choose Effort.

title: Operate Claude Managed Agents inside your security perimeter
abstract: Self-hosted Claude Managed Agents is now available in private beta. Developers can build agents that work directly in their company's code and internal systems, and run those agents in their own environment. Self-hosting is a new way to run Managed Agents , a suite of composable APIs for building and deploying autonomous agents. Managed Agents provides the agent harness, sandboxes, credential handling, and session history to get long-running agents into production. Run your agent control plane in your own environment We first launched Managed Agents as a hosted service on the Claude Platform, where Anthropic runs the infrastructure for you. For teams who needed their code to stay in their own environment, we added self-hosted sandboxes . Since then, agents have become more capable and are taking on more critical work, like fixing broken builds, testing releases, triaging alerts, and working through your bug backlog. They run unattended on your code and need access to your internal systems. For agents with that level of access, some teams want the whole service in their own environment, not just the sandbox. Until now, that meant building the platform themselves. With self-hosted Managed Agents, every part of the service runs in your own cloud or on-premise, including the harness, sandboxes, credentials, and session history. You operate the Managed Agents server, its database, and the workers where agents run their shell and file tools. Model requests go where you choose, whether that's Anthropic directly, your cloud provider (Amazon Bedrock, Google's Agent Platform, or Microsoft Foundry), or your own gateway. Your developers still build agents with the same core APIs as the hosted Managed Agents service. Session history is stored in your own database. If your organization has zero data retention (ZDR) in place with Anthropic, it applies to the requests sent to Claude in the same way as any other Messages API call. Designed for agent security When an agent runs unattended inside your code and systems, you can't rely on a person checking every step, so the limits have to be built into the system itself. That's why agent security starts with architecture, and why we designed Managed Agents around four principles. These principles apply whether Anthropic hosts everything, you host just the sandbox, or you host the whole service. The brain and the hands are split The harness (the brain) calls Claude, and the sandbox (the hands) is where the agent's code runs. They are kept separate by design. The agent's code runs in the sandbox, while the agent loop, session history, and vault secrets stay outside it. Separating them also means an agent doesn't depend on one sandbox surviving its whole run, sandboxes start only when a tool needs them, and session history lives outside the sandbox as an event log. Credentials stay out of the sandbox Vaults are designed to keep credentials out of the sandbox. For MCP tools and supported API calls, a proxy outside the sandbox adds the credential to the request . With self-hosted Managed Agents, you can also store credentials in your own secrets manager. Network access can be limited You can limit each environment to a list of allowed hosts , and requests to any other host are blocked. For an agent that fixes broken builds, that list might be just your git host and your package registry. When you host the sandbox yourself, you set the same limits in your own firewall. Every session leaves a full record Managed Agents keeps a record of every step an agent took, including the tool calls it made and what came back. The record exports over OpenTelemetry , so you can send it to the monitoring tools you already use and review agent activity alongside the rest of your systems. Get started Self-hosted Claude Managed Agents is now available in private beta. Contact your Anthropic account team to request access, or read the docs to learn more.

title: J. Crew brings its signature approach to styling to life with Claude
abstract: Online, shopping usually happens one product at a time, so a customer who finds a sweater has to search again for the pants and shoes that go with it. To change that, J.Crew today launched Style Advisor, an AI stylist on JCrew.com (opens in new tab) that helps customers shop by complete outfit. J.Crew’s team built it with Claude Code (opens in new tab) using multiple Claude models, from Fable to Haiku, each matched to the work it does best. It is available now for women’s and men’s styles in the U.S. For more than 40 years, J.Crew’s own stylists have built complete looks by balancing proportion, color, and layering and by pairing pieces in unexpected ways. Style Advisor brings that expertise online. Customers describe what they need, such as an outfit for a beach wedding or a first job interview, and it answers with complete looks drawn from J.Crew’s own photo shoots. They can keep refining from there, so shopping becomes a visual conversation. How it's built J.Crew’s product team used Claude Fable (opens in new tab) 5.1, Anthropic’s model for complex, open-ended work, to plan how Style Advisor should reason like a stylist, then built a working prototype with Claude Opus (opens in new tab) 5.5 in Claude Code. J.Crew’s engineers took that prototype to production. In each conversation, Claude Sonnet (opens in new tab) 5.5 acts as the stylist and decides each step of the response, while Claude Haiku (opens in new tab) 5.5 handles quick, focused tasks so Style Advisor answers quickly. Because every look comes from J.Crew’s stylists, its recommendations stay consistent with J.Crew’s styling point of view. How customers use Style Advisor Shop complete outfits. Every recommendation starts from looks J.Crew stylists created for the brand's catalog shoots, and Style Advisor shows them in photos so customers see the full outfit. Build from a single piece. A customer can start with one item and get suggestions for the pieces that complete the look. Dress for the occasion. Customers can say where they're going, whether that's a vacation, a holiday party, or a wedding, and get recommendations for it. Get J.Crew's point of view. Style Advisor applies the same styling principles a J.Crew stylist would use in a store. What's next At launch, Style Advisor helps customers find new outfit ideas and shop with more confidence. Over time, J.Crew plans to make it more personal by tailoring suggestions to each customer's preferences and past purchases, and to bring it to more markets and product lines. “As consumer expectations evolve and AI opens up new possibilities for retail, J.Crew is challenging the traditional model of online shopping, moving beyond individual product searches toward a more connected and inspiration-led experience,” said Libby Wadle, Chief Executive Officer of J.Crew Group. “For a long time, we’ve been thinking about how customers will want to shop in the future, and how we can lead that evolution rather than react to it. We see an opportunity to fundamentally rethink the shopping experience. Through our work with Anthropic, we're bringing decades of J.Crew styling, merchandising and creative expertise together to help shape what’s next for customer behavior.” “J.Crew has one of the most recognizable points of view in fashion, and its team used Claude to bring that expertise to customers in a new way,” said Paul Smith, Chief Commercial Officer, Anthropic. “They used a frontier model to build the experience and faster, more efficient models to run it, so customers get quick answers that stay true to the brand’s styling.” Start building with Claude Code (opens in new tab) today.

title: The Claude Tag guide for startups
abstract: Startups frequently work at a fast pace with lean teams wearing many hats. In many ways, Claude Tag (beta) is suited for how startups work. You @Claude to a Slack channel where your context lives, add connectors, and have your team assign and steer tasks together. For startup teams new to using Claude Tag, one of the most frequent questions is “which channels should I add Claude to first?” To help answer it, we spoke with eight high growth startups to see how Claude Tag works inside their teams. Featuring insights from We heard from leaders at companies with visions from reinventing law firms to building the next generation of resource planning software. Some had added Claude to nearly every channel while others had focused deeply on one or two specific use cases. Company On call Thread to PR Company brain Self-serve data Routine reporting Kikoff ● ● ● ● NavigateAI ● ● ● ● Campfire ● ● ● Flagler Health ● ● ● Moritz ● ● Orderful ● ● ● ● Valence ● ● ● Descript ● ● ● But everyone we spoke with shared an “aha!” moment where they realized a minutes-long Claude Tag conversation replaced days of work or uncovered insights that would otherwise have remained hidden. The most common are contained in this guide, each with practical implementation details designed to help founders find and deploy the use cases that will move the needle for their team. Here are some examples of how the needle moved for the startups we spoke with: 21 minutes from Slack mention to open PR 134 pull requests merged from Slack threads 5 minutes for the daily end-of-shift update, down from 1 hour <1 hour from client ask to no-code solution 2 days from Slack question to production Days to hours of recurring reporting prep In this guide, we share the most common use cases, channels, and collective insights from leading startups for using Claude Tag. Top channels to tag Claude The eight startups we spoke with use Claude Tag across Slack, but a handful of channels came up again and again as the best places to start. 01 Claude on call Example setups: Channels #on-call #alerts-ci #deploy-watch #support-escalations Connectors GitHub, GitLab, Sentry, dbt, PagerDuty, Linear, Datadog, Jira, Grafana, incident.io Threads and routines Incident response, morning incident digest, Monday on-call handoff, daily health summary, hourly incident recap Starter instruction @Claude remember for this channel: monitor alerts and immediately triage each one in its own thread. Check for an existing ticket. Query the data first, then theorize, and separate what you verified from what you inferred. If it's real, name the likely root cause with links, tag the owner, and open a draft PR only if the fix is contained. If no action is needed, say so. After each incident, add what you learned to [lessons file]. Triage channels are notoriously noisy. There are constant interruptions from Sentry errors, Datadog alerts, customer bug reports, and support requests making it difficult to find the signal from noise. It's usually the first task teams hand to Claude. With Claude in the channel as a first responder , the first pass is often done before the on-call engineer opens their laptop. Claude reads each item as it lands, investigates the codebase and the tools it has access to, and shares what it found. If the fix is contained, it opens a draft PR; if not, it routes the issue to the right person with the investigation attached. In these setups, a person reviews each fix before it merges, and only genuinely new problems need someone to start the investigation themselves. At Campfire, which builds an AI-native ERP for finance teams, an engineer tagged Claude on a report that some of its AI agent’s finished answers weren’t reaching users. Claude had a PR open 21 minutes later, and it merged that afternoon. Kikoff: A first responder in every triage channel Kikoff is a fintech startup that helps consumers build credit, solve liquidity needs, and achieve financial security. Claude Tag is the first responder in triage channels across the company, including: #deploys : Claude decides what to watch after each release and flags anything it broke. #alerts-ci : When a build fails, Claude finds out why and proposes a fix as a draft PR. #alerts-sentry-backend : Claude takes the first pass on Sentry exceptions and crashes. #dog-fooding : Claude investigates what employees flag while dogfooding and tags the right owner. #support : Claude takes the first pass on support tickets. Kikoff started with Claude contributing to the conversation only when mentioned, and the biggest wins came once the team let it jump in on its own. When sign-up broke, Claude traced it to a backend change, sized the impact, named the team that owned the fix, and opened a draft PR so the app would fail softly in the meantime. Claude flags that sign-up is broken, traces it to a backend change, sizes the impact, names the team that owns the fix, and opens a draft PR so the app fails softly. A recreated conversation from Kikoff. Names and images have been modified. Used with permission from Kikoff. “I’m always hyped when Claude catches an issue before a monitor or human does. One person can only personally manage so much context, Claude Tag helps us organize and own some context, and we manage the outcomes.” Alex Dejeu, engineering manager at Kikoff NavigateAI: Fixing bugs with fragmented context NavigateAI builds AI copilots for construction field teams. They run Claude Tag in about 90 channels for alert triage, bug bashes, quick feature building, and support escalations. Since June, Claude has opened about 223 PRs straight from Slack threads and 134 have merged with a median of two hours from open to merge. Triage has been a particularly valuable use case for NavigateAI. Because Claude has so much context, it can find unintuitive root causes to issues that may have been missed at first glance. “Our biggest ‘wow!’ moment with Claude Tag was when we were trying to debug a load issue, which seemed to be caused by a customer (since their calls were failing). A normal human response would be to continue chasing down that customer. But because Claude had access to so many other data sources, it actually found that it was from an uninstrumented internal cron job that was running during the same time.” Mike Chen, head of engineering at NavigateAI With Claude, mean time to resolve issues has improved. In one case, Claude had the root cause eight minutes after a Sentry alert fired, and the fix was merged 93 minutes after the alert. “Fast-moving startups typically have to pick speed over structure. Claude Tag gives us both. It’s a brain that connects the dots across all our tools, so we get the structure without having to build it ourselves,” said Mike. 02 Thread to PR Example setups: Channels #quick-wins #bug-bash #product-feedback #feature-requests #ux-papercuts #tech-debt #design-polish Connectors GitHub, GitLab, Linear, Jira, Confluence, Notion, Figma, Sentry Threads and routines One request per thread, weekly backlog sweep, daily PR roundup, weekly shipped recap Starter instruction @Claude remember for this channel: when someone describes a bug or small feature, work on it in its own thread. Check for an existing ticket and read the related code first. If details are missing, ask for them or for a real example instead of guessing. If the change is small and contained, open a draft PR with a short summary of what changed and how you tested it. Never merge; a person reviews and approves. If it's too big or risky, say why and suggest a ticket. Speed is one of a startup’s biggest advantages, but often small requests that delight users can get lost in the shuffle. The intelligence is often gathered by customer-facing teams, submitted in Slack, and, if it's not overlooked, eventually makes its way to Linear or Jira where it’s prioritized against hundreds of other tickets. With Claude Tag, anyone can draft the PR, technical or not.

title: Introducing Claude Meetings
abstract: Claude can now join your video calls as a visible participant, follow the conversation and start on work during the meeting. Claude Meetings is now in beta. Your team can ask Claude questions during the meeting, out loud or in chat. By default, Claude answers in writing, and it can use your connected tools with your permission. Claude also works with you live to build docs, whiteboards (opens in new tab) , or other artifacts, while teammates on the invite refine them. Claude writes the notes and action items, so no one on the call has to. Claude Meetings is starting to roll out in beta on Team and Enterprise plans. Support for other video conferencing platforms is coming soon. What it looks like Say your team is planning a customer event, and Claude is on the call. You say, “Claude, start a doc for this plan.” Claude writes up what the team has said so far, and teammates on the invite can edit the plan while you keep talking. When you start discussing the budget, someone asks Claude what last year’s event cost. Claude asks for their approval to look it up, posts it in the meeting chat, and compares it to the current plan. When you start discussing timelines, someone asks Claude to put it on a whiteboard, and the team works on the schedule alongside the doc. Before the meeting ends, someone asks Claude to share a recap with the team. After the call, any notes, action items, plan, and whiteboard are on the meeting’s page in claude.ai (opens in new tab) . Later, you can go back to meetings you were part of and ask Claude about them, or add Claude to the next one from your calendar in claude.ai. We’re working with partners like Gong, Attention, Granola, Fireflies.ai, and Otter so you’ll soon be able to send a meeting’s transcript to the tools your team already uses. Security and privacy Claude adds a separate page for each meeting in claude.ai (opens in new tab) with the notes, transcript, and anything it built. People from your organization on the invite can see it and edit what Claude made, and it can be shared with others in your organization from the page. By default, Claude is set to stay out of calls when someone from outside your organization is invited, and to leave if someone from outside joins partway through. An admin can allow Claude on calls with outside guests. On those calls, Claude posts its notice in the call’s chat but doesn’t reply there, and what guests say is included in the notes and transcript. Claude uses each person’s connected tools with that person’s permission. It asks the first time, and a yes applies going forward. For now, when someone asks out loud, Claude asks each time to confirm who’s speaking. An answer posted in the call’s chat is visible to everyone on the call. When Claude joins, it appears as a participant and posts a notice in the call’s chat. It saves a transcript, summary, and screen descriptions, not audio. Before you add Claude or turn on auto-join, make sure everyone on your calls is OK with being transcribed. Getting started Claude joins when someone adds it or has auto-join on. Support is currently available for Google Meet, with other platforms coming soon. On Team plans, inviting Claude to your meetings is available by default, and an admin can turn it off. On Enterprise plans, an admin turns it on for all or part of the organization. While it’s in beta, it isn’t available to some organizations, including those with zero data retention (ZDR), HIPAA-ready configuration, or customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK). During the beta, Claude’s notes and transcripts are free on Team and Enterprise plans. So are its answers in your calls, unless an answer uses one of your connected tools, which counts toward your plan’s usage. The docs, whiteboards, (opens in new tab) and other artifacts Claude makes in a call are free through February 10, 2027. Setup steps are in the Help Center .

title: Introducing Claude for Manufacturing
abstract: Today we’re launching Claude for Manufacturing (opens in new tab) , a plugin that includes skills for work from pricing a new job to diagnosing a stopped machine. An estimator can now have Claude read a customer’s request, compare costs on similar jobs, and draft the quote. The plugin works from a manufacturer’s own records through connectors to Autodesk Fusion, Infor, Microsoft 365, and Oracle NetSuite. Claude for Manufacturing is built so the person responsible can review and approve the work before it reaches a customer or supplier. Manufacturing teams can spend much of the day gathering information. In a 2025 Manufacturing Leadership Council survey, 79% of manufacturers said they enter data (opens in new tab) manually. With Claude carrying each process to the point of review, an estimator can focus on the price, a quality engineer on the fix, and a technician on what to check first. Skills built for manufacturers The plugin’s 17 skills cover sales, quality, operations, supply chain, design, and setup. Some handle a single task, while others run several in order, so Claude can carry a job through several steps until a person needs to review it. The skills can run processes that include: Quoting a new job : An estimator can ask Claude to read a customer’s request, list what’s missing, compare costs on similar jobs, and draft the quote for release. Investigating a failed inspection : A quality engineer can have Claude document the failure, check past reports for the same problem, rank the likely causes, and draft the corrective action report. Diagnosing a breakdown : A technician can have Claude read the sensor exports, repair notes, photos, and manual, then rank the likely causes for the technician to check and decide on next steps. Sourcing from another supplier : A buyer can have Claude prepare the request for quotes, then compare the bids that come back. Comparing designs with Autodesk Fusion : An engineer can have Claude generate variations from an existing model, score them against the engineer’s targets, and draft a decision memo. Reporting on production : A plant manager can have Claude compile production data into one report showing output against target, equipment downtime, and what the downtime and missed output cost. These skills are a starting point. Organizations can build on them to fit their specific operations, and we plan to add new manufacturing skills over time. Connectors to manufacturing systems Claude for Manufacturing works with the software at the core of manufacturing operations, and that software stays central to how teams run the business: Autodesk Fusion : Engineers can compare more design options before choosing one, because Claude generates variations from their existing model. Infor : Buyers and planners can check purchase orders and stock before they act, because Claude looks them up in Infor. Microsoft 365 : Quality engineers can bring procedures, supplier emails, and exported reports into one job, because Claude finds them in shared folders and inboxes. Oracle NetSuite : Estimators can price new work against actual orders, inventory, production steps, and job costs, because Claude pulls those records when it drafts a quote. Manufacturers can also use the plugin with systems that have no connector. They save regular exports from those systems to Microsoft 365, and Claude works from the files to draft a quote or compile a production report. Making changes in Infor with Claude Infor, which makes core software for manufacturers, is also releasing its own plugin (opens in new tab) . With the Infor connector in Claude for Manufacturing, teams can look up records. With Infor’s plugin, they can also make changes in Infor from Claude. For example, if a steel shipment slips by two weeks, a buyer can ask Claude which customer orders are affected and how much steel other sites have. Once the buyer approves, Claude can release a purchase order to another supplier and reschedule the affected production in Infor. Claude’s access follows the buyer’s Infor permissions. Manufacturing teams stay in control Skills are built to end with a user’s review, so an estimator checks and releases a quote, and a quality engineer verifies a fix for the corrective action report. To support that review, Claude can link figures and claims back to the underlying data and documents. Claude for Manufacturing doesn’t operate equipment. For that, Anthropic is developing the Model Hardware Standard (opens in new tab) , a research preview that gives programmable equipment a standard way to describe its measurements, settings, and safety limits. How to get started On Team or Enterprise plans, install the plugin (opens in new tab) and tell Claude, “Set us up.” Claude asks which systems the team uses, tests the connectors, and reports which skills can’t fully run yet. To see the plugin at work, register for our technical webinar (opens in new tab) on November 17 at 11:00 a.m. ET. To talk through a company’s manufacturing systems, contact our sales team (opens in new tab) .

title: Theoretical Limits of Language Model Alignment
abstract: research area Fairness , research area Methods and Algorithms conference NeurIPS content type paper published November 2026 Theoretical Limits of Language Model Alignment Authors Lucas Monteiro Paes*, Natalie Mackraz*, Barry-John Theobald, Federico Danieli View publication Copy Bibtex Language model (LM) alignment improves model outputs to reflect human preferences while preserving the capabilities of the base model. The most common alignment approaches are (i) reinforcement learning, which maximizes the expected reward under a KL-divergence constraint, and (ii) best-of- N N N alignment, which selects the highest-reward output among N N N independent samples. Despite their widespread use, the fundamental limits of reward improvement under a KL budget remain poorly understood. We characterize the information-theoretic limits of KL-regularized alignment by deriving the maximum achievable expected reward gain for a fixed KL-divergence budget. Our first result provides a closed-form expression for the optimal reward improvement, governed by a Jeffreys divergence term rather than the √ K L √KL √ K L used in prior analyses. We further reformulate this expression as a covariance under the base model, yielding a practical estimator that predicts achievable alignment gains from base model samples alone. We extend our analysis to the proxy reward setting, showing that the gap between ideal and proxy alignment ( reward hacking ) grows with the magnitude of reward error and when the KL penalty factor decreases. We then prove that reward ensembling mitigates reward hacking, providing a theoretical justification for this technique used in practice. Empirically, we compute the KL–reward Pareto frontier for two tasks for LMs, safety and summarization, and show that best-of- N N N closely approaches the theoretical limit, while PPO and GRPO remain substantially suboptimal. Our theoretical results shed light on several empirically observed phenomena in the alignment literature and suggest that algorithmic improvements are needed to achieve optimal alignment without high inference costs. * Equal contribution Related readings and updates. SALSA: Soup-Based Alignment Learning for Stronger Adaptation in RLHF December 5, 2024 research area Speech and Natural Language Processing Workshop at NeurIPS This paper was accepted at the Fine-Tuning in Modern Machine Learning (FITML) Workshop at NeurIPS 2024. In Large Language Model (LLM) development, Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) is crucial for aligning models with human values and preferences. RLHF traditionally relies on the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between the current policy and a frozen initial policy as a reference, which is added as a penalty in policy… Read more On the Limited Generalization Capability of the Implicit Reward Model Induced by Direct Preference Optimization October 9, 2024 research area Methods and Algorithms , research area Speech and Natural Language Processing conference EMNLP Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) is an effective approach for aligning language models to human preferences. Central to RLHF is learning a reward function for scoring human preferences. Two main approaches for learning a reward model are 1) training an explicit reward model as in RLHF, and 2) using an implicit reward learned from preference data through methods such as Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). title: Deploy frontier AI models on AWS Trainium with SGLang-Neuron
abstract: Today, Amazon announced that SGLang-Neuron is publicly available and can be accessed through an AWS Deep Learning Container, released by RadixArk in collaboration with Annapurna Labs. With SGLang-Neuron, you can serve models and generate reinforcement learning (RL) rollouts with SGLang on AWS Trainium using the same SGLang interface you use today. Trainium is a portfolio of AWS AI chips that delivers strong economics for AI training and inference at scale. Now, running SGLang on Trainium follows the SGLang workflow you already know: you launch models through SGLang’s server interface and invoke the endpoint using the same generation APIs. Underneath that interface, SGLang-Neuron runs on native PyTorch. With its out-of-tree plugin design, Trainium support and SGLang core develop independently and iterate faster. SGLang-Neuron is an out-of-tree plugin that connects SGLang with AWS Trainium. Installing the plugin registers the neuron platform through SGLang’s plugin entry points, and setting SGLANG_PLATFORM=neuron selects it when the server starts. SGLang core continues to provide the API server, request lifecycle, RadixAttention, and prefix-cache bookkeeping. The plugin implements the Trainium-specific models, attention, mixture of experts (MoE), and the graph runner. Figure 1: SGLang-Neuron on AWS Trainium TorchNeuron registers Trainium as a native PyTorch device. SGLang-Neuron uses standard PyTorch operations for the model execution path and incorporates kernels written with the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) for performance. It compiles these operations and kernels into executable programs using torch.compile , which the graph runner prepares and executes during serving. SGLang-Neuron also supports PD disaggregation . In this configuration, a prefill server computes the prompt KV cache and transfers it to a decode server using NIXL over Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) . The decode server then generates the remaining tokens. Each server still uses SGLang’s scheduler and request lifecycle, while the plugin manages the Trainium execution and KV-cache transfer path. To follow this walkthrough, you use a Trainium3 Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instance with a pytorch-inference-sglang-neuronx container. Here are the steps: For additional information, please see the SGLang-Neuron getting started guide for setup instructions, and explore the repository documentation for supported models, features, and validated configurations. SGLang-Neuron brings SGLang’s familiar serving workflow to AWS Trainium through native PyTorch. You can get started by launching the SGLang-Neuron container and following the quickstart to serve a supported model. Try it with your workloads, contribute through the project repository, and share feedback to help shape future model and feature support.

title: How Natera designed an agentic AI system for lab ops with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
abstract: At Natera , a leader in cell-free DNA (cfDNA) testing, keeping lab instruments up and running is critical, because equipment downtime disrupts sample processing. Natera’s lab engineering team, led by Ariel Jirau worked with AWS to build SWARM (Systematic Workflow Analytics and Resolutions Manager), an agentic AI system for lab operations. This post walks through how the Natera team built an agentic AI system for lab operations using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that captures and deploys institutional knowledge at scale. It describes the full architecture, from knowledge base construction to automated system deployment and evaluation, so you can apply the same patterns to your own operational workflows. SWARM delivers about 130x faster first response time and 96.2 percent automated coverage across support tickets, giving engineers immediate access to institutional knowledge the moment a ticket arrives. Natera’s lab operations rely on a wide range of precision instruments spanning multiple equipment families, each with its own failure modes, vendor documentation, and resolution patterns. The service engineering team responsible for maintaining this infrastructure is organized around deep individual expertise rather than standardized playbooks. When a senior technician who had spent years diagnosing a particular instrument family departed, the institutional knowledge they carried was effectively lost. No system existed to capture, organize, or deploy that expertise at scale. With over 65 tickets per day across three Jira queues and an average first response time of 17.4 hours, instrument downtime delayed lab samples and patient reporting. Hiring more engineers couldn’t keep pace. SWARM had to respond in minutes, deliver accurate diagnostics across a wide range of equipment types, and improve continuously through a structured evaluation loop. The Natera team chose to build SWARM on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a fully managed, extensible service by AWS designed to build, deploy, connect, secure, and operate AI agents at scale. Three core requirements drove the decision: “We needed a managed runtime that would let us focus engineering effort on diagnostic accuracy rather than infrastructure plumbing—AgentCore gave us that, along with built-in identity management and the flexibility to swap models without rewriting agent logic,” Jirau said. AgentCore provides native integration with services including Amazon DynamoDB , a fully managed NoSQL database service, Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) , and AWS X-Ray , a capability of Amazon CloudWatch. SWARM uses two complementary runtimes sharing a single skill library. The swarm-agent autonomously generates structured diagnostic reports before an engineer opens a ticket, while engineers use swarm-hive to interact in real time, upload images, and explore alternative troubleshooting paths. “The system does not replace engineers—it gives them access to the full depth of institutional knowledge the moment a ticket arrives,” Jirau said. Four layers connect the architecture: Figure 1: Architecture of Natera’s SWARM on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore The Natera team’s first architectural decision was where to run the agents. The team required a managed runtime that would handle container orchestration, scaling, and security without requiring them to maintain custom infrastructure. They chose AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, because it hosts both swarm-agent and swarm-hive in a secure, managed environment with built-in identity management and monitoring, avoiding the need to build and operate a custom agent execution layer. You can adopt this pattern regardless of the framework you choose. The team chose a keyless deployment model because SWARM runs in a clinical environment where credentials exposure is unacceptable. OpenID Connect (OIDC) and AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) generate temporary credentials scoped per deployment, with no long-lived keys in the pipeline. AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) enforces least privilege at the component level. Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) with private subnets and VPC endpoints keeps traffic off the public internet. AWS Secrets Manager rotates the few credentials that exist on an automatic 30-day cycle. GitLab CI runners authenticate to AWS by presenting an OIDC token to an IAM identity provider configured in the account. AWS STS exchanges the token for short-lived credentials scoped to the deployment role (no long-lived access keys are stored in the pipeline). For setup details, see the IAM OIDC provider documentation . The following example illustrates the pattern: an IAM OIDC trust policy for GitLab CI follows this structure: These infrastructure-level security controls work in concert with SWARM’s data governance policies. Together they form the full compliance posture required for operating an AI system in a regulated clinical environment. SWARM runs on HIPAA-eligible AWS services under a Business Associate Agreement ( BAA ), reflecting Natera’s obligations as a clinical laboratory operator. Every agent invocation is audit-logged (a searchable record that satisfies data access traceability requirements). No patient-identifiable information touches the vector index or the language model. Tickets contain only equipment and workflow metadata. Teams building under HIPAA or similar regulatory frameworks should confirm BAA coverage and data separation requirements before designing the knowledge base pipeline. Early prototypes using general-purpose retrieval without equipment-specific metadata produced inconsistent results, so the Natera team built a custom document processing pipeline tailored to technical equipment documentation. Amazon Titan Text Embeddings generates vector representations for semantic search, and Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases provides fully managed Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG), converting documents into embeddings stored in batches of 100, a size chosen to balance indexing throughput against API rate limits. For heavily structured source documents with tables and diagrams, investing in a custom parsing pipeline rather than relying on default chunking compounds accuracy gains across every diagnosis. Amazon Bedrock services, including Amazon Titan Text Embeddings, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore are available in multiple AWS Regions. For the latest information, see Amazon Bedrock supported Regions and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore supported Regions . The Natera team uses the tiktoken tokenizer with the cl100k_base encoding to measure chunk boundaries. The following example illustrates the pattern, the chunking configuration follows a standard structure: For more on batch ingestion patterns, see the Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases documentation . “Diagnostic accuracy is a data quality problem first,” Jirau said. “Adding missing vendor manuals for the lowest-scoring instrument family lifted accuracy from 71% to 75% with no model changes.” This shaped the Natera team’s improvement approach: when accuracy plateaus, the team checks data coverage before model tuning, because gaps in vendor documentation are the most common cause of missed diagnoses. The pipeline reprocesses new or updated documents and refreshes the vector index without disrupting active operations. The Natera team faced a key architectural choice: embed logic directly in agent prompts, or build a separate, versioned skill library. Natera chose the library approach because it makes SWARM auditable and improvable. “When a diagnosis is wrong, we need to point to a specific skill rather than debug the whole system — that’s why we built a versioned skill library from the start,” Jirau said. The library contains 33 skills: 24 instrument-specific skills covering the full range of equipment families Natera supports, plus 9 cross-cutting workflow skills that apply broadly across ticket types.

title: Four Amazon Bedrock inference choices that affect cost
abstract: Your Amazon Bedrock inference bill can keep climbing after you tune prompts and application logic. Request-level choices can still change how many tokens the service processes and the rate applied to them. Cache duration, service tier, reasoning effort, and maxTokens can affect cost without changing your model or prompt. Each choice depends on the model and workload. This post shows how we tested each choice and how to verify its effect from response metadata, logs, and billing data. To try these settings yourself, start with the Amazon Bedrock Samples notebooks Mixed TTL Caching and Tenant Isolation with Prompt Caching . For maxTokens and reasoning effort, see the 01-low-effort folder of the sample-code-for-genai-cost-management-workshop GitHub repo. Each sample sets its own model ID, so change it, and the inference parameters, to match the model you call. For model availability by AWS Region, refer to Models at a glance . For broader decisions such as model selection, batch inference, routing, and distillation, see Effective cost optimization strategies for Amazon Bedrock . Every Amazon Bedrock response carries usage metadata. Input and output tokens bill at the rate for the model and tier that served the request. Cache reads and writes use separate token counters, and reasoning tokens count as output tokens. Repeated system instructions, tool definitions, or reference context can be processed again when the cache expires before the next request. The Prompt caching for faster model inference guide lists 5-minute and 1-hour time-to-live (TTL) values for supported Anthropic models. It also lists a 30-minute minimum TTL for supported GPT-5.6 models. Support and API fields depend on the model, so check the current support matrix before selecting a duration. For supported models, Amazon Bedrock also offers implicit prompt caching , which attempts to reuse eligible prompt prefixes without cache controls in your request. Because implicit caching is best effort and doesn’t guarantee a cache hit, the duration choices in this section apply to explicit caching. This Converse API signature requests a 1-hour entry on models that support it: For supported Anthropic models, InvokeModel places the same ttl value in cache_control . A longer duration is not automatically cheaper. The Amazon Bedrock Pricing page lists separate rates for 5-minute writes, 1-hour writes, and cache reads. For Anthropic Claude Sonnet 5 and Anthropic Claude Opus 5 on Amazon Bedrock, a 5-minute write costs 1.25 times the input rate. A 1-hour write costs 2 times, and a cache read costs 0.1 times. These rates set the break-even, assuming each request reuses the exact prefix and each cache read refreshes the TTL. A 5-minute cache pays back on the first reuse within 5 minutes. When requests for the same prefix arrive more than 5 minutes apart, it rewrites at 1.25 times on every request. The 1-hour cache is then cheaper from the second request within the hour. Cache rates and checkpoint minimums differ by model. Check the Amazon Bedrock Pricing page and the prompt caching guide for the model you call. Rerun the comparison for your model, then confirm it with cache read and write tokens after rollout. Keep stable content before dynamic content, meet the model’s checkpoint minimum, and use on-demand inference because prompt caching doesn’t work with batch inference. Changing a cached prefix, including a system instruction or tool definition, causes a miss and a new write. Checkpoints are evaluated in the order tools, system, then messages, so a change in an earlier section also invalidates the later ones. Version prompts that change often so each version gets its own cache entry. We ran six calls on Claude Sonnet 5 with a 1-hour checkpoint, changing the system prompt once and the tool definition once. Each change produced zero cache reads and a new write. AWS describes cache entries as scoped to your account and Region, not to your tenants. In a multi-tenant application, prepend a tenant-specific SHA-256 hash to the cacheable prefix. The Optimizing cost and latency with Amazon Bedrock prompt caching for Anthropic models post describes this pattern. Enforce tenant authorization before you build the prompt. The hash partitions entries inside one account. If a regulated workload needs a hard data boundary, keep each tenant in a separate AWS account. Keep the 5-minute default for frequent reuse. Move from it to a longer supported duration when the same prefix recurs at least twice an hour with gaps longer than 5 minutes. To beat no caching at all, the 1-hour cache needs three requests an hour. Background jobs, evaluation harnesses, nightly summarization, and backfills don’t always need the latency profile used by interactive requests. For models that support Flex, select it with this request signature: Use default , not standard , to request the Standard tier. You can also omit serviceTier : Tier support is model-specific, so record support by exact model version. The Amazon Nova 2 Lite and OpenAI gpt-oss-120b model cards list Flex as supported. The cards for Anthropic Claude Sonnet 5 and Anthropic Claude Opus 5 on Amazon Bedrock list it as not supported. A Flex request to an unsupported model fails with a ValidationException instead of silently running on Standard. Our request to Anthropic Claude Sonnet 5 returned that error. If your policy allows Standard as a fallback, catch the unsupported-tier error and retry once with default . Don’t retry every ValidationException , because malformed requests raise it too. Cap application-level retries. The bounded retry strategy of the AWS SDK handles throttling and transient errors. Set your own deadline for Flex requests. A supported response reports the resolved tier, which you can also verify with Amazon CloudWatch ResolvedServiceTier . See Service tiers for optimizing performance and cost and the Amazon Bedrock Pricing page for the exact model you call. We tested Flex on Amazon Nova 2 Lite with 200 default requests and 200 flex requests, sent in interleaved pairs. Both tiers processed the same number of input and output tokens. All 400 requests resolved to the requested tier, and the median latency difference was too small to separate from noise. At the time of writing, the published Flex rate for Nova 2 Lite in us-west-2 is half the Standard rate, and our bill reflected that. Check the Amazon Bedrock Pricing page for current rates. Keep latency-sensitive traffic on default . Reasoning tokens bill as output tokens. Claude Sonnet 5 and Claude Opus 5 use adaptive thinking at high effort by default, even when a request omits the thinking field. An application moved from Claude Sonnet 4.6 without changes starts billing thinking tokens, and maxTokens now caps thinking plus response text. Claude Haiku 5.5 defaults to medium . All three models support low , medium , high , xhigh , and max . Lower the effort for a task with this request signature: Keep effort in output_config , not inside thinking . Check Adaptive thinking whenever you change models. We tested a tool-calling agent on Claude Opus 5. Its three tasks follow the design in Build long-horizon agents with Grok 4.7 on Amazon Bedrock , and each has one correct answer. We ran each task eight times at every effort level. The table shows median output tokens: Accuracy at lower effort depends on the model and the task. Measure on tasks shaped like yours. On the Amazon Bedrock Samples Invoke Bedrock model for code generation workload, median output tokens were 676 at low and 743 at high , a difference within run-to-run variation. The programs we graded passed at each effort level. Use per-request output-token counts, CloudWatch AWS/Bedrock OutputTokenCount , invocation logs, and a task pass rate to evaluate the choice. Start below high for routine, well-bounded tasks. Keep high where your quality tests show that the task needs it. A token reduction that breaks the task is not a saving.

title: Tokenomics at scale: Track and cap Amazon Bedrock spend per IAM principal with CUR 2.0 and AWS Budgets
abstract: Generative AI spend is hard to attribute. Before an organization expands AI access, CFOs and CTOs usually want three answers: what do we spend per person or per team, can we cap it, and how much work does it take to get there. In our previous post, Tokenomics at Scale: How Jamf Built Real-Time Spend Enforcement for Amazon Bedrock , we explained a custom enforcement loop built on AWS IAM Identity Center , Amazon Athena over Amazon Bedrock model invocation logs , and AWS Lambda . This approach gives near-real-time control, but it requires code you then own and operate. This post shows how to get per-identity Amazon Bedrock cost visibility and enforceable spend limits using only AWS-native features, with no application code to write for the common case. The approach relies on three things: IAM principal attribution , which Amazon Bedrock records automatically; AWS Cost and Usage Reports (CUR) 2.0 or AWS Cost Explorer for reporting; and AWS Budgets with budget actions for enforcement. By the end, you will have per-identity cost reporting and an automatic guardrail that restricts Amazon Bedrock access when a threshold is crossed. The solution has three parts: attribute, report, and enforce. Attribute. Amazon Bedrock captures the AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) principal identity, the IAM user or role , for every inference request. This happens automatically, with no change to your Amazon Bedrock model inference calls. If several people share one role, you add per-user detail with session tags passed at role assumption time. If each person or application has its own role, principal tags on the role are enough. Report. Activate those tags as cost allocation tags, then read the data either in Cost Explorer for a console-only view, or in a CUR 2.0 data export for detailed line-item analysis and SQL queries. Enforce. Create an AWS Budget scoped to Amazon Bedrock and filtered to one identity or tag value, then attach a budget action that applies a Deny IAM policy when the threshold is crossed. The following sections show each part in more detail, alongside the implementation steps. To deploy this solution, you need: AWS Billing Console access is managed separately from most IAM permissions. Confirm you have it before starting. Before configuring anything, check what you already have. Amazon Bedrock records caller identity for every inference request automatically. Open Cost Explorer, filter Service to Amazon Bedrock, and group by the available identity or tag dimension. For accounts where each application or person already uses a distinct IAM role, this may be all the visibility you need. To configure additional visibility: How you tag depends on how your IAM principals are organized. One role per person or per application. Attach principal tags directly to each IAM role or user. These are static and apply to every request from that principal. Use the IAM console, or the AWS CLI: A shared role used by several people, or a gateway. Principal tags cannot distinguish users on a shared role, because every session carries the same tags. Use session tags instead, passed when the role is assumed. Session tags are dynamic and can vary per session. If a session tag and a principal tag share a key, the session tag wins for that session. The role’s trust policy must allow sts:TagSession . Session tags can be passed three ways: If your organization already captures a claim like saml:sub for other purposes, that alone does not make it available here. Your identity provider must separately map that attribute to a PrincipalTag:* SAML attribute statement, and the role’s trust policy must allow sts:TagSession , before it flows through as a session tag. The two integrations draw from the same SAML assertion but are configured independently. Common tag keys are user, team, Department, CostCenter, and Environment. You can apply up to 50 principal or session tags per IAM user or role. Figure 1: Attribution with principal tags compared to session tags Tags do not appear in billing data until you activate them. In an AWS Organization , activate IAM principal cost allocation tags in the management account (payer). Member accounts cannot activate them independently. Activation does not apply retroactively by default, so activate tags before you need the data. Skip this step if Cost Explorer is enough for your reporting. If you already have a CUR 2.0 export created before enabling identity attribution, it will not include identity data retroactively. Create a new export with the caller identity option selected. In the export, principal and session tags appear as columns prefixed iamPrincipal/ , and resource tags as resourceTags/ . For example, a tag key team appears as iamPrincipal/team . AWS publishes a ready-made query set for this exact pattern in aws-samples/sample-cur-iam-principal-bedrock-tracking . The following diagram compares the two ways to read the data: a console-only path through Cost Explorer, and a SQL path over the CUR 2.0 export with Amazon Athena. Figure 2: Reporting with Cost Explorer compared to CUR 2.0 and Amazon Athena Console path, no custom code. Cost Explorer, filtered to Amazon Bedrock and grouped by your tag key, gives per-team or per-user spend as a chart and table. This covers most recurring reporting needs and requires no query authoring. SQL path, low code. Point Amazon Athena at the CUR 2.0 export to group spend by iamPrincipal/team and usage type: Two notes worth carrying into any query you write. AWS Budgets performs the attach, so there is no custom code for this workflow. Budget actions attach to a specific IAM user, group, or role. This isolates one person’s access only if that person already has their own role. If your Amazon Bedrock traffic runs through a role that many people share, a Deny action attached to that role blocks everyone on it, not only the person who crossed the threshold. The following diagram explains the enforcement workflow. Figure 3: Enforcement with AWS Budgets and budget actions AWS Budgets can run an action when a threshold is crossed. Available actions include applying a custom IAM policy, applying a service control policy (SCP), and targeting Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) or Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) instances. For this use case, the IAM policy action is the relevant one. First, create the Deny policy the action will attach. This example denies the higher-cost models while leaving a lower-cost model available, so the user can keep working: Replace [HIGHER-COST-MODEL-ID] with the model ID you want to deny in your environment. Then set up permissions and the budget itself. There are two distinct roles here, and the AWS managed policy only covers one of them: Your own user or role (the one configuring the budget) needs the AWS managed policy AWSBudgetsActionsWithAWSResourceControlAccess . It grants budgets permissions plus the conditioned iam:PassRole needed to hand your budget action role to AWS Budgets. The IAM role AWS Budgets assumes to perform the action is not covered by a single named managed policy for this use case. Create it with a trust policy that allows the principal budgets.amazonaws.com to assume it (scoped with aws:SourceArn and aws:SourceAccount conditions), and a permissions policy granting iam:AttachRolePolicy and iam:DetachRolePolicy (and organizations:AttachPolicy and organizations:DetachPolicy if you are also using SCPs). Refer to Setting up a role for AWS Budgets to run budget actions for the grantable permissions. You can attach multiple actions to a single threshold, and multiple thresholds to one budget. That is how you build tiers: for example, deny the premium model at 80 percent and the mid-tier model at 100 percent, while never denying the low-cost model. Only the management account can apply SCPs, and from the management account you can apply an SCP to another account.

title: Optimizing cost per task and proving agent ROI on Amazon Bedrock
abstract: Part 1 of this series built the operating model that controls Amazon Bedrock spend: attribution with AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) principal tags and Cost and Usage Report 2.0, observability with model invocation logging, enforcement at three tiers, and a review cadence. That layer answers who spent it, and you can stop them. It can’t tell you whether the spend was well spent. This post answers two questions that Part 1 deliberately left open. First: Why is this workflow expensive? The answer requires thinking in cost per task, not cost per token. Second: Is the agent better than the humans were? The answer requires baselines, controlled experiments, and a scorecard tied to decisions. In this post, you learn a framework for calculating true model cost (including four hidden cost drivers that the pricing page doesn’t show), techniques for reducing cost per task through caching, routing, and output constraints, and a discipline for measuring agent ROI with human baselines, holdout experiments, and a five-dimension scorecard. This post is written for two audiences: the application and platform engineers who own the optimization levers, and the product owners and FinOps partners who need to justify agent spend to leadership. Price per token invites quick comparison, but it doesn’t reflect what you actually pay. The published rate reflects the cost of a single token. Your bill reflects the cost of completing a task. A task is one complete unit of work your application asks a model to do: resolve one support email, extract fields from one invoice, or answer one user question. A task runs from the request through to a usable result, however many model calls it takes. The lower-priced model might not be the cheaper one to run. A cheaper model might fragment your text into more tokens, pad responses with filler, misread your tool schema and loop through corrections, or burn thousands of reasoning tokens before answering.
