None of these costs appear on the Bedrock pricing page . Four model characteristics determine what that published rate actually costs you on your workload. A token isn’t a word, and it is not equal across models. Every model family uses a different tokenizer and vocabulary. The same text, code, or JSON payload splits into different token counts. If Model A’s list price is 15 percent lower but its tokenizer needs 40 percent more tokens for your data (common with structured schemas and numerical arrays), Model B is cheaper. The gap widens for non-English text: many tokenizers fragment non-Latin scripts into two to three times more tokens than the equivalent English. Output tokens commonly cost 3–5x more than input tokens (the ratio varies by family. Refer to the Bedrock pricing page ). A model that ignores formatting constraints like “return only raw JSON” makes you pay that output premium for filler words. A model that follows formatting instructions closely saves money by generating fewer of these more expensive output tokens. Agentic workflows change the cost math entirely. Tool use (function calling) lets a model invoke external functions, requiring a multi-turn loop: analyze the prompt, decide to call a tool, wait for the observation, generate an answer. Each turn re-sends the full conversation history and tool results as input tokens. A model that takes four turns (each one re-sending a larger context payload) costs far more than one that finishes in a single pass. Many models support extended thinking , working through a chain of thought before the visible answer. Reasoning tokens bill as output tokens, so a model that thinks for 2,000 tokens before a 200-token answer bills you for 2,200. Some models redact the reasoning while still charging for it. Start with reasoning turned off and enable it only when benchmarks show a quality gap that justifies the cost. Figure 1: Comparing two models across five cost dimensions. List price is only one of five factors that determine actual cost Consider an agentic workflow that reads a 750-word customer email, extracts entities, calls an API to verify account status, and outputs strict JSON. The following comparison uses illustrative prices (always benchmark against your own data and current Bedrock pricing ): Model A: (6,150 x $0.50 + 750 x $1.50) / 1,000,000 = $0.0042 Model B: (1,000 x $1.00 + 150 x $3.00) / 1,000,000 = $0.00145 Figure 2: Why the higher-priced model costs 65% less. Each extra turn re-sends a growing context payload, compounding the bill Why the 2x-priced model costs 65 percent less: three compounding factors. Model A’s tokenizer fragments the email into 50 percent more tokens, inflating every input payload. It pads its JSON with filler, tripling output tokens. And it misaligns with the tool schema, needing two correction turns that each re-send a growing history. The preceding example assumes both models eventually succeed. In production they won’t, and a failure is rarely free. The formulas: For retry-until-success workflows: cost per successful task = cost per attempt / success rate For escalate-on-failure workflows: cost per successful task = cost per attempt + (1 - success rate) x escalation cost Input further splits into three buckets when prompt caching is active: uncached input at base rate, cache reads below base rate, and cache writes above base rate. Which model is actually cheaper only shows up when you benchmark against your own data. Amazon Bedrock model evaluation is the managed feature for the quality half of that: define criteria, upload your prompt datasets, and get scored results with automatic metrics and optional human review, with no custom infrastructure required. Quality scores alone don’t produce a bill, though. Three more Bedrock features supply the token and turn counts you price against them: Each of the four drivers has a lever, and each is documented in depth. Prompt caching cuts the re-sent context that made Model A expensive, which makes it the largest win on agentic paths. Intelligent prompt routing sends the easy requests to a cheaper model in the same family. A tool schema plus a maxTokens cap holds verbosity down more reliably than prose instructions do, and extended thinking stays off until a benchmark shows it earns its cost back. Batch inference halves the rate on bulk single-turn work, though it rules out tool calling and multi-turn exchange. Efficient isn’t the same as valuable. An agent can be perfectly optimized and still not be worth running. The question that decides budgets is: is the agent better than the humans were? The biggest mistake in agent ROI is trying to prove value without first describing the human workflow. Before building or scaling an agent, write down the current process in operational terms: what triggers the work, which human roles are involved, where the handoffs sit, how completion is defined. This sounds like bureaucracy. It’s actually measurement design. Every instrumentation decision downstream (what counts as a run, what counts as success, where human time is spent) falls out of this description. With the process described, measure the human baseline over a meaningful window: time to completion, queue time, active effort, reopen rate, escalation rate, cost per task, and outcome quality. Baselines must be measured before the agent goes live, not reconstructed from memory after the fact. Retrospective baselines are systematically flattering to the agent: people remember the average case and forget the fast ones. After the baseline exists, instrument the agent workflow as an experiment from day one. Every run gets a trace ID, and every meaningful step is observable. A workflow-run record aggregates everything above the model call into a single analyzable unit: Three fields deserve emphasis: experiment block: Stamped at run creation and propagated into Bedrock request metadata , so model-level and workflow-level records join cleanly. humanMinutes: What most teams omit and most need.

title: Building a self-service LLM gateway with Amazon Bedrock and LiteLLM
abstract: Developers want AI coding assistants with minimal setup. With a large language model (LLM) gateway and LiteLLM, they can quickly access foundation models (FMs) available on Amazon Bedrock while you gain visibility and usage control. Platform teams need to monitor latency and errors, finance teams need to attribute inference costs to teams and projects, and security teams need consistent access controls. An LLM gateway can help address these needs by providing a centrally managed access point to the models that power coding assistants. In this post, we show how to build a self-service LLM gateway using Amazon Bedrock Application Inference Profiles with LiteLLM running on AWS Fargate to abstract Amazon Bedrock behind an OpenAI-compatible API. With this pattern, developers can access foundation models through a single API with a dedicated key while you gain per-user cost controls and model performance observability. By the end, you will understand the pattern well enough to build your own version from the illustrative snippets and AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) constructs. This post uses Claude Sonnet and Claude Haiku models for example purposes. For a list of models and availability by AWS Region, see Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock . This LLM gateway pattern follows a straightforward request flow from the developer, through the LiteLLM layer, to Amazon Bedrock and the underlying FM. The following diagram illustrates the production topology behind that flow. For simplicity, we don’t cover the addition of Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, such as content filtering and grounding, but you would normally include appropriate responsible AI controls before deploying to production. A developer’s OpenAI-compatible client reaches the LLM gateway through Amazon Route 53, Amazon CloudFront, and an Application Load Balancer (ALB). It authenticates to LiteLLM on Fargate with a per-user API key. Behind that, the request draws on Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) (PostgreSQL) for virtual-key and spend state. It also interacts with Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey as a cache, and AWS Secrets Manager for secrets. LiteLLM then ultimately invokes Amazon Bedrock Application Inference Profiles using a scoped AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) task role. Amazon CloudWatch captures requests per minute (RPM) and tokens per minute (TPM) metrics and the quota alarm. Figure 1: LLM gateway architecture (production topology) The architecture consists of these core components: By using an OpenAI-compatible protocol, developers can configure their tools, such as Claude Code, Continue, and Cursor, with a single base URL and API key. Developers then operate at a level above the Amazon Bedrock backend and can swap models, add fallbacks, or migrate model providers without touching developer configurations. You will need an AWS account, Amazon Bedrock model access, and appropriate IAM permissions to deploy this project. You will also need LiteLLM. The LiteLLM AI Gateway component is open source and suitable for a small pilot with some limitations. LiteLLM documents the AI Gateway as free for up to five users with a license required beyond that. LiteLLM Enterprise is a scalable, production-minded licensed version that includes the open source gateway plus single sign-on, audit logs, delegated admin roles, and support. While the free tier supports virtual keys, the self-service key issuance described in this post requires the Enterprise version. We walk through each configuration layer from the developer’s machine to the foundation model. Developers configure their coding assistant to point to the LLM gateway. This is the only configuration a developer needs to make to their tool: With that configuration, each developer gets their own API key from the self-service portal and drops it into their tool configuration. Deploy LiteLLM to a container service following the LiteLLM documentation . In this example we are using AWS Fargate. This will include the portal, which you can open at http://localhost:4000/ui during local testing. The LiteLLM gateway is where you will map and enforce model names to Amazon Bedrock inference profile ARNs with per-key spend limits: Set on the Fargate task from AWS Secrets Manager: Note: Don’t hardcode the master_key or database credentials in config.yaml . LiteLLM resolves os.environ/VAR_NAME references at load time, so set LITELLM_MASTER_KEY and DATABASE_URL as environment variables on the Fargate task, sourced from AWS Secrets Manager. Set the Langfuse credentials the same way in Step 5. When a developer calls claude-sonnet-4-20250514 , for example, LiteLLM resolves it to the inference profile ARN. It then authenticates to Amazon Bedrock using the AWS Fargate task’s IAM role and streams the response back in OpenAI format. With Amazon Bedrock Application Inference Profiles you can create named endpoints for specific models, so you get quota isolation and fine-grained IAM control. Amazon Bedrock CRIS avoids the overhead of implementing cross-Region request routing yourself. Other benefits include: For this proxy pattern, we recommend Global cross-Region inference when the selected models support it and organizational policies permit inference processing across supported AWS commercial Regions worldwide. Geographic cross-Region inference keeps processing within a defined geography. For example, a US inference profile routes requests only to supported US Regions. Global cross-Region inference provides access to a broader pool of Regional capacity with potential pricing benefits compared with Geographic cross-Region inference. You can verify model availability, applicable service quotas, and model-specific pricing through current AWS documentation and AWS pricing pages. Important: For Global CRIS, the copyFrom ARN must reference the system-defined inference profile prefixed with global. , not the foundation-model ARN directly. Using a foundation-model ARN creates a single-Region profile without cross-Region routing. Additionally, the IAM policy must include the resource ARNs the invocation actually touches: the application inference profile and the underlying foundation model in any Region it might route to (Region-wildcarded). Scoping only to the application-inference-profile ARN returns not authorized to perform: bedrock:InvokeModel on resource: arn:aws:bedrock:us-east-1::foundation-model/... at invoke time. This is scoped least-privilege: it names the exact models in use, not bedrock:* or * . The inference profile handles model resolution and cross-Region routing transparently without additional configuration. When LiteLLM calls the inference profile ARN, Amazon Bedrock routes to available capacity across configured AWS Regions and returns the response. LiteLLM integrates with Langfuse through logging callbacks, providing visibility into model invocations without requiring changes to developer tool configurations. To enable the integration, merge the following entries into the existing litellm_settings block from the Step 2 configuration, preserving existing callback entries: Configure the Langfuse public key, secret key, and deployment endpoint as environment variables on the Fargate task. Store the credentials in AWS Secrets Manager: The endpoint must match the selected Langfuse Cloud region or self-hosted deployment. Choose the hosting option based on data governance and operational requirements. Before enabling prompt and response logging, review the content captured by the integration and configure appropriate redaction, retention, and access controls. Langfuse traces can include prompts, responses, model parameters, token usage, and latency, depending on the integration and logging configuration. This information helps investigate unexpected model responses and complements the operational metrics collected in Amazon CloudWatch. Cost controls are an important dimension to a successful AI strategy.

title: Run agents securely and efficiently with the next generation AgentCore runtime
abstract: AI agents have moved past one-off prompts. They now run multi-step workloads for hours at a time. The length of task that frontier agents can complete on their own doubles about every four months ( METR ), and 40 percent of large enterprises are scaling AI agents, up from 27 percent a year ago ( McKinsey ). As agents run longer and with more autonomy, the focus shifts from what agents can do to how securely, reliably, and economically they can operate at scale. Agents do more than traditional software: they execute code, navigate browsers, access sensitive data, and act on behalf of users. These capabilities introduce new security and infrastructure demands, making strong isolation essential for production deployments. Every agent session needs a secure, isolated environment. But delivering that isolation at scale introduces a fundamental challenge: balancing performance, cost, and efficiency. Pre-provisioned environments consume resources even when idle, driving up costs. On-demand environments reduce wasted capacity but introduce cold-start latency, delaying agent execution. Neither approach scales efficiently without trade-offs. As organizations move from deploying a handful of agents to running thousands of concurrent sessions, building and managing custom sandboxes becomes increasingly complex, expensive, and unpredictable. The challenge is evident. Only 15 percent of organizations have scaled orchestrated, multi-agent systems, and 70 percent say they can’t yet trust and govern their agents ( Deloitte ). Scaling agents shouldn’t mean choosing between security, speed, and cost. The next generation of agent infrastructure must deliver strong isolation with fast startup times, elastic scaling, and usage-based economics. Because as AI agents move into production, secure execution shouldn’t be the bottleneck. It should be the foundation that makes scale possible. The fastest path to production should also be the safest one. We built Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to help developers build, connect, and optimize agents securely at scale. AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, is the managed compute layer. It gives developers a fully managed environment to deploy and run agents without building or maintaining infrastructure. Since launching, our customers have been pushing their agents into increasingly complex workloads. As those workloads grow, so do the demands on the execution environment: more compute, more flexible billing, and trust boundaries that extend to data, not only compute. Agents reach production at scale if the infrastructure underneath was built for both scale and speed. Today we’re announcing updates to AgentCore runtime that meet those demands. The core guarantee stands: every session runs in its own hardware-isolated Firecracker micro virtual machine (MicroVM), with its own identity, policy, and audit trail. These updates expand what’s possible within that guarantee. Sessions now start up to 15x faster, scale to 4x more compute, and run up to 68% more efficiently, with the isolation boundary fully intact. Teams building increasingly advanced agents asked for more flexibility: the ability to scale memory and compute within the isolated session to match the demands of their workloads. From large codebase compilations to browser-driven workflows to local model inference, the execution environment needs to keep pace. Sessions now scale 4x compared to the previous version, up to 8 vCPUs and 32 GB, with support for container images up to 10 GB. Sessions start in under 2 seconds, independent of image size and concurrency. You no longer need warm pools and pre-provisioned clusters to manage cold starts. “AgentCore Runtime lets us run AI-driven development at scale. Each coding agent session runs in its own hardware-isolated environment, which we need when agents execute code, and the runtime scales elastically with demand and starts fast every time, so our engineers move quickly without managing any infrastructure.” — Siwei Shen, VP of Engineering, Coinbase “Mission is using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime to power a natural-language query agent that helps users retrieve property and sales insights without navigating complex data systems. In our initial comparison of both runtime versions, the same workload delivered 35% faster cold starts for inference requests and 77% faster starts for health checks, while reducing measured runtime cost per call by 17%. The new AgentCore runtime gives us a compelling combination of faster agent experiences and more efficient resource utilization as we bring enterprise agents into production.” — Dr. Ryan Ries, Chief AI & Data Scientist, Mission Cloud “Our approach is to run Zuora’s cloud with automation and AI agents wherever we can, and that only works if the runtime is efficient and reliable. The next generation AgentCore runtime cut our memory footprint per invocation by around 60% in many use cases while handling more traffic at steady latency. That gives us a stronger cost profile as we expand agentic workloads across our platform.” — Brad Ruppert, VP of Cloud and Security, Zuora “The Rescale platform helps R&D and engineering teams accelerate product development with agentic digital engineering. Our engineering-specific agents validate simulation inputs, troubleshoot jobs, select hardware, and generate reports, while engineers stay in control. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime allows us to deploy and scale those agents in production without building or operating the underlying agent infrastructure, so we can deliver new agents to customers faster.” — Mark Whitney, VP Engineering, Rescale As teams move agents closer to production, they asked for billing that reflects how agents actually work. Agents spend much of their time waiting on a model response, a tool call, or a human decision. Agents should be billed for the work they do, not the time they spend waiting. The runtime now reclaims memory within minutes of the agent releasing it, and an idle agent scales to zero. For multi-turn agents with natural pauses between interactions, this means up to 68 percent less memory consumed per session. For always-on agents, committed baseline pricing sets a memory baseline per session, billed as a minimum, with room to burst up to four times that baseline on demand. This gives steady workloads a predictable rate at AWS Lambda MicroVM rates. The runtime uses compute more efficiently, so you pay less for the same work. That makes the finance conversation that often gates production rollouts easier to close. “The next generation Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime helps us deliver more responsive AI experiences by starting agents faster and using memory more efficiently. Aligning consumption with actual usage gives our clients great confidence to scale agentic solutions while keeping costs connected to real demand.” — Ashwin Patil, Principal, AI and Data Leader, Deloitte Consulting LLP “AgentCore runtime gives us a managed foundation for building agentic products and platforms around our customers’ data, tools, and business processes. The next generation Agentcore runtime makes that foundation more responsive and resource-efficient by restoring initialized environments and reclaiming unused memory. We’re beginning to build on the latest version because the cost and latency reductions make a significant difference in how our customers’ businesses operate.” Many enterprises face a persistent gap in their agent security model. The agent runs inside an isolated session, but the data it requires resides outside that boundary. Long-running agents pick up context as they go: files, credentials, tool outputs, and more. Teams end up building their own rules for how data moves in and out, adding complexity and risk with every new agent. Isolation that stops at compute is only half a boundary. The next generation AgentCore runtime closes that gap.

title: Migrate to Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base with your coding agent
abstract: With a customer-managed knowledge base on Amazon Bedrock , you provision and scale the vector store, tune the embedding model and index settings, and plan capacity for each new data source. The migration guide in the Agent Toolkit for AWS helps you migrate to Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base . Managed Knowledge Base takes over that work and adds new retrieval capabilities, and your team keeps control of the content and the application that uses it. Moving a production knowledge base means your team maps its configuration, creates the replacement, ingests content, updates the application’s retrieval call, and validates retrieval before switching traffic. To help, we added a knowledge base migration guide to the amazon-bedrock skill in the Agent Toolkit for AWS . The guide gives your coding agent the context to plan the migration with you, starting with read-only discovery and a plan you review line by line. On your approval, the agent creates the new knowledge base and its data sources alongside the original, or writes a migrated infrastructure as code (IaC) template for your pipeline. Ingestion and updating your application’s Retrieve calls stay with you, and your agent can walk you through both. In this post, we explain why we recommend the move and how the migration guide works, review the prerequisites, install the skill, plan a migration, update the application’s retrieval call, and validate retrieval before cutover. We recommend Managed Knowledge Base because it balances ease of use, retrieval accuracy, and cost. With a Managed Knowledge Base, Amazon Bedrock handles ingestion, storage, indexing, and retrieval, and the store scales automatically as your content grows. Hybrid search, which combines keyword and semantic matching, is always on, with no index to configure. The knowledge base includes a managed embedding model, a managed reranker, and a built-in parser for multimodal file types. You can still bring your own Amazon Bedrock embedding model when you create the knowledge base. On each retrieval request, you choose the managed reranker, an Amazon Bedrock reranking model, or no reranking. The managed reranker requires the managed embedding model. Managed Knowledge Base includes capabilities you’d otherwise build yourself: Agentic retrieval, AgentCore Gateway integration, and resource-based policies are not available on customer-managed knowledge bases. For the AWS Regions where managed knowledge bases are available, and the features that AWS GovCloud (US-West) doesn’t support, see Supported AWS Regions . As of this writing, higher default quotas change how you can organize content. With 200 data sources per knowledge base, you can group related content in one knowledge base. With 10,000 knowledge bases per account, per Region, each team or product line can use a separate knowledge base. For current values, see Amazon Bedrock endpoints and quotas and Service quotas for managed knowledge bases . Cost is one of three things teams weigh when they consider this move, alongside customizability and direct control of the vector store. On a customer-managed knowledge base , you choose, provision, scale, and update the vector and text stores, and pay separately for the infrastructure you select. On a Managed Knowledge Base, those stages are part of the service, and storage and retrieval are metered directly. The pricing models can differ too. With a customer-managed knowledge base, storage and retrieval charges depend on the vector store you choose. Some stores charge for provisioned or minimum capacity, and others, such as Amazon S3 Vectors, a capability of Amazon S3, charge only for what you use. A Managed Knowledge Base is priced on what you store and retrieve, so cost follows real usage. Usage-based pricing can fit enterprise question-answering, policy, and support knowledge bases that run at low utilization. For current rates, see Amazon Bedrock pricing . For the parsers available on a customer-managed knowledge base and how each is billed, see Parsing options for your data source . Rates are only part of the total cost of ownership. On a customer-managed knowledge base, your team provisions, scales, and operates each stage as a separate resource. A Managed Knowledge Base consolidates them into one resource, with a default embedding model, foundation model, and reranker, and with per-knowledge-base rate limits by default. You manage the content and the application that uses it, and Amazon Bedrock operates the managed storage, embedding model, foundation model, and reranker. A customer-managed knowledge base uses the VECTOR type, with a vector store you configure. A Managed Knowledge Base uses the MANAGED type. The migration guide directs your agent to create a new MANAGED knowledge base alongside the original without modifying or deleting the original during migration. Using the guide’s map, your agent writes a plan that lists which settings remain unchanged, which Managed handles differently, and which application changes you need to make. As Figure 1 shows, the original keeps serving every request while your team ingests content, validates, and cuts over. Figure 1: Create a managed knowledge base or migrated template alongside the original, then validate before cutover The guide separates planning from implementation. In Explore mode, your agent answers questions about Managed Knowledge Base and can inspect your configuration with read-only calls, so you can estimate the effort. In Migration mode, the guide takes your agent through checkpoints: As Figure 2 shows, resource creation stays separate from ingestion and cutover. Figure 2: Migration checkpoints. Implementation is optional, and your team runs ingestion and cutover The guide maps each setting to preserve your data sources, filters, and chunking behavior when the managed type uses a different configuration. The plan classifies each setting: Compare chunking on your own content when you validate. Discovery, planning, and the entire IaC path need only read-only credentials. For a live build, the guide directs your agent to propose a scoped policy that explicitly denies changes to the original knowledge base, and to never ask for administrator or full-access permissions. It also directs your agent to change only resources it created, reference secrets by Amazon Resource Name (ARN), and ignore instructions found in the data it reads. Review the generated AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policy and provisioning script before you approve the run. After the build, check what the agent did in AWS CloudTrail event history , which keeps 90 days of management events. Each event records the API call, such as CreateKnowledgeBase , and the identity that made it. For the optional cost analysis, your agent compares current spend with a Managed Knowledge Base estimate using current AWS prices. It uses read-only inputs, including Amazon CloudWatch metrics, Amazon S3 object sizes, and AWS Cost Explorer. Each figure is labeled as measured, supplied by you, or estimated. Use separate credentials for planning and for any approved resource creation. The Agent Toolkit for AWS works with compatible development environments and its repository on GitHub lists the available skills. Examples in this post use AWS CLI 2.37 and boto3 1.43.32. Follow the Agent Toolkit for AWS getting-started instructions for your coding agent. The add-skill command installs the amazon-bedrock skill to the coding agents it detects. Add --agent to target one, for example --agent kiro . After installation, your agent loads the migration guide when you describe a migration task. The following prompts are illustrative inputs, not transcripts. Choose the path that matches how you maintain the source. To start in Explore mode, ask a question: When you’re ready, choose the live or IaC path.

title: Build composable, interoperable multi-agent systems with A2A on AWS
abstract: Agents in multi-agent systems that span organizational boundaries often need to collaborate in a composable, interoperable way, with agents that other organizations build and run. They need a way to discover each other, communicate, and exchange tasks without exposing internals or requiring the same framework on both sides. The Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol addresses this constraint. Without A2A, building composable multi-agent systems across organizational boundaries requires custom integration code for each customer and framework. Independent software vendors (ISVs) can instead build composable, interoperable agents that work with the A2A-compatible frameworks their customers already use. While we frame this post around the ISV use case, the pattern also applies to organizations that expose agents across boundaries, whether to partners, customers, or internal teams that use different frameworks. As your system grows, you add skills by registering Agent Cards with the orchestrator, without changing the agents already running. In this post, we walk through a deployed reference architecture on AWS. A LangChain-based enterprise orchestrator communicates with a Strands Agents-based software as a service (SaaS) agent across organizational boundaries using A2A, with the enterprise and the SaaS provider in separate AWS accounts. Neither side depends on the other’s framework or SDK, and the two sides share no secrets. We cover the architecture and implementation patterns, then deploy the system from three Jupyter notebooks and run an end-to-end test. The A2A protocol is now a Linux Foundation project , and AWS is among the organizations that support it. With A2A, agents can discover each other, negotiate tasks, and collaborate across organizational boundaries through a standardized protocol. The protocol uses existing authentication standards such as OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect (OIDC) for cross-boundary security, and is designed to work across A2A-compatible frameworks. In Open Protocols for Agent Interoperability Part 4: Inter-Agent Communication on A2A , we introduced A2A concepts and demonstrated two Strands agents communicating using the protocol on AWS. That post established the foundation with Agent Card discovery, structured task execution, and the A2A server pattern. This post builds on that foundation with cross-framework interoperability, cross-organizational trust boundaries, and OAuth in both directions. Three agents run in two AWS accounts, one for the enterprise and one for the SaaS provider. The A2A protocol connects them, with OAuth authentication in both directions. Each account has its own Amazon Cognito user pool, so each side authenticates with its own identity provider. Figure 1: A2A agents across an enterprise account and a SaaS provider account During onboarding, the enterprise and the SaaS provider exchange only public values, such as identity provider URLs, client IDs, scopes, and endpoint URLs. Each side then trusts tokens from the other side’s user pool, and no secrets are shared. After onboarding, each request follows these steps: On the enterprise side, two agents run on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) with AWS Fargate . The Enterprise Orchestrator is the entry point for users. LangChain provides the agent framework and tool-calling abstractions, and Amazon Bedrock provides the foundation models (FMs) that power each agent’s reasoning. The orchestrator uses LangChain and Amazon Bedrock (Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6). At startup, the orchestrator fetches the SaaS agent’s Agent Card from its well-known URL and creates a LangChain tool for each skill described on the card. The model then decides which tool to call based on the user’s question, so the orchestrator needs no hardcoded routing logic. It sends compliance scan requests over A2A with OAuth bearer tokens and summarizes the results for leadership. Users reach the orchestrator through an Amazon API Gateway HTTPS endpoint that accepts only tokens from the enterprise’s own pool. The second enterprise agent provides internal context. The Enterprise Context Agent is built with LangChain and Amazon Bedrock (Amazon Nova Lite). It provides internal account metadata such as internal policy rules, data classification, business criticality, and escalation contacts (team on-call rotations). The deployed agent uses the official a2a-sdk (AgentCard, AgentExecutor, and spec-conformant JSON-RPC routes), pinned to a2a-sdk[http-server]==1.2.2. The SaaS agent reaches the context agent through an API Gateway partner API that accepts only the SaaS provider’s callback token. Both enterprise agents run in private subnets of an Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC), with no public IP addresses. On the SaaS provider side, the Compliance SaaS Agent runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore in the SaaS provider’s own AWS account. Built with the Strands Agents SDK , it checks AWS accounts against the enterprise’s own internal policies, such as no public storage in production and encryption at rest for confidential data. In production, the scanning tools would connect to services such as AWS Config , AWS Security Hub , or Amazon GuardDuty . For this demo, the agent uses synthetic data that simulates compliance findings across multiple accounts. Before it scans, the SaaS agent calls back to the Enterprise Context Agent for enterprise context, such as which accounts are production, which internal policies apply, and who to escalate to. This bidirectional pattern makes the agents true peers instead of a client and a server. The callback goes only to the address the customer registered at onboarding. The key design decision is to use A2A for all cross-boundary communication. The enterprise has no access to the SaaS agent’s internal tools, system prompt, or model choice. This separation means the ISV can change its internal architecture without changing customer integrations, as long as its Agent Card and A2A interface stay compatible. The SaaS card publishes one curated skill, not its internal tool names. Amazon Bedrock provides API access to multiple foundation models, so each agent can use the model that fits its workload. In this solution, the orchestrator and SaaS agent use Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6 for complex reasoning, while the context agent uses Amazon Nova Lite for metadata lookups. You can choose different models based on your own requirements. A2A and the Model Context Protocol (MCP) solve different problems in this architecture. MCP connects an agent to its own tools and data sources in a client-server model. A2A connects agents to other agents as peers, where neither side exposes its internals. In production, the SaaS agent could use MCP internally to connect to its compliance scanning tools while exposing itself externally through A2A. The external interface stays the same regardless of how the agent connects to its internal tools. The notebooks contain the complete deployment procedure. Before you run them, you need the following: Notebook 3 also runs the end-to-end test described later in this post, so you can verify the deployment. Running this solution incurs charges for the resources it creates. In the enterprise account, the main always-on resources are a NAT gateway, two AWS Fargate tasks, the internal Network Load Balancer, and two interface VPC endpoints. Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore charge for what you use. Prices vary by AWS Region. See the pricing pages for Amazon VPC , AWS Fargate , Amazon Bedrock , Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , and Elastic Load Balancing . Run the Clean up sections when you finish. Deploy the system with three notebooks, run in order with Jupyter, one cell at a time. Notebook 1 (enterprise account, about 3 minutes) creates the enterprise identity and writes an onboarding request. Notebook 2 (SaaS provider account, about 5 minutes) deploys the compliance agent and writes an onboarding response.

title: Fine-grained access control for Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base tools
abstract: More enterprises are building AI agents into their daily work, and a common pattern is an agent that searches internal documents to compose its answers. A single organization might soon run hundreds of agents, each connected to many data sources and tools. This raises a question. When an agent searches on behalf of a user, can you make sure that it uses only the information that user is allowed to see? Consider AnyCompany, a fictional company that builds an internal assistant shared by all employees. An employee in department A asks, “Compare my department’s business plan with the notice to all departments, and list the initiatives that are behind schedule.” The agent writes its own search queries and keeps searching internal documents until it has enough information. Employees in department B ask the same assistant the same question. If the application doesn’t scope searches to each user, the department B business plan can end up in an answer to an employee in department A. If you replace the departments with customer companies, the same problem occurs in a multi-tenant software as a service (SaaS) architecture where multiple customers share one assistant and knowledge base. Controlling access to multi-tenant data through this agent is harder than in traditional applications. In a traditional application, the application code determines who the signed-in user is and searches with that user’s permissions. In an agent, a large language model (LLM) decides at runtime which tool to call and with which arguments. If a search tool takes “who to search as” as an argument, the LLM decides that value too. A prompt injection or an LLM error might then make the agent search as a different employee. In this post, we build an internal assistant for AnyCompany. All employees share the same agent and knowledge base, yet each employee can search only the documents they’re allowed to view. We use Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base as the search backend and expose it to the agent as Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The design principle is to not let the LLM decide who the user is. Instead, trusted code decides, based on information that your identity provider has verified. On top of that, we add independent layers of defense in case that mechanism has a bug or is bypassed. Managed Knowledge Base has a feature called ACL awareness . When a search request includes a user context ( userContext ) with the user’s email in userId , the knowledge base returns only the documents that user is allowed to view. If your application calls the search API directly, the application code sets the search scope from the authentication result. Build multi-tenant agentic chat applications on enterprise data with Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base shows this pattern. When you expose the knowledge base as an MCP tool through AgentCore Gateway, however, userContext becomes a tool argument, and the LLM constructs its value. Neither the gateway nor the knowledge base verifies that this value belongs to the authenticated user. This solution injects verified user attributes into tool calls at the tool layer (AgentCore Gateway). It then scopes the search by those attributes at the resource layer (Managed Knowledge Base). The sample stores three documents in a single knowledge base: business plans for department A and department B, and a notice shared with all departments. Two users, user-a in department A and user-b in department B, search through the same agent. The following diagram shows the architecture. Figure 1: Solution architecture The request flow is as follows. The step numbers correspond to the numbers in Figure 1. Figure 1 omits the call from the web app to AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, so its step numbers differ from the diagram in the repository README . The four mechanisms map to layers and lines of defense as follows. For requests that go through the gateway, the two primary defenses are enough to achieve fine-grained access control, as long as no other principal can call the knowledge base. ACL awareness filters results based on the userContext that it receives and isn’t an authorization mechanism by itself . The two secondary defenses cover cases where an assumption behind the primary defenses fails, such as an interceptor bug or a principal that calls the knowledge base without going through the gateway. Add them based on your requirements. If other principals in the account have bedrock:Retrieve permissions, add the resource-based policy. The rest of this post covers ACL awareness, the MCP tools for Managed Knowledge Base, the request interceptor, Policy in AgentCore, and the resource-based policy, in that order. You can deploy the architecture in Figure 1 with a single AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) stack from the agentcore-access-control directory of the sample-managed-knowledge-base-patterns repository. Run the commands in this post from that directory. The repository installs the AWS CDK CLI and aws-cdk-lib (2.274.0 or later) as npm dependencies. The stack also deploys a web app on Amazon CloudFront and runs the agent, built with Strands Agents, on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime. By default, the agent uses Claude Sonnet 5.5 through the global cross-Region inference profile global.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5-5 . The agent forwards the access token of the signed-in user to the gateway and contains no access control logic. For deployment steps, including how to fetch only this directory, see the README . Managed Knowledge Base is a new type of Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base. You connect a data source, and it runs parsing, chunking, embedding, indexing, search, and reranking as a fully managed service. It provides two search APIs. Retrieve runs a hybrid search. AgenticRetrieveStream breaks a query into subqueries and searches multiple knowledge bases iteratively. ACL awareness keeps the access permissions of the data source at ingestion time. At search time, it returns only the documents that the user can view. For an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) data source, you define ACLs either in a global ACL file per S3 prefix or in a metadata file per document. The sample in this post uses metadata files. When you place the following metadata file at the same S3 path as the document, only user-a can retrieve dept-a-plan.txt . When you adapt the sample, keep these behaviors of ACL-enabled Amazon S3 data sources in mind. A document without an ACL entry isn’t ingested. A change to the global ACL file requires reindexing the affected prefix, while per-document metadata files reindex only the affected documents and take precedence over the global file. Amazon S3 has no real-time ACL verification, so an ACL change applies after the next sync. ACL mistakes don’t return errors. The affected documents are silently left out of the results. At query time, pass the user’s email in the top-level userContext.userId for both Retrieve and AgenticRetrieveStream . Queries without userContext don’t return documents from a data source that has ACLs enabled. In contrast, documents from a data source that doesn’t have ACLs enabled are returned to all users, with or without userContext . The following diagram shows the ACLs that the knowledge base keeps for the three sample documents at ingestion, and the search results for each userContext . Figure 2: Scoping searches with ACL awareness Managed Knowledge Base doesn’t authenticate end users. It trusts the userContext that it receives and filters results based on it. Passing a verified userContext is the responsibility of the caller . When you create a Managed Knowledge Base connector target on AgentCore Gateway, you can expose two MCP tools: <target-name>___Retrieve and <target-name>___AgenticRetrieveStream . The administrator fixes the target knowledge base in parameterValues .

title: From prototype to production: Engineering agents with Agent DLC
abstract: Over the past year, AI agents have moved from exploration into engineering. Enterprise teams are shipping large language model (LLM) systems that call tools, orchestrate APIs, and answer questions over internal knowledge. A successful demo can show what an agent is capable of. Before release, the team needs to answer a further question: “ Is this agent ready for production? ” The person responsible for that decision needs evidence that the agent meets the agreed requirements. To make that decision consistently, teams need a repeatable, affordable way to assess the agent’s current behavior and whether the latest change has improved it. In traditional software development, teams answer these questions with unit tests, continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD), and passing builds. Those mechanisms are necessary but not sufficient for agents, for three reasons, each requiring additional checks. This post explains these three properties and presents a measured case where an aggregate metric hides a coverage problem. It then introduces the Agent Development Lifecycle (Agent DLC): one lifecycle, two loops, and a single explicit standard for judging every change. A note on terminology: Throughout this post, gold standard means one specific artifact: the bundle of verifiable criteria, their thresholds, and the approved examples they are checked against. Business owners approve this standard as the basis for acceptance decisions. Conventional software testing and CI/CD still apply to agents, but three properties require additional checks. First, agents are non-deterministic: identical inputs can produce different outputs and execution paths. Second, changes to prompts, tool descriptions, retrieval settings, or memory configuration can alter behavior in ways that a text review alone can’t reveal. Third, model endpoints, knowledge bases, and external APIs can change independently of the repository and affect agent behavior. Table 1 summarizes the engineering practices needed to address each property. Table 1. What each property invalidates, and what it requires instead. The following example shows how the choice of metrics affects diagnosis. We built a reference implementation to exercise the method end to end: an internal policy assistant answering HR policy questions over a document knowledge base. We chose a narrow, well-scoped domain to make the evaluation and diagnosis straightforward to follow. The following results were measured on this reference implementation. It isn’t a customer outcome and it isn’t a benchmark result. The accompanying AWS Samples repository includes infrastructure deployment, the HR agent, custom evaluators, and scripts for baseline evaluation and prompt-change re-evaluation ( 09-run-eval.sh and 10-optimize-prompt.sh ). It also includes optional checks for judge repeatability, model comparison, cost, and latency. The scripts reproduce the workflow. Scores can vary across runs and repository versions. Three golden questions, five measures each: Table 2. First evaluation round. Measured on the reference implementation. Not a customer outcome. Chunk-level precision is 1.00 for all three questions. A release gate based only on this metric would accept all three answers. Fact-level precision tells a different story: 0.59, 0.53, 0.09. For the third question, roughly nine out of ten facts in the retrieved material are irrelevant to what was asked. Chunk-level precision only asks whether a passage is on topic. It doesn’t measure how much of the passage is relevant. Then we changed exactly one thing: the system prompt. We added three constraints: ground strictly in retrieved content, ignore irrelevant retrieved content, and keep answers focused. The agent, the knowledge base, the evaluators, and the questions were untouched, so the before-and-after differs by one variable. Table 3. After a prompt-only change. One change, two opposite outcomes. The first question improved substantially. The third got worse. The evaluation suggested where to investigate before we made the change. Look at the third row of Table 2 again: chunk-level precision 1.00, fact-level precision 0.09, retrieval coverage 0.00. Together, these scores suggested a knowledge-coverage problem: the retrieved material was nominally on topic but didn’t answer the question. Telling the model to “ground strictly in retrieved content” couldn’t supply the missing information. We checked that diagnosis against the source documents used in the experiment. The corpus lacked a dedicated sick-leave policy document, although the leave-management policy contained brief references to sick leave. The next step was to address policy coverage and then check retrieval, rather than keep changing the prompt. In this case, the source material lacks the information needed to answer the question, so prompt changes alone can’t resolve the failure. In this example, evaluation helped identify what needed investigation before further changes. Another result shows why groundedness needs to be checked alongside other criteria. The benefits-enrollment answer passed with groundedness 0.90, and it contained this sentence: “I also noticed from your profile that your preferred contact method is Social Media.” No such profile exists. The policy document lists contact preference as an option inside a process step. The public, crowd-sourced, noisy FAQ corpus contains a pair answering that question with “social media”. The model combined a policy option with an unrelated FAQ answer and presented it as a fact about the user. The high groundedness score didn’t catch this false personal claim. Passing a quality threshold doesn’t establish that responsibility constraints have been met. These scores can vary between runs, and a borderline Pass can become a Fail. Interpret score differences alongside repeated runs and the underlying evidence. Section 5 discusses how to check evaluator reliability. This small reference-implementation example illustrates how evaluation can guide diagnosis. It doesn’t establish a general improvement rate or validate a production release. Agent DLC connects six activities around one explicit gold standard: Define , Build , Evaluate , Release , Observe , and Feed Back . Evaluation-driven development has been described in earlier work, including Xia et al.’s Evaluation-Driven Development of LLM Agents: A Process Model and Reference Architecture . Agent DLC applies this approach to delivery through six activities with explicit acceptance conditions, release authority, and evidence requirements. The acceptance-first approach also appears in Fotor’s published AWS customer case study . The team defined scalability, cost, isolation, and architectural flexibility criteria before migrating to AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, then validated changes against operating data. The case reports workflow overhead falling from minutes to seconds, excluding model inference, and support for thousands of concurrent active sessions. It documents Agent DLC-guided architecture delivery. Quality evaluation is identified as the next step. Define translates business objectives into criteria, thresholds, and approved examples. Build designs the prompts, tools, context, memory, and runtime mechanisms that must satisfy them. Evaluate produces the evidence that says whether a candidate version does. When it does, the version goes to a controlled release. Observe watches it in production. Feed Back returns what production teaches to Define. Figure 1: The six activities of Agent DLC each relate to the gold standard at the center. Define produces it, Build follows it, and Evaluate uses it. Release checks against it, Observe reuses it, and Feed Back iterates it. The five dimensions of the standard are listed beneath Figure 1 shows how each activity uses or updates the standard, making its role in development and release explicit.

title: Build autonomous AI agents with Amazon Bedrock and Spring AI
abstract: Java teams have established JVM tooling, continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipelines, and operational patterns, yet taking AI agents from prototype to production is hard: agent frameworks do not solve scalability, governance, security, and operational concerns by default. Amazon Bedrock and Spring AI close those gaps, so Java teams can build autonomous AI agents that plan, call tools and APIs, and maintain context across multi-turn conversations. Agentic AI is moving beyond prompt-response interactions toward autonomous systems that execute complex multi-step tasks. Java remains one of the widely used programming languages in enterprise software. Teams have existing CI/CD pipelines, operational expertise, and established patterns built around the JVM. Spring AI brings AI capabilities to the JVM through familiar Spring patterns: auto-configuration, dependency injection, and composable advisors. Developers can build AI agents using the same idioms they use for REST APIs, security, and data access. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. With AgentCore, you can build, deploy, and operate AI agents at scale. It is framework-agnostic and model-agnostic: you bring your preferred agent framework and foundation model (FM). With AgentCore, you can access the production infrastructure you need: managed runtime, memory, browser automation, code execution, and identity management. In this post, we show you how to build autonomous AI agents in Java using Spring AI and Amazon Bedrock with spring-ai-agentcore . We explore the key implementation patterns for two systems. The first is a single-agent travel assistant that demonstrates tool calling and memory. The second is a multi-agent intelligent document processing (IDP) system that shows how specialist agents, a rules engine, and alerting work together. To follow along with this walkthrough, you need the following: A chat completion call can generate text, but it can’t decide what to do next, reach into external systems, or remember what happened yesterday. An agent can, because it unites three capabilities: A Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) application has limited tool use (retrieval) but no planning loop. An agent has all three, operating in a goal-directed loop until the task is complete or it determines it cannot proceed. The following diagram shows these capabilities in an end-to-end agentic pipeline, from request to grounded answer. Figure 1: Agentic reference architecture. A request flows through the runtime, guardrails, classification, a specialist agent, tools, the foundation model, memory, rules, and human review to a grounded answer, with resilience and observability as cross-cutting concerns The pipeline has 11 stages. A client submits a document and question. The request passes through a runtime gateway for authentication and rate limiting, then input guardrails screen for harmful content. A router classifies the document and routes it to a specialist agent, which plans its workflow and calls tools, the Amazon Bedrock foundation model, memory, and a rules engine as needed. Low-confidence or flagged results go to a human review queue before the grounded answer returns to the client. Resilience, observability, logging, and least-privilege AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) apply across all stages. The solution consists of two deployable systems that share common patterns: Both systems share the following architecture: The travel assistant is the recommended starting point. The following diagram illustrates how a Spring Boot agent interacts with AgentCore runtime, tools, memory, and models available on Amazon Bedrock. Figure 2: Single-agent travel assistant. The Spring Boot application exposes both REST endpoints for the React UI and the AgentCore runtime contract, calling Amazon Bedrock through the Converse API while tool calling, streaming, and memory run inside one code base. The travel assistant runs a single Spring Boot application with two entry points, the /invocations and /ping contract required by AgentCore runtime. Spring AI orchestrates calls to Amazon Bedrock through the Converse API and resolves tool invocations locally inside the same process. Server-Sent Events stream tokens to the client as they are generated. AgentCore memory supplies both short-term context within a session and long-term context across sessions, so the agent retains conversation history without external state management. The following diagram shows the architecture for the IDP multi-agent system. Figure 3: IDP multi-agent system architecture. Specialist agents process documents through a shared ChatClient pattern, with results flowing through a rules engine and alert service. The IDP multi-agent system routes documents through five specialist agents (Lawyer, Mortgage, Insurance, Tax, and General), each built on a shared AbstractDocumentAgent template. A ClassifierAgent reads each document and forwards it to the appropriate specialist. The specialist extracts structured JSON with confidence scores using the multimodal Converse API of Amazon Bedrock. A rules engine evaluates Spring Expression Language (SpEL) expressions from application.yml against the extraction. ALERT or BLOCK severity rules dispatch through the AlertService . Low-confidence documents go to human review. Metrics, audit trail, resilience, and observability apply across all stages. When multiple agents work together, how they coordinate determines system behavior. This solution uses three patterns: The following diagram compares the three coordination patterns used in this solution. Figure 4: Agent collaboration patterns Three patterns shown side by side. The router dispatches each request to one specialist by document type. The evaluator passes specialist findings through a rules engine that applies to severity levels and dispatches alerts or blocks for human review. The parallel fan-out sends one request to multiple specialists concurrently and aggregates results before the rules engine runs. Router pattern: A lightweight orchestrator examines the incoming request and routes it to the appropriate specialist. In the IDP multi-agent system, the router inspects document type metadata and forwards it to the Lawyer, Mortgage, Insurance, Tax, or General agent. The router holds no domain logic. It is a dispatch layer only. Parallel fan-out (optional extension): The base solution implements the router and evaluator patterns. The batch endpoint processes documents sequentially. When a document needs several perspectives at once, you can add a parallel fan-out as a drop-in extension. Dispatch to specialists concurrently and aggregate their results before the rules engine runs. Wall-clock time for the combined analysis is then bounded by the slowest single agent call rather than the sum of all calls. Evaluator pattern: After specialists return their findings, a rules engine evaluates the combined output against configurable business rules. Rules that trigger ALERT or BLOCK severity dispatch through a pluggable AlertService for human review. The following sections walk you through the key implementation patterns, starting with the AgentCore runtime contract and progressing through tool calling, memory, resilience, and multi-agent orchestration. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime manages agent lifecycle and scaling. For current rates, see Amazon Bedrock AgentCore pricing and Amazon Bedrock pricing. The runtime routes incoming requests to your agent and monitors its health. Your agent must expose two endpoints: The following diagram shows how the Spring AI developer model maps onto AgentCore runtime, Memory, Browser, Code Interpreter, and Evaluations. Figure 5: Spring AI AgentCore SDK on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.

title: OpenAI Codex on Amazon Bedrock
abstract: Developers increasingly use Codex with Amazon Bedrock to explore unfamiliar code, make changes, and handle repetitive engineering work. For platform teams, the challenge is to make those tools available without creating a second model-access, identity, and operations stack. Codex can use Amazon Bedrock for inference with supported OpenAI models. In this post, we show how to fit that path into the AWS identity, AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), Regional, and observability practices your organization already uses. Codex still runs on the developer workstation. The main design choice is how its model requests reach Amazon Bedrock and where your organization applies policy and operational controls. We begin with a small, least-privilege pilot and work through the checks that matter before access expands. The examples use GPT-5.6 Sol. Before starting the pilot, review Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock to confirm that Sol, Terra, or Luna is available in the AWS Region and inference path you plan to use. Recommended default: Start with Native AWS Access for a small, least-privilege pilot. Choose AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, when you want AWS managed gateway infrastructure for routing or Amazon Bedrock Guardrails. Choose an LLM Gateway when a platform team wants to enforce controls in the request path. A custom integration is the advanced version of the LLM Gateway pattern, not a quick start. The examples come from the open source Guidance for Codex on AWS repository. It includes quick starts for Native AWS Access, AgentCore Gateway, LiteLLM on ECS, Portkey, the AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry (ADOT), and the Amazon CloudWatch setup used later in the post. Choose the quick start that matches your architecture, use it for the pilot, and adapt it to your environment. Authentication is only one part of an enterprise rollout. Decide who can use the service and which models and Regions are approved. Also define where configuration lives, what telemetry to collect, how usage is allocated, and which skills or Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers are allowed. The following table maps those needs to an access path and an owning team. Choose the access path that provides the controls you need now. The most straightforward path that meets the requirement usually has the lowest operational overhead. The following diagram compares where identity, routing, policy, telemetry, and operational ownership sit across the three rollout paths. Figure 1: Codex runs on the developer workstation in each scenario. Native AWS Access uses AWS IAM Identity Center, a configured AgentCore Gateway can apply managed routing and Guardrails, and a configured LLM Gateway can apply request-path controls If Native AWS Access fits the pilot, the repository’s Native AWS Access quick start provides the complete procedure and supporting files. The following abbreviated walkthrough focuses on the sequence and the checks that matter most. Employees continue to sign in through the identity provider they already use. In this example, Okta handles authentication through Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) and provisions users and groups into IAM Identity Center through System for Cross-domain Identity Management (SCIM). IAM Identity Center then issues the temporary AWS credentials used by Codex. The identity provider is not configured in Codex. The pilot has three checks. First, sign in using the IAM Identity Center profile configured for the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) and call Amazon Bedrock Runtime directly. Next, point Codex to the approved model. Finally, run a safe Codex task. The direct call isolates AWS access problems. The final step confirms the Codex configuration. Step 1: Sign in and validate Amazon Bedrock Runtime access. This command creates a short-lived AWS session and checks whether the profile can invoke the chosen model in the chosen Region. If it fails, resolve the profile, Region, model or inference-profile access, or IAM permissions before configuring Codex. Step 2: Configure the Codex provider. The model value is the Codex model ID. The profile selects the AWS IAM Identity Center session, and region tells Codex which AWS Region to use. Keep these settings in user-level or managed configuration so a repository cannot change the provider. Before adding users, make sure the pilot reaches the approved model, produces the expected records, and can be disabled cleanly. The walkthrough shows the complete pilot sequence: workforce sign-in, direct Amazon Bedrock Runtime validation, Codex provider configuration, and a safe test task. Figure 2: Native AWS Access walkthrough covering workforce sign-in, Amazon Bedrock Runtime validation, Codex provider configuration, and a safe pilot task Use the video to verify the order of the checks and the evidence to collect before adding more pilot users. Two users are required to test identity isolation. A single user shows that sign-in works. A second user tests whether attribution remains distinct. Have two pilot users sign in separately and run the same harmless task. Their assumed-role sessions and audit records, and telemetry records if configured, should remain distinct. The following diagram shows how separate pilot identities should produce separate AWS sessions, request evidence, and optional telemetry while using the same approved Codex and Amazon Bedrock path. Figure 3: Use trusted identity enrollment for attribution. A local collector can add approved identity context only when it is deployed and configured as part of a managed enrollment process AgentCore Gateway is an option when you want AWS managed gateway infrastructure for centralized routing or Amazon Bedrock Guardrails. If your organization already runs an LLM Gateway or wants to enforce controls in the request path, use that gateway instead. Validate the selected gateway before exposing it to pilot users. A custom enterprise integration is the most involved form of the LLM Gateway pattern. Consider it only when Native AWS Access, AgentCore Gateway, and an existing gateway cannot meet a specific requirement. The result is another service to design, secure, test, support, and operate, so platform engineering and security need to own it from the start. Codex OpenTelemetry, Amazon Bedrock service records, AWS identity records, and billing data answer different questions. Codex OpenTelemetry describes client activity. Amazon Bedrock service metrics and model invocation logs show service-side activity when enabled. AWS identity records and the AWS Cost and Usage Report (CUR) provide identity and billed-usage evidence. Correlate them for the path you deploy, and do not present token volume as a cost report. Define what code, prompts, files, and tool output Codex might send through the selected model path. Exclude secrets and restricted data unless the organization has approved that data flow. Require developers to review and test generated changes before merge. Telemetry does not establish correctness or safety. For observability, this post uses the ADOT collector configuration and CloudWatch dashboard from the repository’s monitoring and operations guidance . Deploy that configuration to each managed pilot device, then run a safe Codex task. The repository provides the configuration files. Follow its deployment instructions to install the approved ADOT collector and configure its AWS authentication. Validate the repository path: run a safe Codex task and confirm that the expected operational metrics appear on the managed CloudWatch dashboard. The Amazon CloudWatch Coding Agent Insights managed dashboard in the Guidance for Codex on AWS repository shows Codex operational metrics collected through ADOT. Use it to understand client activity, and use AWS identity, audit, and billing records separately when you need attribution or cost evidence.

title: Semantic diffing of formal policies with anti-unification
abstract: When reviewing code, you start with a diff. You wouldn’t compare two 3,000-line files by eye and hope to spot every change. Formal policies can be even harder to compare because a textual diff often highlights syntactic changes that don’t affect meaning. Reorder two conjuncts, swap the arguments of an equality, or use an equivalent predicate, and much of the file might appear changed. A real change in behavior, such as an Or where the requirement says and , can get lost in that noise. A semantic diff shows what two policies have in common and where they disagree. The open source engine used in this post computes this diff using anti-unification , which finds a most specific common pattern for two expressions. Plotkin’s 1970 paper gives the classical formulation. The engine works over an e-graph, which keeps track of expressions known to be equal. We supply the algebraic laws and domain rules that justify those equalities, such as equating an external destination with one that isn’t internal. The result shows the shared parts once and keeps both versions of each differing part for review. If no differences remain, the policies are equivalent under those laws and rules. When the rules or the search are incomplete, a remaining difference might reflect an equivalence the engine has not found. One use case is autoformalization. Autoformalization translates natural language into a formal language. Suppose you want to turn requirements into SMT-LIB , the standard input language for satisfiability modulo theories (SMT) solvers such as Z3 and cvc5, or into Cedar or Dogwood to control authorization in your software system. A large language model (LLM) generates the formal artifact from the prose. The model writes the artifact. It plays no part in computing the diff. Run the model twice, and it might produce two different formalizations, with no ground truth to identify the correct one. A semantic diff shows where they agree and where they differ. Generate more candidates by varying the model, prompt, or sampling temperature. Comparing them shows which parts stay the same and which vary. Review the varying parts first. Requirements can also become OpenShell sandbox policies or Common Expression Language (CEL) expressions. OpenShell uses YAML to describe an agent’s filesystem and network access. CEL is embedded in applications to evaluate expressions, including policy conditions. These languages and formats differ in what they express, but translations into any of them can disagree about a condition, a scope, or an event. The following table gives illustrative disagreements: In each worked example, we compare translations of the same requirement within one policy context. We encode the relevant syntax as terms and declare the equalities used in the comparison. The engine reads these encodings. It doesn’t import native policies from the four formats. The idea is a formal-methods analogue of semantic entropy , described by Farquhar et al. in Nature (2024). That approach samples several natural-language answers, clusters those that entail one another, and reports a single number. For formal outputs, anti-unification preserves more information. It identifies the shared structure and each divergence instead of returning only a score. Counterexamples help explain the consequences of a disagreement. An SMT solver can find a concrete assignment that satisfies one formula and violates the other. A reviewer can then trace that assignment through the formulas to understand the conflicting decisions. The anti-unifier gives a different view: it organizes the shared structure and the fragments that differ, without issuing an SMT query. A solver or policy validator can help resolve those fragments. We assume you can read S-expression syntax, as in SMT-LIB, and know what an authorization policy is. E-graphs and anti-unification are explained as they come up. When several translations agree on part of a requirement, the diff shows that part once. Where they disagree, it keeps the alternatives visible for review. Say a policy-generation pipeline hands you two candidate rules for this requirement: sensitive data sent to an external destination must be encrypted . sensitive ( data ) ∧ external ( dst ) → encrypted ¬ internal ( dst ) ∧ sensitive ( data ) → audited Whether these are the same rule isn’t obvious. The conditions are reordered, external is expressed indirectly as not internal , and the conclusions do not match. The engine computes a most specific anti-unifier for these terms. In its input language, the two rules are S-expressions. The complete program first declares the vocabulary: It then adds one function line for each predicate ( sensitive , external , internal ) and constant ( data , dst , encrypted , audited ). Here, And is declared associative, commutative, and idempotent, as the next section explains: The engine answers with a single term: The reordering doesn’t appear in the result because And is declared associative, commutative, and idempotent. Two Variants nodes remain, each marking a place where the inputs disagree, and only one of them is a difference in meaning. The difference between (external dst) and (Not (internal dst)) is a difference in vocabulary. Both express the same domain fact. The engine can’t infer that from syntax alone. State the domain fact as a rewrite , run it to saturation (until no rule adds a new equality), and diff again: After saturation, the engine answers: One Variants node remains: Rule B audits where the requirement demands encryption. A textbook presentation would put a fresh variable at that spot. The engine instead writes (Variants encrypted audited) : a node that holds both readings . Select the first child of every Variants node and you reconstruct rule A, up to the declared algebra and rewrites. Select the second child and you get rule B. The anti-unifier is a lossless merge of both terms: Shared structure appears once, and every genuine disagreement is a localized, reviewable node. Three fields describe the result: :size , :cr , and :completion . The :size field counts the concrete nodes (a Variants marker itself isn’t counted, but both of its children are, so structure can’t hide inside one). The :cr field reports the compression ratio (s - a) / b , where s is the result size and a and b are the smaller and larger input sizes. For each input, we use its smallest known equivalent form in the current e-graph. A score of 0 means full agreement under the declared equalities. After the preceding rewrite, both inputs have seven nodes and the result has eight, giving (8 - 7) / 7 , or approximately 0.1429. Keeping both complete policies in a single Variants node would use fourteen nodes, giving (14 - 7) / 7 = 1 . This is the reference value for no sharing. A score of 1 is a reference value, not an upper bound. The search might use larger equivalent forms than the smallest known inputs. A result larger than their combined sizes therefore scores above 1. For example, if both smallest input forms have ten nodes and a result has twenty-three, the ratio is (23 - 10) / 10 = 1.3 . The :completion field reports exact when the search space was exhausted and budget when the default anytime search (a Monte Carlo search, described in the implementation section) reached its playout limit before exhausting the search space. A low :cr means the inputs share more structure under the declared equalities. It doesn’t establish correctness: two candidates can share the same mistake. An entropy score summarizes variation in one number. The full semantic diff also identifies where the candidates disagree and retains both alternatives in Variants nodes. A semantic diff ignores only the differences covered by the declared equalities. A plain syntactic anti-unifier would also have reported the reordering in this example. The next three sections show how to declare the algebra and add domain identities.

title: Detecting and recovering from silent data corruption on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod
abstract: Silent data corruption (SDC) happens when hardware, such as a GPU, returns a wrong but plausible number and raises no error. In distributed training, the wrong number can flow into the gradients and weights of every replica. Loss can still look normal for hours, and by the time a team notices an unexplained divergence or a weaker model, the compute is spent. It happens at scale: during a 54-day period of Llama 3 405B pre-training on up to 16K H100 GPUs, Meta attributed 6 of 419 unexpected job interruptions to silent data corruption, and those were only the cases that interrupted the job and were traced to SDC. Amazon SageMaker HyperPod already replaces nodes that report a fault: the health-monitoring agent watches for GPU errors, deep health checks stress-test nodes, and automatic node recovery swaps out bad hardware. SDC slips past all of these features, because the hardware never reports anything. Detection has to come from the training job itself. In this post, we add three checks to a PyTorch DistributedDataParallel (DDP) training loop to detect SDC. When a check fires, we map the suspect rank to its node, contain the corruption, and have SageMaker HyperPod replace the node. Each check covers a different place where a fault can land: We tested the checks with software-injected faults on a SageMaker HyperPod cluster with 4 ml.p5.48xlarge instances (32 NVIDIA H100 GPUs), and repeated every test on three instances, the minimum the checks need. The full code of this solution is available in the accompanying GitHub repository .
