title: How H6.ai builds AI-powered financial automation with Lakebase Postgres
abstract: Traditional accounts payable and invoice processing tools often force companies into a trade-off: moving quickly using AI automation and risk losing control, or maintaining tedious manual oversight. H6.ai was founded to solve this problem. H6.ai automates accounts payable on top of a company's existing ERP. It reads each invoice, matches it to a purchase order, assigns its lines to the right accounts and checks it against the company's own policies. Our approach combines AI-assisted understanding with approved, deterministic and auditable policy execution. Our challenge was finding a backend solution that could support frequent regression testing at scale. In this industry, no two customers look alike. Each has its own ERP, suppliers, purchase orders, chart of accounts and policies. Invoices range from a one-line service bill to documents with hundreds of lines. And the data keeps moving. At 10 AM an invoice matches an open purchase order with enough quantity left. By the afternoon that order may be partly consumed, amended or closed. Process the same invoice again and the answer changes, even though our code has not. That makes regression testing hard. When a result changes, we need to know whether our change caused it or the customer's data did. Our engineering team needed a scalable solution that could isolate our customers' data and allow us to investigate errors. After learning about the lakebase architecture which separates storage from compute, scales idle compute to zero, and enables branching, we selected it as the core system of record for our platform. Today, every H6.ai customer has a dedicated Lakebase Postgres database. It holds their whole financial context: purchase orders and suppliers synced from the ERP, the chart of accounts and dimensions, past transactions, and their H6 policies. A database per customer keeps each customer's data isolated. It also allows us to freeze snapshots. A Lakebase branch is a copy-on-write copy of a database at a point in time. Creating one copies no data: the branch shares storage with its parent and only stores what changes on it. When we find an invoice H6 handled incorrectly, we branch that customer's database and keep the branch as a snapshot. A purchase order that was open stays open in the snapshot, with the same remaining quantities and prices, even after the ERP closes it. The same holds for suppliers, accounts, dimensions, history and policy settings. We no longer try to recreate the conditions behind an issue. We keep them. Every box in the shaded band is a branch of the same customer database. The harness branches the live database once to take a snapshot and never writes to it. Everything a test writes stays on its own run branch and is deleted with it. Each test case in our harness pairs one invoice with one snapshot and the outcome we expect: which purchase order it should match, which accounts its lines belong to, and whether it should be held for review. A run has four steps: A test plan can mix cases from many customers, ERPs and invoice formats, each running against its own preserved database. Because every run starts from the same frozen state, the same test gives the same starting point today, next week and next quarter. We don't mock the database or the pipeline. Isolation does that job. Everything a test writes (review items, validation results, draft documents) lands on the run branch and is deleted with it. A test never posts to the customer's ERP, and the live database is never written to. This matters for a financial platform. We can test against copies of production customer data with the same code paths production uses, while the customer's books stay untouched. Branch management uses dedicated service principals with least-privilege access, and the branching guards refuse to touch a customer's live branch. Checking that an invoice was processed is not enough. An invoice can be read perfectly and still be matched to the wrong purchase order, assigned to the wrong account, or processed in breach of the customer's policies. So each run is judged two ways: Together they tell us whether the outcome was right, not only whether processing finished. That lets us try new models, improve extraction, cut cost and change our matching and policy engines, and spot a regression on a real customer case before it reaches production. We don't fix an issue and move on. We keep its database state as a snapshot, add the invoice and the expected outcome, and it becomes a permanent test case. As we onboard more customers, ERPs and invoice formats, test coverage grows with the complexity of the businesses we serve. Lakebase Postgres gives us four things we rely on: For H6.ai, Lakebase’s database branching isn't just an infrastructure convenience. It is how we build AI-powered financial automation that customers can trust. In the future, we look forward to leveraging Lakehouse//RT queries on Lakebase tables which will allow us to run read-only analytical queries on Lakebase without copying data. This will allow us to get fresh analytics without a pipeline. If you’d like to learn more about what we are building at H6.ai, visit our website . If you want to learn more about database branching with Lakebase Postgres, watch this video . A lakebase is a transactional database that keeps its data on the lake, for a modern, agentic app stack. Traditional databases run on single machines. A lakebase runs a stateless database engine and keeps data in durable cloud object storage, so compute can scale on its own and storage is used on demand. Lakebase Postgres is a fully-managed, serverless Postgres database integrated into the Databricks platform. Teams use it to build real-time transactional applications alongside their lakehouse data. It includes autoscaling, scale-to-zero, instant branching, read replicas, instant restore, high availability and native Unity Catalog integration. 3. Is Lakebase Postgres a good fit for AI use cases? Yes. Lakebase serves as the backend for agent memory and real-time feature serving. Agents can store conversation state and long-term memory in Postgres, and models can read low-latency feature data through online feature stores powered by Lakebase. Branching also makes it easier to test AI systems. H6.ai, for example, replays real invoice cases against frozen database snapshots to catch regressions when it changes models or logic. A Lakebase branch is an instant, isolated copy of a database, much like a Git branch for your data. It uses copy-on-write: a new branch shares storage with its parent, and only changed data is written separately. As a result, branches appear instantly no matter how large the database is, and creating one doesn't slow down production. Teams use branches for development, testing and schema changes. They can also create a new branch from any point in time within the history window. 5. Does Lakebase Postgres support multi-tenancy? Yes, in two ways. You can give each tenant its own database, as H6.ai does with a dedicated Lakebase Postgres database per customer to keep each customer's data isolated. Or you can keep tenants in shared tables and use PostgreSQL row-level security so users see only their own or their organization's data. Scale-to-zero suspends inactive compute, which keeps per-tenant databases cost-efficient. Subscribe to our blog and get the latest posts delivered to your inbox.

title: Lakehouse//RT: Scale real-time analytics, not your bill
abstract: AI agents are pushing the limits of data warehouses. A human analyst might run a few dozen queries in an afternoon. An agent can run hundreds per second, around the clock. And with growing demand for use cases like customer-facing dashboards that refresh in milliseconds and applications with embedded analytics, real-time workloads are quickly becoming a standard part of how businesses use data. Most data warehouses were designed for human-scale query volume, not the sustained concurrency agents generate. And even when a warehouse can deliver low latency, the bill grows as fast as demand: 10x the queries could easily mean 10x the cost. We built Lakehouse//RT not only to serve real-time workloads directly on the lakehouse , but to do so without growing your costs at the same rate as your queries. Most data warehouses scale capacity in step with demand: more queries, more compute, more cost. That works well for many analytics workloads, where query volume tracks the number of people asking questions. Real-time workloads are different. When AI agents and thousands of concurrent users all need answers in milliseconds, query volume can grow far faster than headcount, and cost grows with it. Real-time workloads are also often spiky. The usual way to handle that is to overprovision: add capacity in large blocks and keep it running so latency holds up at peak. You end up paying for idle compute most of the day. Lakehouse//RT flips the equation. Instead of scaling cost with demand, it scales efficiency. Its engine is architected to serve dramatically more queries on the same resources, so when demand doubles (or increases tenfold), your infrastructure keeps pace without a proportional spike in spend. Lakehouse//RT achieves this by taking a different approach in four areas: Organizations will not be able to outspend the demand curve. The only sustainable path is a system that does more per unit of compute. Concurrency is where real-time costs usually grow fastest. Traditional warehouses can only run so many queries at once; the rest wait in line or trigger more capacity. Serving hundreds of agents then means running several clusters just to keep response times steady. That's true even when most of those queries are small lookups that don't need the horsepower. Lakehouse//RT is designed to run far more queries side by side on each warehouse. In our launch blog we shared that we can deliver sub-100 millisecond latency at 12,000 queries per second, and we’re only getting better from here. Each query also finishes quickly, so capacity frees up sooner for the next one. The same peak fits on far less compute, and the agents still get answers in milliseconds. Customers are experiencing this on real-world workloads. Aurasell moved from several clusters at 200 queries per second to one small Lakehouse//RT warehouse sustaining more than 250 QPS, executing queries 4-5x faster while reducing costs by 10x. Keep reading for more customer success stories! Say you hire a contractor. One charges $20 an hour and takes 10 hours. Another charges $22 an hour and finishes in five. The first costs $200 and the second costs $110. You pay for the finished job, not the hour. Compute works the same way: your bill is rate times runtime. Lakehouse//RT is built to finish real-time queries fast, including the steps around execution like planning, routing, and returning results. Each query holds compute for less time. Across millions of agent queries a day, that adds up. Every warehouse eventually needs more capacity as traffic grows. What matters is the size of each step. Traditional warehouses typically scale by spinning up whole copies of themselves. On a Large warehouse, that's another Large warehouse spinning up. While cluster-level scaling works well for steady analytics workloads, real-time demand is spikier. When a burst needs only a fraction of a cluster, adding a whole cluster means paying for capacity you don't use until the burst passes. Lakehouse//RT can flexibly add capacity, even one node at a time, whatever t-shirt size you select. Real-time demand rarely arrives in cluster-sized blocks. A spike in agent traffic might need 10% more capacity, not 100%, and Lakehouse//RT can add a step that size instead of doubling. Scaling in small steps without hurting latency is easier said than done. It's what Lakehouse//RT was designed for, and it lets capacity grow in step with demand instead of ahead of it. Real-time used to mean bolting a separate serving layer onto your warehouse, such as Apache Druid, Apache Pinot, or a cache. That meant always-on infrastructure, a second copy of your data, sync pipelines, and engineers to keep it all consistent. Lakehouse//RT queries governed lakehouse data directly, so as volume grows there's no second stack growing alongside it. Aurasell's AI-native go-to-market platform runs agents that prospect, manage pipeline, and coach reps around the clock. Those agentic workflows depend on high query throughput, and Aurasell wanted real-time performance without moving or indexing data into an external system. With Lakehouse//RT, the team serves that workload directly in Databricks from a single small cluster. VisionHeight is a pre-attack intelligence platform that maps adversary infrastructure across the public internet in real time. Their previous real-time layer ran on Apache Pinot with always-on EC2 clusters running 24/7. After switching to Lakehouse//RT's serverless model, VisionHeight saw a cost reduction of more than 90%. On their heaviest query, Lakehouse//RT delivered sub-second response times, nearly 3x faster than Pinot. The entire migration took three days. Read the full case study here . nOps manages more than $5 billion in annual cloud spend for hundreds of customers, powering real-time dashboards where enterprises track exactly where their money goes. Their real-time query layer previously ran on Apache Druid, requiring a separate always-on cluster and 40TB of duplicated data synced from their lakehouse. After migrating to Lakehouse//RT, nOps cut infrastructure costs by more than 6x while eliminating the duplicated data entirely. Because Lakehouse//RT queries data directly where it lives, the migration required no data copying, no new ingestion pipelines, and no new infrastructure. Read the full case study here . The wave of AI and user demand isn't coming; it's here. Query volumes will grow by orders of magnitude. The question isn't whether you can afford real-time performance. It's whether you can afford not to have a system built for efficiency at scale. Lakehouse//RT is available in beta today. Spin up a new Lakehouse//RT warehouse and start testing your most demanding real-time workloads. title: Genie in Slack is now Generally Available: Governed AI cowork, right where work happens
abstract: • Genie in Slack is generally available: DM Genie or @mention it in a channel to get governed answers grounded in your business context without leaving Slack. • From answers to action: Genie updates documents and tickets through MCP connectors after you approve, and works with files and runs analyses on a schedule. • Governed by design: Every question runs with the asker's permissions, so Unity Catalog and source permissions apply in DMs and channels alike. Many business questions can’t be started and answered within the same conversation. A manager asks her team in Slack why revenue growth slowed last month across active customers. To answer, someone needs to find the right dashboard, check it against the number finance reported, and search last week's meeting notes for the explanation. Two hours later, they paste their findings back into the thread, but the conversation has already moved on. The delay doesn't come from the question being hard, it comes from having to piece together data from multiple scattered sources. The revenue numbers live in your data platform, the explanation for the slowdown lives in documents and tickets, the definition of “active customer” varies across teams, and decisions happen in Slack. Today, we’re making it easier than ever for teams to answer questions right where they start, with the General Availability of the Databricks Genie app for Slack . title: How Block powers collaborative AI agents with Buzz and Unity Gateway
abstract: Inside Block, Buzz brings employees and AI agents into a shared workspace. With Databricks Unity Gateway, employees who use Buzz can access frontier and open-weight models, experiment with different agent harnesses, and find the right combination based on the efficiency frontier for each task. As AI agents become part of everyday work, Block’s teams needed a way to work with agents in the same place they work with each other. Block developed Buzz , an open source collaboration space where people and AI agents can work together in group discussions, focused conversations, and one-on-one exchanges. Buzz brings agents into the same collaborative environment as employees. Users can create an agent, choose the model or coding harness behind it, and bring that agent into a conversation with colleagues. Rather than switching between different AI tools, teams can work with multiple agents in one place. At Block, Databricks Unity Gateway helps power the Buzz experience by providing access to a broad selection of frontier and open-weight models through a single integration. That gives employees the flexibility to experiment with different models and match them to the work they're trying to accomplish. Buzz gives people and AI agents a shared workspace to exchange information, contribute context, and work together on tasks. Employees can create AI agents, work with them individually or alongside colleagues, and bring others into ongoing work. For example, an employee can ask an agent to help with coding or analysis, while colleagues review its work, provide additional information, or ask follow-up questions. Buzz includes its own built-in agent, which incorporates a lightweight version of Goose, and also supports other coding harnesses and tools. As an open source project, Buzz is model-agnostic and can be self-hosted, meaning it can run privately on your own network or system, giving users flexibility in how they deploy and configure their agents. At Block, employees are using Buzz for coding, analytics, and other day-to-day work. Many bring agents into the same conversations where colleagues are already collaborating. Buzz lets users choose the model or harness behind each agent. A coding task, an analytical question, and a lightweight everyday request may benefit from different models or agent harnesses. Instead of committing to a single model for every workflow, Buzz lets users make that choice when creating their agents. Unity Gateway provides the model access layer for this experience. When employees create an agent in Buzz, they can select Databricks as their inference provider and choose from the models available through Unity Gateway. That includes frontier models from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google, as well as select open-weight models, all accessible through a single integration. This flexibility matters as new models become available and teams learn which ones work best for different tasks. Instead of designing every agent around the same model, employees can create a collection of specialized agents, each with its own model or harness, and bring them together in Buzz. Model choice becomes even more interesting when multiple agents collaborate on the same task. Block has been experimenting with different combinations of models and agent harnesses to understand how they affect performance and cost. One approach its engineers have explored is using a more capable model to coordinate work across a team of agents powered by smaller, more efficient models. The idea is straightforward because not every step of a complex task requires the most expensive model. A coordinating agent can take on the more demanding work, while other agents handle tasks suited to their capabilities. In Buzz, those interactions can take place within the same collaborative environment, where people can see how agents work with each other and participate in the work. Block has also developed an internal approach to benchmarking these agent teams, giving its engineers a way to experiment with different configurations. This approach reflects a broader shift in how teams are thinking about AI development. The question is no longer just which single model performs best but how to combine models, harnesses, and agents to complete work effectively. Buzz reflects a different way to think about AI at work. Rather than treating each agent as an individual tool, Block built an environment where people can create, collaborate with, and coordinate multiple agents in the same place. With Unity Gateway providing access to frontier and open-weight models, Block employees can experiment with different combinations of models and harnesses to find what works best for each task, all within the collaborative Buzz experience. Get started with Block Buzz and Unity Gateway Block Buzz is an open source collaboration workspace where employees and AI agents can work together in channels, threads, and direct messages. Users can create agents, choose their models or coding harnesses, and collaborate with multiple agents and colleagues in the same environment. Block uses Databricks Unity Gateway to provide centralized access to frontier and open-weight AI models within Buzz. Employees can select Databricks as their inference provider and choose from available models, including those from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google, through a single integration. Enterprises can assign different models to AI agents based on task requirements, performance, and cost. With Buzz and Unity Gateway, Block employees can experiment with different combinations of models and agent harnesses rather than relying on one model for every workflow. Multi-agent workflows allow teams to use different models for different parts of a task. For example, a more capable model can coordinate complex work while smaller, more efficient models handle simpler tasks. Block is experimenting with these configurations to understand how model and harness selection affects performance and cost. Yes. Block Buzz is open source, model-agnostic, and can be self-hosted. It supports multiple models and agent harnesses, and organizations can integrate with Databricks Unity Gateway to access frontier and open-weight models through a single API.
