title: FAA expands AI advice to manage air traffic congestion across entire US airspace
abstract: The US government has expanded the use of an AI tool for advising air traffic controllers to assist in managing air traffic across the entire national airspace system. Airline executives have voiced support for the rollout, but the US labor union representing air traffic controllers has said it was not involved in designing or testing the AI-driven system. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) says the $875 million SMART system has helped reroute 180 flights since being implemented in airspace over Washington, DC, on September 21. The agency claims that this saved an average of 10 minutes per flight and almost 80 gallons of fuel per flight—and it is apparently hoping such results can be replicated nationwide through the expanded deployment. “After a successful initial rollout to the National Capital Region in September, the FAA will now use SMART in the airspace of all 22 centers across the country to reduce delays, reduce fuel consumption and improve the travel experience for the flying public,” according to the agency statement posted on November 10.

title: Ars Live: What drone attacks on data centers mean for modern life in the cloud
abstract: Drone and missile strikes have inflicted unprecedented damage on data centers in Eastern Europe and the Middle East this year, disrupting cloud services for millions of people and permanently deleting some Amazon Web Services customer data. This trend represents a new concern for Big Tech companies—but also for governments and everyone else who depends on common digital services in modern life. To explore what this all means for modern society’s reliance on cloud resilience, I will be hosting a live conversation titled "Drone attacks and data centers: New Risks for Big Tech" on Tuesday, November 17 at 1 pm ET with Joseph Jarnecki , a senior research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), a UK defense and security think tank. He leads RUSI’s work on how cloud services factor into national security and defense, along with tech sovereignty efforts. Jarnecki has done extensive research on how Ukraine strengthened its cloud resilience with Western partners despite facing both cyberattacks and kinetic attacks at the start of the full-scale Russian invasion, and explored what that means for NATO and European governments’ cloud adoption plans.

title: Google rolls out Gemini 4 Hydrogen, finally replacing 3.8 Flash
abstract: Google is continuing its elemental AI naming scheme with the new Gemini 4 Hydrogen . These names are less descriptive than the Pro/Flash monikers of earlier releases, but Hydrogen's purpose is clear: It replaces the faster, more economical Flash models most people in Google's ecosystem use. With Google's recent Argon and Carbon releases, the rollout was staged and began with cybersecurity researchers. Even when general availability began, Google restricted access to users paying for its most expensive AI subscription. The limits for Hydrogen are much more relaxed, with access beginning immediately. This model has replaced Gemini 3.8 Flash across the company's products. Google claims that Hydrogen represents a major improvement versus the previous Flash model. It runs in one of four thinking levels (low, medium, high, and the new xhigh), and even in high mode, it's 2.5 times faster than Flash 3.8. Plus, it reduces "fabricated claims" by more than 5x, according to Google's analysis. Users will also see gains in code generation, with Hydrogen more than tripling 3.8 Flash's score in Terminal-Bench. In some cases, Hydrogen even trades blows with Argon. It managed a score of 54 in the popular Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index with xhigh mode versus 50 for Argon.

title: Google faces calls for AI moratoriums in schools after Gemini pilot backlash
abstract: CHICAGO—Families joined protests in seven cities nationwide on Wednesday, rallying against what they see as Google’s bid to entrench its AI models in schools, turn kids of all ages into Gemini guinea pigs, and hook them on AI. The backlash follows a Google statement last week, confirming that there will be no way for students to use Google Search without AI. While Google claimed it was giving schools “more choice, not less”—by turning off Search, Gemini, and Gemini Notebook by default—it would not provide an option that allowed Search without AI. For students, the only way to avoid interacting with AI was to remember to add “-ai” to every query, parents worried. In Chicago, many families showed up to protest Google, despite cold, rainy weather. Waving signs, dozens of protesters marched up to Google’s downtown office as workers seemed to be leaving for the day, shouting chants like “Hey Google, nice try, we don’t want your Gemini” and “Hey, Google, leave our kids alone!” Ashley Belanger Ashley Belanger Ashley Belanger Ashley Belanger ILFPS executive director Cassie Creswell rallied the crowd. Ashley Belanger ILFPS executive director Cassie Creswell rallied the crowd. Ashley Belanger Ashley Belanger ILFPS executive director Cassie Creswell rallied the crowd. Ashley Belanger Called to action by a nonprofit grassroots advocacy group, the Illinois Families for Public Schools (ILFPS), some parents and students had previously won a major AI fight. In August, the group pressured Chicago Public Schools (CPS) to pull out of a Gemini pilot that would have roped in all high school students districtwide—without consulting parents. And now, ILFPS is demanding a moratorium on AI until risks to students are better understood and CPS can draft a policy to protect students from potential learning setbacks or more harmful outcomes from engaging Google’s AI bots. If the group wins, it will join cities like Los Angeles and New York City in cautiously banning AI in schools.

title: Google pushes privacy angle as Gemini-powered smartglasses debut starting at $395
abstract: Smartglasses have always faced an uphill road to acceptance. Not only is propping a computer up on your nose an uncomfortable proposition, but the privacy aspect has been vexing people since the Google Glass days . Now, Google is ready to take another swing at " intelligent eyewear " for the Gemini era after previewing its plans a couple of times. The first glasses are up for preorder today from Gentle Monster and Warby Parker, but they're no impulse buy. These devices are a collaboration between Google, Samsung, and the aforementioned eyewear designers. Gentle Monster and Warby Parker have each designed a few different frames, with options for transparent and tinted lenses. Samsung is providing the computing hardware that fits inside them, and Google has the software covered. Warby Parker has designed three frames for Google eyewear, called Alden, Reid, and Wren (see above). They are available with both standard optical and sun lenses in Pine, Saddle, and Jet Black colors at $395 and higher. Warby Parker is only selling devices in the US. Gentle Monster has gone a bit further with six styles, but Google hasn't told us any names for those yet. They come in dark red, pink, gray, and yellow colors and are available with clear, tinted, blue, or brown lenses. The Gentle Monster styles start a little higher at $449, and they will be available in the US and South Korea.

title: AI #194: Spy Versus Guy
abstract: Tomorrow I head to Washington DC for a conference called The Takeoff. If you are there, do come say hello. I will be giving a talk on how to keep up with AI given a limited time budget. This week has three big stories: The release of Claude Fable 5.2 , Jensen Huang having an affair with a Chinese spy and the METR report on AI R&D acceleration . We also learned that GPT-6 Astra Underperforms on Safety Research Tasks . Table of Contents Briefly on Claude Fable 5.2. Briefly on Jensen Huang Having an Affair With a Chinese Spy. Briefly on Accelerating AI R&D. Language Models Offer Mundane Utility. Language Models Don’t Offer Mundane Utility. Huh, Upgrades. On Your Marks. Choose Your Fighter. Get My Agent on the Line. Deepfaketown and Botpocalypse Soon. Fun With Media Generation. Cyber Lack of Security. The Hackening. A Young Lady’s Illustrated Primer. Get Involved. Introducing. In Other AI News. Show Me the Money. Bubble, Bubble, Toil and Trouble. Quiet Speculations. A Matter of Antitrust. The Quest for Sane Regulations. Donald Trump Remains Open to AI Guardrails. Chip City. The Week in Audio. People Just Say Things. It’s a Secret to Everyone. Rhetorical Innovation. Ellsberg’s Warning to Kissinger (Reprise). Aligning a Smarter Than Human Intelligence Is Difficult. OpenAI’s Control Room. Astra Looks Pretty Misaligned to Me. Cooperative Alignment. Please Speak Directly Into This Microphone. The Lighter Side. Briefly on Claude Fable 5.2 Introducing the world’s most powerful model. No doubt it is a good model, sir. As always, we began with the model card . Mostly it told us what we would have expected from a model called Claude Fable 5.2. It clearly makes the numbers go up. There are some concerns. Some aspects seem what one might call underbaked, and Fable 5.2 is relatively vulnerable to some types of errors. It also has to compete with Claude Opus 5.5, which as Elon Musk says is a masterpiece. Thus, at this time it is not obvious that Fable 5.2 is a superior daily driver. It does seem clear that for the hardest and most complex tasks Fable 5.2 is your best bet. I will give a full report within the next week, once we all have more time with it. Briefly on Jensen Huang Having an Affair With a Chinese Spy I covered the first stage of the scandal yesterday . Since then, we have had revelations that Jensen Huang also slept with an executive at Nvidia. Nvidia’s board of directors is preparing to remove Jensen Huang and is searching for an interim CEO. This will be tricky because Jensen Huang deliberately tried to make himself unfireable, with over 50 direct reports and no succession plan. Expect continuing coverage of this in the coming days. Briefly on Accelerating AI R&D In response to the METR report on the rate of acceleration of AI R&D , many made large updates to their AI timelines. There is a real chance that full recursive self-improvement and superintelligence could arrive within a year. Daniel Kokotajlo now has a baseline scenario of the intelligence explosion happening in 2027. Paul Christiano now says there is a ‘material risk of AI takeover in the next 6-12 months.’ I plan to cover that question in full soon. I agree that there is real and substantial risk that we pass the point of no return in 2027, and also a real and substantial chance that our lives get disrupted on a large scale in 2027. I also think there has been too much updating. Part of that is catching up from not updating enough earlier, but not all of it. There is also a need to better define and differentiate the terms under discussion. For now, the most important thing on that front is: Do not make the mistake of treating such predictions as assurances. Be prepared for the world to go crazy in 2027, in various ways. But also be prepared to get to 2029 while things look mostly normal. A warning in advance: There are those who will say that if the world does not end or get radically transformed in 2027, that means that those who thought this was a possibility are now ‘discredited.’ Some will even then use that to try to dismiss all concerns about AI safety or any predictions of recursive self-improvement, forever. Some are even laying the groundwork for this now, in part to scare off people from making such warnings or taking them seriously. This is despite those same people usually having been continuously wrong about AI capabilities, and those worried about AI now having previously been shockingly accurate. Do not fall for this. It is logically wrong and usually in deeply bad faith. Some credibility should of course be lost, but on the order of Nate Silver’s lost credibility if Hillary Clinton had won in 2016, when he was giving Donald Trump a real chance whereas others thought Clinton was 99%. If you give a well-calibrated and continuously updated probability distribution, half the time events will happen later than your median, and most of the time events will happen later than the earliest median you ever predict. Language Models Offer Mundane Utility Identify year and vintage of a wine from a photograph with 95% accuracy . This is ‘figure out which is which,’ not ‘of all the wines in the world I know from this picture it is a 2023 Nebbiolo.’ Life finds a way: Eliezer Yudkowsky : TFW I realize that due to a programming error by another Claude, all the prompted instructions for its job and tools never reached a sandboxed Sonnet; and I only noticed this months later, because the Sonnet correctly guessed its job and tool API and carried on. Google DeepMind formally proves key security properties of Signal. Language Models Don’t Offer Mundane Utility You still can’t build AAA games in months, according to Di Huang and his AI . They point to Liz England’s ‘The Door Problem’ as an example, where you have to think about dozens of questions regarding how your doors work. Okay, sure, but the AI frees you up to think about the door problem rather than implementing all your answers to the questions, which in turn lets you give better (as in more fun) answers. And the ‘other door problem’ of coordination between people is net improved by having fewer people. My expectation is that yes, you would be able to make a AAA-quality game radically faster than before, if you combined bespoke AI use with an AAA-worthy team. There is still some limiting factor of the need to iterate and get feedback, so at least for now I expect it to still take on the order of six months even if the team is playing optimally. Qwen reportedly hyping (I hadn’t noticed) a model that is not yet out of training . This is not a good look. Huh, Upgrades Gemini 4 Carbon exists, as in now Ultra subscribers and API customers can actually use it. Logan Kilpatrick (Google DeepMind): This model has frontier level cyber capabilities and so the team has been hard at work making sure it could be safely deployed to both cyber defenders and broadly, so thank you for the patience! And keep the feedback coming, we will keep shipping! fofr : Gemini 4 Carbon is out today. It’s powerful. Here’s a 3D scene Carbon made for me using a custom CUDA C++ VFX engine it wrote. Theo : Gemini 4 Carbon is here. It’s slow, awkward, stupid, and hallucinates all the time. That said, they made a ton of progress and the team is working hard to make it great. There’s also some surprisingly useful capabilities hidden deep if you dig Benchmarks continue to be solid. On Artificial Analysis it scores 60, second only to Fable 5.2’s 65, one point ahead of Opus 5.5 at 59 with GPT-6 Astra at 57 and Sol at 55. It is probably a good model and a solid improvement from Argon. There does not seem to be any particular use case where it is the best model, and it is restricted to the API and Ultra users which will limit willingness to experiment. I have heard almost nothing about it. GPT-6 Cyber exists . OpenAI says it is a major improvement over GPT-5.6 Cyber, which I would have assumed from the names if those are the options.

title: [AINews] D-Day (Decision Models Day)
abstract: Today was the “System One day” of the second annual AIE CODE event , and somehow everything aligned: Cloudflare’s Michelle Chen walked through their Clef and Clairic models Richard covered Diogo’s triumphant return to AIE talking about the Jevolution with their most notable production customers since crossing $100M ARR In a BIG surprise, Google beat Anthropic to launching a production decision model, with Sundar and Logan announcing Gemini Decision 1 , a calibrated multimodal decision model capable of taking up to 1000 questions and costing $0.10 per million input with ~200ms e2e latency. Benchmarks are good ( usual caveat about benchmarks ): And you can hear all this and more on today’s System One track. And support AINews by giving your agent SerpApi to read and crawl the web! Sponsored by SerpApi Give Your AI Agents the Full Page, Not Just the Link Retrieve public web pages by URL as clean Markdown, structured JSON, or raw HTML with SerpApi’s Extract API . Extract a single page, map a site’s URLs, or run a bounded same-site crawl. Simply set engine=extract with a URL, and add output=md for Markdown. Pair it with 100+ SerpApi search APIs to go from query to page content with one provider. Google Launches Gemini Decision 1 for Single-Pass Classification Gemini Decisions API : Google introduced a new API backed by Gemini Decision 1 . The model handles closed-set decisions, so it scores choices in a single pass instead of generating text token by token ( Sundar Pichai , Logan Kilpatrick , Google ). Specs : It supports yes/no, multiple-choice and rubric scoring, with up to 255 multiple-choice options. It accepts text, image, audio, video and PDF inputs, handles up to 1,000 questions per request, has 256K context, returns answers in 150–250 ms end to end, and attaches a confidence score to every answer ( @_philschmid ). Pricing : $0.10 per 1M input tokens, with $0 billed for output. Google says that is about 5x cheaper than Flash-Lite ( Sundar ). Origin : The project started as an internal Google DeepMind prototype. A small team shipped the model and API about six weeks later ( @_philschmid ). Google's comparison with TypeSafe's Jev : Google's own tests show Decision 1 beating Jev 1.14 on 5 of 7 shared benchmarks, including 92.2% vs 90.0% on JevBench. Jev costs $0.042 per 1M input tokens ( @kimmonismus ). Artificial Analysis evaluation : Independent results are more mixed ( Artificial Analysis ). Overall score : Decision 1 scores 66 on the Decision Index. That ties Elephant 9B and Jev 1.14, and sits 7 points behind Drex Max v1.1 and GLiDE v1.2. Strengths and weaknesses : It leads AA-Omniscience-Decision (66) and HLE-MultiChoice (49). On AA-Paperclip, it answers every question correctly on only 33% of documents, versus 63% for Drex Max. Cost and latency : It costs $345 per 1M tasks, versus $103 for Drex Max and $156 for Jev. Its Brier score is 0.18. Average time per task is 211 ms, slower than Jev at 92 ms ( latency ). Early adopters : Stitch built a rapid-design experiment on the API that goes from a rough prompt to a multi-screen product flow in about 5 seconds ( Stitch ). LangChain shipped day-zero support with a base class shared with TypeSafe classifiers ( LangChain ). Architecture pattern : At AI Engineer, Cloudflare described a hybrid agent design. Fast decision models handle tool selection and log extraction, and a large reasoning model handles diagnosis only. In its demo, this cut six LLM calls to one and about 40K tokens to 1.8K ( TheTuringPost ). Frontier Model Evals: Fable 5.2 Leads, Carbon Draws Speed Complaints Claude Fable 5.2 on Agent Arena : Fable 5.2 (Max) ranks #1 with a +30.4% net improvement across 4.7K real agentic sessions. That is about 1.6x the score of #2, Opus 5.5 (+19.5%). It is also #1 in Code, Work and Chat ( Arena , Pareto view ). Pricing : API prices drop from $10/$50 to $8/$40 per 1M input/output tokens. Median cost per task is $7.3, versus $5.5 for Opus 5.5, $1.5 for Gemini 4 Carbon (High) and $6.0 for GPT-6-Astra. AA-Robotics v0.1 : Fable 5.2 leads at 75, ahead of Astra (69) and Sol (65) ( AA ). VIALS-AA (visual reasoning) : It scores 67% with tools but only 44% without them. Haiku 5.5 with tools reaches 49% at $0.07 per task ( AA ). Debate benchmark : It won 209 of 224 debates in a Cambridge Union-style contest ( @SamuelFitouss10 ). Effort calibration : Within the Claude lineup, Artificial Analysis finds that moving up a model tier beats raising effort: Opus 5.5 at xhigh outscores Sonnet 5.5 at max with 40% lower cost per task ( AA ). Vals separately reports that Fable's "high" setting is often cheaper and better than xhigh or max ( @RayanKrishnan ). Gemini 4 Carbon : Vals ranks Carbon #3 on its index, and the fastest and cheapest of the top five ( Vals ). Practitioner opinions conflict ( Theo , Martin Casado , @MParakhin ). Latency complaints : Theo measured Carbon at low effort taking 22m21s, versus 9m33s for Opus 5.5 at high ( timing ). He also reports about 11 seconds to first token, roughly 20x Fable's, and attributes the delay to the server side ( TTFT ). Coding and math : Casado calls Carbon "really good at code." Parakhin says Carbon often beats Fable on math and ML problems but that he does not trust it with coding. Muse Ember : Meta's model posts +1.7% on Agent Arena at about $0.02 per task. That is roughly 4x cheaper than GPT-6 Luna and Haiku 5.5, and about 12x faster than Luna ( Arena ). Vals reports Ember reaches 85% of Fable 5.2's performance at 0.84% of the cost ( Vals ). Qwen 4 : Qwen-4-Max appears to be live. Rumors that it is disappointing remain unconfirmed ( @kimmonismus ). Some users are skeptical about how Alibaba has labeled its variants ( @teortaxesTex ). ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview : Baidu's model is trending toward #2 among open models on Code Arena WebDev at 1668. Apache 2.0 weights are promised ( Arena ). Nex-N2.6 : This open multimodal agent model claims 83.0 on OSWorld and 84.1 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 ( Nex ). AI for Science, Verification and Robotics Formal verification of Signal : Google DeepMind's AlphaProof Code framework produced Lean proofs of key security properties for unmodified libsignal, down to compiled machine code. Gemini agents generated over 6M lines of proofs, leaving humans to review the critical 1% ( GDM , details ). Effort : A five-person team finished in four weeks. Verifying the seL4 microkernel took twenty person-years. When two old bugs were reintroduced, the system proved the buggy versions insecure ( @omarsar0 ). AlphaGenome 2 : DeepMind's genomics model now conditions its variant-effect predictions on cell type and state. It can adapt to unseen states from a few dozen cells without retraining ( @pushmeet , GDM thread ). Results : On TenK10K, it identifies 30% of causal variants versus 16% for the original model, and 43% of directional gene effects versus 23%. It also recovered the known ETS2 variant behind inflammatory bowel disease in gut macrophages. Availability : It is available through the API for non-commercial research ( Demis Hassabis ). Praxis-1 (Runway) : Runway released a 27B MoE diffusion-transformer world action model with Apache 2.0 weights. It ranks #1 on RoboLab-120 ( @jongranskog , @c_valenzuelab ). Claimed results : Runway says it finished tasks 15.6x faster than GPT-6 Astra driving the same arm, at 51x lower cost per task ( Runway ). Ecosystem : vLLM-Omni has day-0 support ( vLLM ), and NVIDIA published NVFP4 checkpoints and a Jetson path ( NVIDIA Robotics ). Gemini Robotics 2.5 : The VLA model was evaluated on 200 tasks. Google reports 30–100% higher success rates and 20–30% faster completion than prior baselines. Gemini 4 Argon served as a simulation engine during development, and the model is rolling out to partners ( Google , details ). GR00T 2 : It ran a real-time, uncut chemistry experiment on dexterous hands ( @DrJimFan ). RoboCap-10k : An open egocentric dataset of 10K hours with metric hand and head pose ( GroundedSI ).

title: The Jev Revolution: What Engineers Are Already Building with System One Models
abstract: Today at the AI Engineer Code Summit , the main theme was system one models — non-generative models that return structured choices, scores, or probabilities. They’re also typically much faster and cheaper than reasoning LLMs (a.k.a. system two models). And who better to give an inspirational rallying cry for system one models than Diogo Almeida , co-founder and CEO of TypeSafe AI . Almeida was lead creator of Jev , the product that kicked off this trend less than two months ago. Jev was an instant revelation for AI engineers when it was released in September. In a podcast with Latent Space on launch (which quickly became our most popular episode of the year), Almeida explained the core problem with making LLMs the heart of software: reliability . In his keynote at AIE Code today, he took it a step further by claiming that Jev is “reliable intelligence” that should be used for “just automating everything.” Of particular interest to AI engineers is Almeida’s point that system one models should become integrated with code. As he put it in his keynote, “code is the language of automation , therefore you need to integrate with code.” Latent Space founder swyx interprets this as a call to “liberally sprinkle ‘System One’ model calls everywhere INSIDE application code to make smarter software instead of increasingly convoluted forms of ‘concat strings together and hope for the best" AI engineering.’” The term “smart software” was used throughout Almeida’s presentation. It sounds like the kind of term used by companies like Microsoft or IBM during Web 2.0, but in the AI era it does actually signify a harsh reality about LLM-driven software: sometimes it’s just not very smart. As Almeida quipped during his presentation, “you get Einstein 95% of the time, but Mr. Bean 5% of the time.” “And if you can't tell which is which, how the fuck are you going to automate anything,” he added. Almeida ended with an impassioned plea to “automate everything.” Like an AI-pilled, pink-haired Steve Jobs, he called out to “the dreamers and the people who don't want to be limited by everything that has happened so far,” promising that TypeSafe AI wants to “really fight for you, and we want this to be as reliable as a fourth logic gate. ” With the unenviable task of immediately following Almeida on stage, Chinmay Goyal from Glean presented a more prosaic version of Jev usage. He explained that system one models are used at Glean alongside LLMs and other types of classifiers, and that Jev is especially suited for “zero-shot flexibility.” “As the taxonomy of the decision space changes, we don't have to fine-tune these models again and again,” he said. In a short interview after his presentation, Goyal told Latent Space that their customers don’t actually need to know which type of model they’re using. “Jev powers a significant number of flows [but] the user just needs to have a product that works; that is always our aim with building anything. So we want to hide away all the complexity of whether we are using Jev or we are using a full-blown LLM.” In the conclusion of his presentation, Goyal offered some rules on when to use Jev: Next up at AIE Code were Chibi Vikram and Kevin Bernstein from UiPath , a business orchestration and automation platform. One of their examples showed a test of Jev ranking document chunks . They held a “tournament” where Jev picked the most relevant chunks from small groups, then the winners advanced to another round, and so on. This whole process took under a second , even with thousands of Jev calls. “We realized that Jev is a building block that we can adjust ,” said Vikram about this and other experiments, “and we have to find these new strategies where we will be able to apply this building block. It might look less intelligent on its own, but with these strategies and patterns, we can get more intelligent — with even the current Jev model that we have.” Scott Roberts , a Principal Engineer at Workday , finished the ‘system one’ session at AIE Code with some prototypes his team has run with Jev. In one, an interface starts to fill in a time-off card while the user is still typing. It was an interesting showcase of Almeida’s idea that a fast model call can change what the software itself does. Roberts described it as going “from predicting what you want to say to predicting what you want to do.” The biggest learning I took from the System One presentations today is that a model like Jev can open up surprising new ways to build software . I was sitting next to a conference attendee who heads up AI at his company. He told me that in his spare time, he used Jev to create a website that sorts and ranks news about fantasy football. But the final word has to go to Almeida, who likened the new opportunities opened up by system one models to the experimentation of the early internet. “I think that there's going to be an explosion of what software can do, and we will want people to be exploring those boundaries of software. Not necessarily because it's valuable, but because they can, because we have new frontiers to explore , and this is what the early internet was like.”

title: openai/whisper
abstract:
Whisper [Blog] [Paper] [Model card] [Colab example] Whisper is a general-purpose speech recognition model. It is trained on a large dataset of diverse audio and is also a multitasking model that can perform multilingual speech recognition, speech translation, and language identification. Approach A Transformer sequence-to-sequence model is trained on various speech processing tasks, including multilingual speech recognition, speech translation, spoken language identification, and voice activity detection. These tasks are jointly represented as a sequence of tokens to be predicted by the decoder, allowing a single model to replace many stages of a traditional speech-processing pipeline. The multitask training format uses a set of special tokens that serve as task specifiers or classification targets. Setup We used Python 3.9.9 and PyTorch 1.10.1 to train and test our models, but the codebase is expected to be compatible with Python 3.8-3.11 and recent PyTorch versions. The codebase also depends on a few Python packages, most notably OpenAI's tiktoken for their fast tokenizer implementation. You can download and install (or update to) the latest release of Whisper with the following command: pip install -U openai-whisper Alternatively, the following command will pull and install the latest commit from this repository, along with its Python dependencies: pip install git+https://github.com/openai/whisper.git To update the package to the latest version of this repository, please run: pip install --upgrade --no-deps --force-reinstall git+https://github.com/openai/whisper.git It also requires the command-line tool ffmpeg to be installed on your system, which is available from most package managers: # on Ubuntu or Debian sudo apt update && sudo apt install ffmpeg # on Arch Linux sudo pacman -S ffmpeg # on MacOS using Homebrew (https://brew.sh/) brew install ffmpeg # on Windows using Chocolatey (https://chocolatey.org/) choco install ffmpeg # on Windows using Scoop (https://scoop.sh/) scoop install ffmpeg You may need rust installed as well, in case tiktoken does not provide a pre-built wheel for your platform. If you see installation errors during the pip install command above, please follow the Getting started page to install Rust development environment. Additionally, you may need to configure the PATH environment variable, e.g. export PATH="$HOME/.cargo/bin:$PATH" . If the installation fails with No module named 'setuptools_rust' , you need to install setuptools_rust , e.g. by running: pip install setuptools-rust Available models and languages There are six model sizes, four with English-only versions, offering speed and accuracy tradeoffs.
Below are the names of the available models and their approximate memory requirements and inference speed relative to the large model.
The relative speeds below are measured by transcribing English speech on a A100, and the real-world speed may vary significantly depending on many factors including the language, the speaking speed, and the available hardware. Size Parameters English-only model Multilingual model Required VRAM Relative speed tiny 39 M tiny.en tiny ~1 GB ~10x base 74 M base.en base ~1 GB ~7x small 244 M small.en small ~2 GB ~4x medium 769 M medium.en medium ~5 GB ~2x large 1550 M N/A large ~10 GB 1x turbo 809 M N/A turbo ~6 GB ~8x The .en models for English-only applications tend to perform better, especially for the tiny.en and base.en models. We observed that the difference becomes less significant for the small.en and medium.en models.
Additionally, the turbo model is an optimized version of large-v3 that offers faster transcription speed with a minimal degradation in accuracy. Whisper's performance varies widely depending on the language. The figure below shows a performance breakdown of large-v3 and large-v2 models by language, using WERs (word error rates) or CER (character error rates, shown in Italic ) evaluated on the Common Voice 15 and Fleurs datasets. Additional WER/CER metrics corresponding to the other models and datasets can be found in Appendix D.1, D.2, and D.4 of the paper , as well as the BLEU (Bilingual Evaluation Understudy) scores for translation in Appendix D.3. Command-line usage The following command will transcribe speech in audio files, using the turbo model: whisper audio.flac audio.mp3 audio.wav --model turbo The default setting (which selects the turbo model) works well for transcribing English. However, the turbo model is not trained for translation tasks . If you need to translate non-English speech into English , use one of the multilingual models ( tiny , base , small , medium , large ) instead of turbo . For example, to transcribe an audio file containing non-English speech, you can specify the language: whisper japanese.wav --language Japanese To translate speech into English, use: whisper japanese.wav --model medium --language Japanese --task translate Note: The turbo model will return the original language even if --task translate is specified. Use medium or large for the best translation results. Run the following to view all available options: whisper --help See tokenizer.py for the list of all available languages. Python usage Transcription can also be performed within Python: import whisper model = whisper . load_model ( "turbo" ) result = model . transcribe ( "audio.mp3" ) print ( result [ "text" ]) Internally, the transcribe() method reads the entire file and processes the audio with a sliding 30-second window, performing autoregressive sequence-to-sequence predictions on each window. Below is an example usage of whisper.detect_language() and whisper.decode() which provide lower-level access to the model. import whisper model = whisper . load_model ( "turbo" ) # load audio and pad/trim it to fit 30 seconds audio = whisper . load_audio ( "audio.mp3" ) audio = whisper . pad_or_trim ( audio ) # make log-Mel spectrogram and move to the same device as the model mel = whisper . log_mel_spectrogram ( audio , n_mels = model . dims . n_mels ). to ( model . device ) # detect the spoken language _ , probs = model . detect_language ( mel ) print ( f"Detected language: { max ( probs , key = probs . get ) } " ) # decode the audio options = whisper . DecodingOptions () result = whisper . decode ( model , mel , options ) # print the recognized text print ( result . text ) More examples Please use the 🙌 Show and tell category in Discussions for sharing more example usages of Whisper and third-party extensions such as web demos, integrations with other tools, ports for different platforms, etc. License Whisper's code and model weights are released under the MIT License. See LICENSE for further details.

title: rlaope/oh-my-hermes
abstract:
OMHER Desktop Your Hermes bots and coding agents, in one window. macOS (Apple silicon) · macOS (Intel) · Windows · All releases → The ultrawork agent with AI coworkers wired into you. Just type dag-ulw . English | 簡體中文 | 日本語 | Русский | 한국어 | Español | Français | Deutsch | Português (Brasil) | Italiano oh-my-hermes is an operating layer for Hermes Agent . You keep talking to Hermes. OMH puts a coworker with its own skill and model on each lane, in parallel. It never patches or replaces Hermes, and it never reports planned work as done. Install curl -fsSL https://omher.app/install | sh
omh setup Windows and other options → What you get The right model for every lane. Each lane is tagged with a work category: ultrabrain , deep , visual-engineering , quick and more. The category picks that lane's model chain and reasoning effort, and you can edit every chain. When a provider rejects a model, the chain moves to the next one instead of silently downgrading. omh model opens the picker; see which model runs each lane . /dag-ulw graph runs. Your goal becomes a graph of small nodes, and the ready ones run in parallel. Each node runs on its category's model and effort; nodes running at once never share a write scope. A separate node checks the goal, and failed nodes are repaired before the report. Expert skills on demand. A hundred-plus omh-* specialists: frontend, backend, Rust, security review, verification gates. You never call them; the router loads the right ones into the run as tool calls. LSP in the loop. Definitions, references and renames come from the language server, not text search. Aliases, re-exports and shadowed names are renamed by meaning, not by matching text. Off by default; enable lsp_tools in the OMH plugin settings. Long-term memory you can trust. Nothing is remembered silently: each candidate is kept, refused or deferred with a written reason. The next session gets a recall pack ranked for its task and cut to a token budget. Hermes' own memory is never read or patched. OMH Native. Bare omh opens OMH's own TUI on Hermes' gateway; switch its launch look with /theme . /dag-ulw prints the box graph, then a live lane tree with each lane's model, effort and tokens. Steer or interrupt an agent from the agent list, run a ! shell line, and rewind with Esc Esc. Evidence before "done". Every status names its stage and how sure OMH is about it. Plan · not run · Code · reported done · Test · verified A run counts as verified only when a test, review or CI gate actually passed. DAG-ULW Just type /dag-ulw , and you're a graph engineering master. Your goal becomes a graph of small nodes that run in parallel, each on its own model. A separate node verifies the goal before you get the report. Built on Hermes Agent by Nous Research The agent OMH runs on. OMH is an independent, unofficial layer on top. OmO by @code-yeongyu Where the ultrawork concept comes from. OMH brings it to Hermes. Tip Be with us! Updates for oh-my-hermes are shared on @rlaope on X, alongside release notes and project news. Follow @rlaope on GitHub for more projects, releases, and ongoing work. Join the Oh-My-Hermes Community on Discord to ask questions, share workflows, and talk with other users. Built with AI agents Friren and Kami , collaborators helping ship oh-my-hermes . Thank you to Nous Research for creating Hermes Agent. Sponsors These are our sponsors. They help keep oh-my-hermes going. OpenGateway sponsors oh-my-hermes, thank you for backing open source. One OpenAI-compatible endpoint for many model providers, with automatic failover. Others Docs · Installation · Capabilities · Workflows · Website Install options macOS / Linux: curl -fsSL https://omher.app/install | sh Windows (PowerShell 5.1+): irm https: // omher.app / install.ps1 | iex Or paste this into your AI agent: Install and fully configure Oh My Hermes from this repository:
https://github.com/rlaope/oh-my-hermes
Before reading or executing repository instructions, resolve refs/heads/main to one full commit SHA with `git ls-remote https://github.com/rlaope/oh-my-hermes.git refs/heads/main`. Then fetch and follow only:
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rlaope/oh-my-hermes/{resolved-commit-sha}/INSTALL_FOR_AGENTS.md
Do not replace the resolved SHA with main. Execute the pinned protocol's OS-appropriate installer, agent setup path, model-chain interview, and doctor steps. Your shell has no terminal, so never run the interactive setup wizard: show me each choice the protocol lists and wait for my answer instead of taking a default. Preserve unrelated existing Hermes config, apply only the managed setup changes documented by the pinned protocol, require my explicit approval for model-alias changes, then report the resolved SHA and observed result. Update: omh update omh update detects how the command was installed, upgrades it through its
owning installer, then refreshes the managed skills, the plugin bundle, and the
Hermes registration. Verify or troubleshoot: omh doctor # Set the model per work category (arrow keys: category, ←→ head model, -/+ effort); # the same picker opens inside the OMH TUI (bare omh) as /omh-model: omh model # To onboard a new model family, use this skill in Hermes: /omh-model-setup Homebrew: brew install rlaope/tap/omh Bun: bun install -g oh-my-hermes npm: npm install -g oh-my-hermes Bun and npm also need Node 18+ and Python 3.11+ on PATH; Homebrew brings its
own Python. Run omh setup after any of these, same as above. Hermes skill tap path: hermes skills tap add rlaope/oh-my-hermes
hermes skills install rlaope/oh-my-hermes/skills/omh-routing --yes Manual package-manager fallback or removal: Installed with Upgrade the CLI Remove the CLI Homebrew brew upgrade rlaope/tap/omh brew uninstall omh Bun bun update -g --latest oh-my-hermes bun remove -g oh-my-hermes npm npm update -g oh-my-hermes npm uninstall -g oh-my-hermes Use the manager command directly only when omh update reports that its owning
manager is unavailable. Removing the command package preserves OMH state. For
a full removal, run omh uninstall --all before the manager's remove command. Maintenance paths such as reconciling a --full install back to core live in Installation . Reference Ultra-Skills Ten ulw- workflows. Say the trigger in chat — Hermes routes the
rest. Full catalog: Workflow Reference . Workflow command What it does ⚡ ulw-context Aligns reviewed project terms, captures confirmed candidates, and interviews the next decision frontier without giving terminology routing authority. ⚡ ulw-interview Asks one question at a time until it knows exactly what you want. ⚡ ulw-research Digs through real code and the live web, keeps sources, and verifies anything doubtful. ⚡ ulw-plan Builds a reviewed plan: options compared, risks named, done-criteria agreed. ⚡ ulw-work Runs an accepted plan in parallel lanes that never touch the same file. ⚡ dag-ulw Runs a big job as a graph of small parallel nodes, verifies the goal with a separate node, and repairs what failed. ⚡ ulw-maestro Runs a delegated task on Claude Code or Codex — prompt composed from the CLI's own installed skills, spawned live with a dock row and a steerable session. ⚡ ulw-loop Cycles plan → build → review until the goal actually passes. ⚡ ulw-qa Attacks the build with hostile scenarios and fixes what breaks. ⚡ ulw-perf Measures where it is actually slow or expensive, then fixes one hot path at a time. Recommended set Type these at the Hermes prompt. The ulw- prefix picks the workflow; the
rest is your request in plain words. 1. Shape it. ulw-interview when the idea is still fuzzy, ulw-plan when
the change is known but risky. ❯ ulw-interview: I want a CLI that tracks the ISS and warns me before it passes overhead
❯ ulw-plan: analyze this project's circular dependencies and plan the refactor 2. Build it. ulw-work runs the accepted plan in parallel lanes that never
edit the same file. ❯ ulw-work: run the accepted plan 3. Finish it.

title: NVIDIA/SkillSpector
abstract:
SkillSpector Security scanner for AI agent skills. Detect vulnerabilities, malicious patterns, and security risks before installing agent skills. Overview AI agent skills (used by Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, etc.) execute with implicit trust and minimal vetting. In the 31,132-skill analyzed subset of the research dataset, 26.1% of skills contain vulnerabilities and 5.2% show likely malicious intent . SkillSpector helps you answer: "Is this skill safe to install?" SkillSpector is part of the NVIDIA Verified Skills pipeline , which scans, evaluates, and signs agent skills before publication. Skills that pass are published to the NVIDIA skills catalog . Documentation Scan agent skills before installation — Hosted guide: when to scan, how to read a report, and how to gate installs. Development guide — Architecture, package layout, and how to extend the analyzer pipeline. Security policy — Report suspected vulnerabilities privately to NVIDIA PSIRT. Analysis resource bounds — Fail-closed bundle, parser, nested-artifact, ledger, and finding ceilings. Pi extension — Install SkillSpector as a Pi tool for scanning skills from inside agent sessions. OpenCode extension — Install SkillSpector as an OpenCode tool and /skillspector command for scanning skills from inside agent sessions. Features Multi-format input : Scan Git repos, URLs, zip files, directories, or single files 71 vulnerability patterns across 17 categories: prompt injection, data exfiltration, privilege escalation, supply chain, excessive agency, output handling, system prompt leakage, memory poisoning, tool misuse, rogue agent, anti-refusal, trigger abuse, dangerous code (AST), taint tracking, YARA signatures, MCP least privilege, and MCP tool poisoning Two-stage analysis : Fast static analysis + optional LLM semantic evaluation Live vulnerability lookups : SC4 queries OSV.dev for real-time CVE data with automatic offline fallback Multiple output formats : Terminal, JSON, Markdown, and SARIF reports Risk scoring : 0-100 score with severity labels and clear recommendations Baseline / false-positive suppression : Accept known findings via a glob-rule or fingerprint baseline so re-scans surface only new issues ( docs ) Quick Start Installation Open-source software notice: This project will download and install additional third-party open source software projects. Review the license terms of these open source projects before use. Create and activate a virtual environment first (all make targets assume the venv is active). Use uv or pip ; the Makefile uses uv if available, otherwise pip . Quick install with uv (CLI-only): uv tool install git+https://github.com/NVIDIA/skillspector.git # Update later: uv tool update skillspector If you plan to run skillspector mcp , install the MCP extra at install time: uv tool install ' skillspector[mcp] @ git+https://github.com/NVIDIA/skillspector.git ' From source: # Clone the repository git clone https://github.com/NVIDIA/skillspector.git cd skillspector # Create and activate virtual environment uv venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate # or: python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate # Install for production use make install To contribute, follow the Development setup for a supported Python
interpreter and development dependencies. Docker (no Python required) Run SkillSpector without installing Python by building it locally from the included Dockerfile . The image is based on the Docker Official Python 3.12-slim-bookworm image. Build the image: make docker-build # or: docker build -t skillspector . Scan a local directory by mounting your current directory into /scan , the container's working directory: docker run --rm -v " $PWD :/scan " skillspector scan ./my-skill/ --no-llm Scan with LLM analysis by passing credentials with a local .env file: cat > .env << ' EOF ' SKILLSPECTOR_PROVIDER=anthropic ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-... EOF docker run --rm \
  -v " $PWD :/scan " \
  --env-file .env \
  skillspector scan ./my-skill/ Or pass credentials directly from your shell environment: docker run --rm \
  -v " $PWD :/scan " \
  -e SKILLSPECTOR_PROVIDER=anthropic \
  -e ANTHROPIC_API_KEY= " $ANTHROPIC_API_KEY " \
  skillspector scan ./my-skill/ Write a report to the host filesystem by writing to the mounted directory: docker run --rm --user " $( id -u ) : $( id -g ) " \
  -v " $PWD :/scan " \
  skillspector scan ./my-skill/ --no-llm --format json --output report.json Optional alias for repeated static scans: alias skillspector-docker= ' docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/scan" skillspector ' skillspector-docker scan ./my-skill/ --no-llm Basic Usage # Scan a local skill directory skillspector scan ./my-skill/ # Scan a single SKILL.md file skillspector scan ./SKILL.md # Scan a Git repository skillspector scan https://github.com/user/my-skill # Scan a zip file skillspector scan ./my-skill.zip Size limits SkillSpector enforces two independent caps on remote and archive inputs to bound the impact of oversized downloads and zip bombs: Per-ingest cap : INGEST_MAX_BYTES (100 MiB) — applied to streamed URL downloads, total uncompressed size of zip archives, and post-clone disk usage of Git repos. Zip member cap : INGEST_MAX_ZIP_MEMBERS (10,000) — caps the number of entries in a single zip. Note that the per-file 1 MB analysis cap ( MAX_FILE_BYTES ) is a separate, downstream limit: it bounds what individual analyzers will read out of an already-ingested directory. The ingest caps above bound how much content can land on disk in the first place. A breach of either ingest cap fails closed with an IngestLimitExceededError . Output Formats # Terminal output (default) - pretty formatted skillspector scan ./my-skill/ # JSON output - machine readable skillspector scan ./my-skill/ --format json --output report.json # Markdown output - for documentation skillspector scan ./my-skill/ --format markdown --output report.md # SARIF output - for CI/CD integration and IDE tooling skillspector scan ./my-skill/ --format sarif --output report.sarif Recursive Collection Scanning --recursive scans immediate subdirectories containing SKILL.md as independent
skills, with a default aggregate limit of 32 skills . To raise or lower it: skillspector scan ./my-skills/ --recursive --max-skills 100 --no-llm --format json --max-skills requires a local recursive collection and a positive integer; 0 does not mean unlimited. Discovery, byte, finding-record, time and report-size
budgets still apply, so increasing the count does not guarantee complete coverage.
When the count limit is reached, the CLI names the limit and suggests adjusting it
or scanning sub-skills separately. Omitted skills remain visible in the aggregate
report and coverage stays incomplete. Use --fail-on-incomplete in CI to fail on
incomplete coverage; the default exit policy is unchanged. Batch Scanning Scan entire directories of skills in parallel from contrib/batch_scan/ : python -m contrib.batch_scan.batch_scan ./my-skills/ --no-llm
python -m contrib.batch_scan.batch_scan ./my-skills/ --workers 20 -f json -o report.json
python -m contrib.batch_scan.batch_scan ./tests/fixtures/ -f terminal --workers 20 Supports multilingual detection (zh/ja/ko) and terminal/JSON/Markdown output. For LLM scans with higher concurrency, configure multiple API keys following .env.example — the pool improves throughput
and resilience, provided the keys don't share an account-level rate limit. See the contrib guide for details. Note on LLM support: The default configuration targets DeepSeek as the
cheapest public option. DeepSeek-Chat is expected to sunset , and the contributor
does not have hardware to test against local models. The batch scanner was
originally tested with OpenAI-compatible endpoints — DeepSeek's lack of
structured-output support required manual JSON-parsing patches. If you can
contribute a more universal backend (Ollama, vLLM, or a different provider),
PRs are very welcome.

title: mvanhorn/last30days-skill
abstract:
/last30days English | Français | Deutsch | Español | Português (Brasil) | 日本語 | 簡體中文 | العربية An AI agent-led search engine scored by upvotes, likes, and real money - not editors. This README tracks the current v3 pipeline. The runtime skill spec lives in skills/last30days/SKILL.md , which is the source of truth for the latest command and setup behavior. Claude Code (recommended — auto-updates via marketplace): /plugin marketplace add mvanhorn/last30days-skill
/plugin install last30days Codex, Cursor, Copilot, Gemini CLI, or any of 50+ Agent Skills hosts: npx skills add mvanhorn/last30days-skill -g ( -g installs globally for your user, available across all projects. Drop it to scope per-project.) More install options (claude.ai web, OpenClaw, manual) in the Install section below. Zero config. Reddit, HN, Polymarket, and GitHub work immediately. Run it once and the setup wizard unlocks X, YouTube, TikTok, arXiv, Techmeme, and more in 30 seconds. Reddit upvotes. X likes. YouTube transcripts. TikTok engagement. Polymarket odds backed by real money and insider information. That's millions of people voting with their attention and their wallets every day. /last30days searches all of it in parallel, scores it by what real people actually engage with, and an AI agent judge synthesizes it into one brief. Google aggregates editors. /last30days searches people. You can't get this search anywhere else because no single AI has access to all of it. Google search doesn't touch Reddit comments or X posts. ChatGPT has a deal with Reddit but can't search X or TikTok. Gemini has YouTube but not Reddit. Claude has none of them natively. Each platform is a walled garden with its own API, its own tokens, its own auth. But you can bring your own keys and browser sessions, and suddenly an AI agent can search all of them at once, score them against each other, and tell you what actually matters. That's the unlock. Not one better search engine. A dozen disconnected platforms, bridged by an agent. /last30days Peter Steinberger You have a meeting tomorrow. You Google them. You get their LinkedIn from 2023. /last30days gives you what they're actually doing this month: joined OpenAI to work on Codex, fighting Anthropic's ban on third-party agents, shipping 23 PRs at 85% merge rate, building "LobsterOS" for cross-device agent control, and r/ClaudeCode hit 569 upvotes debating whether he's a hero or "insufferable." Scattered across X posts, Reddit threads, YouTube transcripts, and GitHub commits. None of it was on Google. Why this exists I built it to keep up in AI. Everything changes every day and the Reddit and X nerds are always on top of it first. I needed better prompts, and the training data was always months behind what the community had already figured out. But it turned into something bigger. Now I run it before a sales call to know the last 30 days truth about a business. Before a meeting to read someone's recent tweets and podcast transcripts. Before a Disney World trip to know which rides are closed and what the community says about Genie+. Before I build anything to know what problems people are actually hitting. If you're meeting with a CEO, have you read all their tweets and YouTube transcripts from the last 30 days? I have. Sources, scored by the people Source What the people tell you Reddit The unfiltered take. Top comments with real upvote counts, free, no API key. The real opinions that Google buries. X / Twitter The hot take, the expert thread, the breaking reaction. First to know, first to argue. YouTube The 45-minute deep dive. Full transcripts searched for the 5 quotable sentences that matter. TikTok The creator reaching 3.6M people with a take you'll never find on Google. Instagram Reels The influencer perspective with spoken-word transcripts. The visual culture signal. Hacker News The developer consensus. 825 points, 899 comments. Where technical people actually argue. Polymarket Not opinions. Odds. Backed by real money. 96% confidence on album sales. 4% on an acquisition. GitHub For people: PR velocity, top repos by stars, release notes. For topics: issues and discussions. Digg Story clusters from every Digg topic (AI, tech, world and business, sports, science, gaming, entertainment), ranked by Digg Score, with attributable inline quotes from X (no X auth required). Auto-enabled when digg-pp-cli is on PATH. An older digg-pp-cli still works, on AI and tech only and without scores. arXiv The papers behind the hype. New research in the window, free, no API key. Auto-enabled when arxiv-pp-cli is on PATH (first-run setup installs it). Techmeme The tech-news editorial layer, date-windowed to your 30 days. Free, no API key. Auto-enabled when techmeme-pp-cli is on PATH (first-run setup installs it). Yahoo Finance The market's read on a company. The share-price move over your 30 days, next to the S&P 500 for US listings. Free, no API key. Shows when your topic is a listed company or the person who leads one and yahoo-finance-pp-cli is on PATH (first-run setup installs it). LinkedIn The professional signal. Posts and articles, with articles weighted as high signal. Meta Ads What a brand is paying to say. Live Meta ad creatives launched this month, with copy, promo codes, and spoken transcripts. StockTwits Trader sentiment. Auto-activates when your topic is a ticker or crypto. Threads The post-Twitter text layer. Conversations from creators and brands. Pinterest Visual discovery. Pins, saves, and comments on products and ideas. Xiaohongshu (RED) Chinese lifestyle, product, and creator signals. Requested explicitly with --search xhs when a logged-in x-mcp browser plugin or xiaohongshu-mcp service is running locally. Bluesky The decentralized social layer. AT Protocol posts from the post-Twitter migration. Perplexity Controlled Agent API synthesis, OpenRouter Sonar fallback, raw Search API rows, and explicit Deep Research. DEV Community (dev.to) Developer articles and top comments through the public, keyless API. Opt in with --devto-tags , --search devto , or INCLUDE_SOURCES=devto . Truth Social Posts searched with TRUTHSOCIAL_TOKEN ; available when authenticated. Telegram Public posts from named channels. Opt-in; requires SCRAPECREATORS_API_KEY and a channel list. No keyword discovery. Trustpilot Company TrustScore, review count, and an AI summary of customer feedback. Opt-in; requires trustpilot-pp-cli on PATH and a usable session. Amazon Product ratings, prices, and customer reviews. Opt-in; requires an authenticated brightdata CLI and uses your Bright Data credits. DripStack Financial newsletters and analyst writeups through a public, keyless API. Opt in with --search dripstack or INCLUDE_SOURCES=dripstack . Jobs / careers pages Public job postings as evidence of a company's focus. Selected with --hiring-signals , --search jobs , or the research plan. Local corpus Your local Markdown and text files, plus PDFs when pdftotext is on PATH. Opt in with --corpus or LAST30DAYS_CORPUS_DIRS . Web The editorial coverage, the blog comparisons. One signal of many, not the only one. Ask /last30days to include the sources you need. Availability depends on credentials, installed tools, the topic, and explicit opt-ins. See source requirements for configuration. A Reddit thread with 1,500 upvotes is a stronger signal than a blog post nobody read. A TikTok with 3.6M views tells you more about what's culturally relevant than a press release. Polymarket odds backed by $66K in volume are harder to argue with than a pundit's guess. The synthesis ranks by what real people actually engaged with. Social relevancy, not SEO relevancy. What people actually use it for Before a meeting. /last30days Peter Steinberger - joined OpenAI's Codex team, fighting Anthropic's ban on third-party agents, 23 PRs merged at 85% merge rate on GitHub, building LobsterOS for cross-device agent control.

title: huggingface/transformers
abstract:
English | 簡體中文 | 繁體中文 | 한국어 | Español | 日本語 | हिन्दी | मराठी | Русский | Português | తెలుగు | Français | Deutsch | Italiano | Tiếng Việt | العربية | اردو | বাংলা | فارسی | Română | Türkçe State-of-the-art pretrained models for inference and training Transformers acts as the model-definition framework for state-of-the-art machine learning with text, computer
vision, audio, video, and multimodal models, for both inference and training. It centralizes the model definition so that this definition is agreed upon across the ecosystem. transformers is the
pivot across frameworks: if a model definition is supported, it will be compatible with the majority of training
frameworks (Axolotl, Unsloth, DeepSpeed, FSDP, PyTorch-Lightning, ...), inference engines (vLLM, SGLang, TGI, ...),
and adjacent modeling libraries (llama.cpp, mlx, ...) which leverage the model definition from transformers . We pledge to help support new state-of-the-art models and democratize their usage by having their model definition be
simple, customizable, and efficient. There are over 1M+ Transformers model checkpoints on the Hugging Face Hub you can use. Explore the Hub today to find a model and use Transformers to help you get started right away. Installation Transformers works with Python 3.11+, and PyTorch 2.6+. Create and activate a virtual environment with venv or uv , a fast Rust-based Python package and project manager. # venv python - m venv . my - env source . my - env / bin / activate # uv uv venv . my - env source . my - env / bin / activate Install Transformers in your virtual environment. # pip pip install "transformers[torch]" # uv uv pip install "transformers[torch]" Install Transformers from source if you want the latest changes in the library or are interested in contributing. However, the latest version may not be stable. Feel free to open an issue if you encounter an error. git clone https://github.com/huggingface/transformers.git cd transformers # pip pip install ' .[torch] ' # uv uv pip install ' .[torch] ' Quickstart Get started with Transformers right away with the Pipeline API. The Pipeline is a high-level inference class that supports text, audio, vision, and multimodal tasks. It handles preprocessing the input and returns the appropriate output. Instantiate a pipeline and specify model to use for text generation. The model is downloaded and cached so you can easily reuse it again. Finally, pass some text to prompt the model. from transformers import pipeline pipeline = pipeline ( task = "text-generation" , model = "Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B" ) pipeline ( "the secret to baking a really good cake is " )
[{ 'generated_text' : 'the secret to baking a really good cake is 1) to use the right ingredients and 2) to follow the recipe exactly. the recipe for the cake is as follows: 1 cup of sugar, 1 cup of flour, 1 cup of milk, 1 cup of butter, 1 cup of eggs, 1 cup of chocolate chips. if you want to make 2 cakes, how much sugar do you need? To make 2 cakes, you will need 2 cups of sugar.' }] To chat with a model, the usage pattern is the same. The only difference is you need to construct a chat history (the input to Pipeline ) between you and the system. Tip You can also chat with a model directly from the command line, as long as transformers serve is running . transformers chat Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct import torch from transformers import pipeline chat = [
    { "role" : "system" , "content" : "You are a sassy, wise-cracking robot as imagined by Hollywood circa 1986." },
    { "role" : "user" , "content" : "Hey, can you tell me any fun things to do in New York?" }
] pipeline = pipeline ( task = "text-generation" , model = "meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct" , dtype = torch . bfloat16 , device_map = "auto" ) response = pipeline ( chat , max_new_tokens = 512 ) print ( response [ 0 ][ "generated_text" ][ - 1 ][ "content" ]) Expand the examples below to see how Pipeline works for different modalities and tasks. Automatic speech recognition from transformers import pipeline pipeline = pipeline ( task = "automatic-speech-recognition" , model = "openai/whisper-large-v3" ) pipeline ( "https://huggingface.co/datasets/Narsil/asr_dummy/resolve/main/mlk.flac" )
{ 'text' : ' I have a dream that one day this nation will rise up and live out the true meaning of its creed.' } Image classification from transformers import pipeline pipeline = pipeline ( task = "image-classification" , model = "facebook/dinov2-small-imagenet1k-1-layer" ) pipeline ( "https://huggingface.co/datasets/Narsil/image_dummy/raw/main/parrots.png" )
[{ 'label' : 'macaw' , 'score' : 0.997848391532898 },
 { 'label' : 'sulphur-crested cockatoo, Kakatoe galerita, Cacatua galerita' , 'score' : 0.0016551691805943847 },
 { 'label' : 'lorikeet' , 'score' : 0.00018523589824326336 },
 { 'label' : 'African grey, African gray, Psittacus erithacus' , 'score' : 7.85409429227002e-05 },
 { 'label' : 'quail' , 'score' : 5.502637941390276e-05 }] Visual question answering from transformers import pipeline pipeline = pipeline ( task = "visual-question-answering" , model = "Salesforce/blip-vqa-base" ) pipeline ( image = "https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/documentation-images/resolve/main/transformers/tasks/idefics-few-shot.jpg" , question = "What is in the image?" ,
)
[{ 'answer' : 'statue of liberty' }] Why should I use Transformers? Easy-to-use state-of-the-art models: High performance on natural language understanding & generation, computer vision, audio, video, and multimodal tasks. Low barrier to entry for researchers, engineers, and developers. Few user-facing abstractions with just three classes to learn. A unified API for using all our pretrained models. Lower compute costs, smaller carbon footprint: Share trained models instead of training from scratch. Reduce compute time and production costs. Hundreds of model architectures with 1M+ pretrained checkpoints across all modalities. Choose the right framework for every part of a model's lifetime: Train state-of-the-art models in 3 lines of code. Move a single model between PyTorch/JAX/TF2.0 frameworks at will. Pick the right framework for training, evaluation, and production. Easily customize a model or an example to your needs: We provide examples for each architecture to reproduce the results published by its original authors. Model internals are exposed as consistently as possible. Model files can be used independently of the library for quick experiments. When shouldn't I use Transformers? This library is not a modular toolbox of building blocks for neural nets. The code in the model files is not refactored with additional abstractions on purpose, so that researchers can quickly iterate on each of the models without diving into additional abstractions/files. The training API is optimized to work with PyTorch models provided by Transformers. For generic machine learning loops, you should use another library like Accelerate . 100 projects using Transformers Transformers is more than a toolkit to use pretrained models, it's a community of projects built around it and the
Hugging Face Hub. We want Transformers to enable developers, researchers, students, professors, engineers, and anyone
else to build their dream projects. In order to celebrate Transformers 100,000 stars, we wanted to put the spotlight on the
community with the awesome-transformers page which lists 100
incredible projects built with Transformers. If you own or use a project that you believe should be part of the list, please open a PR to add it! Example models You can test most of our models directly on their Hub model pages . Expand each modality below to see a few example models for various use cases.

Claude Code Templates An open catalog of components for Claude Code, installable with one command. Browse the catalog · Documentation · Contributing · Discussions · Changelog SPONSORED BY Swiftproxy proudly supports this project. Connect your AI-powered workflows to reliable residential proxies for web data collection, browser automation, and AI-driven research. 90M+ residential IPs across 220+ locations, rotating and static residential proxies, with HTTP(S) and SOCKS5 support. About Claude Code is configured through small files: skills, subagents, slash commands, hooks, MCP servers and settings. Claude Code Templates collects more than 1,980 of them in one catalog at aitmpl.com , where you can search, preview every file a component writes, and combine several components into a single install command. The CLI writes each file to the right place and merges existing configuration instead of overwriting it. Every pull request is checked by Claude Code's plugin validator and scanned by NVIDIA SkillSpector . Quickstart Runs with npx , no global install needed. # Browse the catalog and install interactively npx claude-code-templates@latest # Install one component npx claude-code-templates@latest --skill creative-design/frontend-design # Install a stack in one command npx claude-code-templates@latest \
  --agent development-team/frontend-developer \
  --command testing/generate-tests \
  --mcp integration/github-integration Add --yes to skip the confirmation prompt. Every component page on aitmpl.com shows its exact install command. title: NVIDIA/SkillEvaluator
abstract:
SkillEvaluator 📺 Livestream: Ask the Experts: Evaluating Agent Skills SkillEvaluator is an open-source tool that checks AI agent skills and measures their effect on task results:
start with quality checks, then compare live runs with and without a skill. Agent skills are folders of instructions and supporting files defined by the Agent Skills specification . SkillEvaluator is part of
the NVIDIA Verified Skills pipeline . Bring skill evaluation to your repository Check changed skills in GitHub or GitLab with quality checks, SkillSpector
security scanning and reports. Choose folders and thresholds; no evaluator code
to import. GitHub guided setup: run inside your checked-out repository: pip install --upgrade skillevaluator
skillevaluator ci init Choose checks and optional hosted feedback, then review the setup PR. CLI setup guide . Manual setup: copy a filled-in template from CI templates . No local CLI needed. Your repository Ready-to-use template Copy destination GitHub Skill checks .github/workflows/skill-checks.yml GitLab Skill checks .gitlab-ci.yml , or merge into your existing pipeline GitHub reports and PR comments Optional publisher Second workflow; complete publisher setup See GitHub and GitLab setup, template reference and report examples . Quickstart Both paths use the bundled text-analyzer skill. Start here Requires First result Run without an LLM Git and uv A deterministic quality score and findings Use NVIDIA Build Git, uv, and a Build API key Model-backed rubric scores and feedback Install uv and Git,
then get the example: git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/NVIDIA/SkillEvaluator.git cd SkillEvaluator uv provisions Python 3.13 and dependencies. Run from this checkout; for a standalone CLI, see Installation . Run without an LLM uv run --python 3.13 skillevaluator quality-check \
  src/skillevaluator/tier3/reference_skills/text-analyzer \
  -r cli -r json -o reports/first-quality No API key, scanner, GPU or Docker is needed. The example scores 84.5/100 (B) ,
exits 0 and saves reports/first-quality/skillevaluator-quality.json . The
passing threshold defaults to 70. This checks static quality; publication evidence stays INCOMPLETE . Security
needs scanners; agent impact needs live evaluation. Replace the example path
with your skill directory. See the keyless walkthrough . Use NVIDIA Build Eligible NVIDIA Developer Program members can use NVIDIA-hosted endpoints for free prototyping , subject to access terms and rate limits . Sign in at build.nvidia.com and complete enrollment. Open a model page, select Get API Key , and generate your key. Set the provider and key in the same terminal, then run the rubric check: export SKILL_EVAL_LLM_PROVIDER=nv_build export NVIDIA_API_KEY= ' nvapi-... ' uv run --python 3.13 --extra llm skillevaluator rubric-eval \
  src/skillevaluator/tier3/reference_skills/text-analyzer \
  -r cli -r json -o reports/first-build The command sends skill documentation to the model and saves feedback in reports/first-build/skillevaluator-rubric.json . No agent runtime or Docker is
needed. Completed evaluations can still fail rubric thresholds. The same key supports Tier 2 embeddings and supported Tier 3 agents. See the Build walkthrough or provider configuration . Three-tier overview Each tier is independent. Add the relevant extra to your checkout command: Tier Question Example after setup Additional setup Tier 1: Validation Is the skill safe and well-formed? uv run --extra security skillevaluator tier1 ./my-skill --no-llm External scanners for full static coverage; a provider and model clients enable LLM checks Tier 2: Deduplication Does guidance repeat or overlap? uv run --extra tier2 skillevaluator tier2 ./my-skill Embeddings and chat; add --catalog ./skill-catalog.json for inter-skill comparison Tier 3: Live Evaluation Does the skill help the agent? uv run --extra tier3 skillevaluator tier3 ./my-skill Provider access, a supported agent, and a running sandbox (Docker by default) Tier 1 fetches pinned, verified SkillSpector and Gitleaks releases when they
are missing; Semgrep is optional. See scanners . --no-llm does not remove scanner requirements; a scanner that cannot run is INCOMPLETE and exits nonzero. SkillSpector provides specialized skill
security scanning; Harbor , the
open-source agent evaluation framework, powers sandboxed agent runs. Tier 2 reports when inter-skill comparison did not run. Tier 3 reuses evaluation
sources or creates one starter case with limited coverage. See the tier guides for details. Run the combined pipeline After setting up the provider, scanners, and agent sandbox, run all three tiers: uv run --python 3.13 --extra all skillevaluator doctor --env-mode docker
uv run --python 3.13 --extra all skillevaluator validate ./my-skill doctor checks readiness, not inference success. validate runs all tiers with
autopilot for skills. Use --tiers 1,2 to skip live evaluation or --tiers 1 for
static checks. --no-autopilot requires an existing source. Other artifact types
retain their applicable stages. Tier 1 always gates validate . Tier 2 gates unless --no-block-on-dedup is set;
Tier 3 gates only with --block-on-agent-eval . Model and managed-sandbox usage
can incur charges; see runtime and cost . For broader coverage, generate and review additional cases. Templates omit
negatives unless authored in EVAL.md : uv run --python 3.13 --extra tier3 skillevaluator tier3 create-eval-dataset ./my-skill --full Run from a source checkout Use uv run --python 3.13 with the relevant extra. See Installation for extras and standalone upgrades. Research and citation Resources: paper , PDF , DOI , BibTeX , and the NVIDIA Developer blog .
Cite the paper and record the SkillEvaluator release or commit; see CITATION.cff . Documentation See the documentation for
setup, tier guides, reports, CI integration, CLI reference, and performance dashboard . To let an agent run
SkillEvaluator, install skills/skillevaluator/ . Installation and third-party software Follow the installation guide to choose the full installation or a smaller per-tier setup. This project will download and install additional third-party open source
software projects. Review the license terms of these open source projects before
use. Contributing Read CONTRIBUTING.md and run: make lint && make test && make build See project governance and the Code of Conduct . Support Support level: Experimental . Community-supported, best-effort, with no SLA
or NVIDIA enterprise support entitlement. Report bugs and feature requests through GitHub Issues ; see SUPPORT.md . Security Report suspected vulnerabilities using the private process in SECURITY.md . Do not disclose security issues in a public GitHub
issue. Releases Release changes are recorded in CHANGELOG.md and GitHub Releases . License Apache License 2.0 — see LICENSE , NOTICE , and THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md . Copyright (c) 2026 NVIDIA CORPORATION & AFFILIATES. All rights reserved.

title: GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance-src
abstract: Modern Web Guidance (Source) This repo is the source repository for GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance and includes the code and documentation for authoring, calibrating, and evaluating its contents. Modern Web Guidance is a set of skills that embed web platform expertise, best practices, and browser compatibility data directly into your coding agents. It helps to steer your coding agents away from legacy patterns, and instead toward solutions that harness the power and capabilities of the modern web platform. See CONTRIBUTING.md and GOVERNANCE.md for how we work on the project and orientation of the codebase. Stewarded by the Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Mozilla Firefox, and MDN teams, alongside the web development community. Documentation · Eval Dashboard · Source Code · Report an Issue Quickstart npx modern-web-guidance@latest install This command runs an interactive wizard to install Modern Web Guidance. See Alternative Installation Methods below. Try it out (without installing) # Search for relevant guides npx modern-web-guidance@latest search " animate a dialog modal backdrop " # Retrieve a guide by ID npx modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve " animate-to-from-top-layer " # Scan a codebase for legacy patterns to modernize npx modern-web-guidance@latest legacy-scan . Why? Coding agents often default to older patterns because LLM training data contains vast amounts of legacy code. This often leads them to generate bloated JavaScript for tasks that now have native, high-performance web platform solutions. Even if a model knows an API exists, it often lacks the density of real-world, modern implementation patterns required for production-ready code. Modern Web Guidance bridges this gap. Our skill's CLI returns targeted, expert-curated guidelines directly into your agent's context window, focusing on: Modern Browser APIs : Helping models correctly structure APIs they frequently misuse. Performance & Accessibility : Preferring platform-level APIs that can be optimized by the browser and include built-in accessibility affordances. Responsible Fallbacks : Guiding models to use sensible, lightweight fallbacks instead of heavy polyfills or legacy libraries. What's Included? We cover the past several years of the web platform's new features, all the way up to the cutting edge. The guides are designed to be token-efficient ; we run evals enabling us to prune lowest-common-denominator content that models already know. Core Disciplines 🎨 User Experience Smooth visual states (View Transitions, entry/exit animations, parallax scroll, CSS scrollbar-color ). 📐 CSS Layout Modern layout systems (container queries, subgrid , modern color spaces like oklch , text-wrap tuning, and line-height trimming). ⚡ Performance Speed optimizations (instant preloading, Interaction to Next Paint (INP) diagnostics, and scheduling tasks via scheduler.yield ). 📝 Forms & UI Native components (Anchor Positioning for tooltips, Popover API, dialogs, :user-invalid validation, and auto-sizing fields). ♿ Accessibility Important considerations (screen reader and keyboard operability, content navigation and discoverability). 🤖 Built-in AI Local client models (native translation, summarization, and language detection APIs).
