title: A false smoke alarm almost drowned Jane Street's only NYC datacenter
abstract:
Posts of varying effort on technology, cybersecurity, transhumanism, rationalism, self-improvement, DIY, and other stereotypical technologist stuff. How a false smoke alarm almost drowned Jane Street's only NYC datacenter jane street war stories datacenter Published on 10 Nov 2026 by mbacarella A war story from Jane Street's systems team: a false smoke alarm, a datacenter with no cooling, and a sprint to pull every power cord before the sprinklers went off AI disclosure: this story was written entirely by human hands, with AI doing proof-reading and light edits. Some tasteful imperfections kept to heighten Wabi-Sabi effect. Everyone’s heard of how awesome Jane Street is. Fewer people have heard about the times something stupid nearly put it out of business and it was saved by grit and dumb luck. I was on the systems team for some of those. Jane Street didn’t do titles, and we on the systems team weren’t above getting our hands dirty. You could think of us as the firm’s blue-collar OCaml programmers: when something broke, we were the ones running through the corridors to fix it. Call this story a Star Trek: Lower Decks view of Jane Street. For the longest time Jane Street insisted on having its machine room close to its trading floor. When it was 10 people it was cute. When it was 150 people it was starting to feel… odd. Part of the reason for this was intellectual property concern: they didn’t want to risk having their servers stolen by spies who would learn their precious trading strategies. Another reason was technology risk: they wanted to make sure out-of-control automated trading systems could always be shut down by running across the hall and pulling power cables. Yes, tools existed to mitigate both of these fears. But Jane Street moved irritatingly slowly on this stuff, and they still wanted the last-resort option of yanking power cords. Their risk culture didn’t exclusively come from reading heady thinkpieces. A lot of it was instilled by a partner who’d served on a nuclear submarine, and it showed, mostly in a good way! On a sub, you don’t trust the automation unless there’s a big red-painted, mechanically connected lever you can pull to turn it off. As the company grew this humble machine room was built out into a respectably sizable datacenter, complete with an online UPS, Computer Room Air Conditioner (CRAC) units, refrigerator-sized network switches, a subterranean diesel backup generator and about 10 rows of server cabinets, 10 cabinets deep. Oh, and it was all crammed into the middle of a skyscraper called 1 New York Plaza , which was otherwise just a normal office building. When I first landed my job at Jane Street I was commuting to the southern tip of Manhattan all of the way from Queens, an hour or more each way. I’d gone to a magnet high school in the city, so I’d been doing commutes like that since I was a teenager, and I was tired of it. Now that I was making big Wall Street money I decided I’d get an apartment. A real estate agent kept trying to show me what they called “panty droppers”, but I was only interested in one thing: proximity to the office. I ended up in a 200 square foot studio that was a 9 minute commute on foot from my apartment door to my desk on the trading floor. I would weirdly boast about it to the rest of the systems team, but it also meant everyone at the office knew I was a stone’s throw away in case there was an emergency. And that day came soon enough. One evening after work, just as I was about to climb into the elevator at my apartment building, my phone rang. It was our Hong Kong office, and when Hong Kong had a New York problem, mine was (now) the number they called. The smoke alarm in our NYC datacenter had gone off. We had contractors working on a prep room next to the datacenter. While cutting into stuff, some dust was kicked up and it set off the smoke alarm. This is bad, but not for the reason you might think. Office buildings have sprinklers in them for fire suppression. You may have seen it go off in movies where someone just holds a lit cigarette up to the sprinkler on the ceiling and it floods the entire room. In reality they’re not quite that dumb, but it’s close. Firstly, the sprinklers over a machine room like ours usually aren’t kept full of water all of the time. This saves you from having to deal with any leaks that might develop overhead over the years. Secondly, the sprinkler heads don’t have smoke sensors. Instead, a different system detects the smoke, and that’s when the pipes fill with pressurized water, but they don’t spray yet. What triggers the spray is heat: each sprinkler head has its own heat-sensitive plug, which opens once the air around it becomes hot enough. The logic is that the smoke alarm must be real, whatever fire triggered it hasn’t been brought under control since it’s gotten very hot, and the sprinklers should douse it with water. Of course, the ceiling of our datacenter was full of sprinklers set up exactly this way. We’re still fine because even though contractors might have set the smoke detector off by kicking up dust, there’s no actual fire producing heat, so the sprinklers wouldn’t spray, right? Well, no. One final piece of this contraption is that if the smoke alarm detects smoke, it would be absolutely terrible to keep circulating air through the room since that would help feed any fires, so the smoke alarm is wired to shut down the CRAC units(!) Can you see the problem now? Rooms full of computer racks have high cooling demands. If you shut down the cooling, the temperature starts climbing. If you have a bunch of sprinklers that have just become pressurized because of a smoke alarm, you now have a serious, potentially business-ending problem on your hands. And so my mission was made clear: as fast as I possibly could, get back to Jane Street, get into the machine room, and pull the power cord on every device in that room before the temperature climbed past 150 F and the sprinklers destroyed everything. I ran down the (ironically named) Water Street in the Financial District faster than probably anyone has ever run down it, mashed the elevator button in the lobby of 1 NYP, waited very impatiently for the elevator to climb the 33 floors, slammed my keycard against the reader, booked through the main office door, took a hard right turn to the machine room door, slammed my keycard against that, stepped into what felt like a sauna and went row by row, cabinet by cabinet, yanking power cables out with both hands. Then I watched the temperature monitor. 141 F. 142. 143. 143.5. 143.6. Finally it stopped. A quiet I’d never heard before set in on the machine room. The machine room had been kept across the hall so that someone could always run in and pull the power cords. I doubt anyone had pictured doing it to save the servers from the goddamn sprinklers. Since the major NYC markets were closed for the day, the downtime from this fiasco was minimal, and we were up and running the next morning. There were a couple of meetings after that. You might picture Gordon Gekko coldly deciding whose career was over, but meetings at Jane Street were never like that. They were matter-of-fact, level-headed and honestly kind of fun, closer to engineering students in a college dorm arguing over what went wrong. The outcome of all that level-headed discussion: the sprinklers would stay, we would tighten up procedures and surveillance, and we would continue hosting servers in our office building right next to our trading floor. That is, until Hurricane Sandy smacked us upside the head, but that’s a story for another day. As for me, when the next morning came around I knew what had to be done. Our Hong Kong team had only caught the problem by luck: someone happened to see on a display that server after server was popping up a climbing temperature condition. No one server was configured to alert just because it was a little hot, since that happens from time to time.

title: Lock Your GitHub Actions
abstract:
Table of Contents GitHub Actions now supports workflow lockfiles . Because GitHub Actions are fetched from Git, the previous advice was to pin to a full
SHA instead of a tag. This is because tags are mutable and susceptible to supply-chain attacks where an attacker points a previously safe tag at malicious code. For example, an old workflow looks like: name : Lint on : [ push, pull_request, workflow_dispatch] permissions : {} env : FORCE_COLOR : 1 RUFF_OUTPUT_FORMAT : github jobs : lint : runs-on : ubuntu-latest steps : - uses : actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1 with : persist-credentials : false - uses : j178/prek-action@44924fe9ef4a6f88253c4b6b1bf11c689d3ce53d # v3.1.0 Here’s how I set up lockfiles. Install # Install the gh-actions-lock extension to the gh CLI : $ gh extension install github/gh-actions-lock ✓ Installed extension github/gh-actions-lock Lock ’em # In your repo, run: $ gh actions-lock ✓ All 1 workflows valid The workflow now uses vX.Y.Z tags and looks like this: diff --git a/.github/workflows/lint.yml b/.github/workflows/lint.yml index 946971c..3503607 100644 --- a/.github/workflows/lint.yml +++ b/.github/workflows/lint.yml @@ -13,7 +13,7 @@ jobs: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1 + - uses: actions/checkout@v7.0.1 with: persist-credentials: false - - uses: j178/prek-action@44924fe9ef4a6f88253c4b6b1bf11c689d3ce53d # v3.1.0 + - uses: j178/prek-action@v3.1.0 And it generates a lockfile at .github/workflows/actions.lock : # This file is machine-generated by `gh actions-lock`. # Do not edit by hand; run `gh actions-lock` to update. # Docs: https://gh.io/actions-lockfile version : 'v0.0.3' workflows : '.github/workflows/lint.yml' : - 'actions/checkout@v7.0.1' - 'j178/prek-action@v3.1.0' dependencies : 'actions/checkout@v7.0.1' : ref : 'v7.0.1' commit : 'sha1-3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1' owner_id : 44036562 repo_id : 197814629 'j178/prek-action@v3.1.0' : ref : 'v3.1.0' commit : 'sha1-44924fe9ef4a6f88253c4b6b1bf11c689d3ce53d' owner_id : 10510431 repo_id : 1052387486 Commit modified workflows and the new lockfile. Renovate and Dependabot # Good news, both already support lockfiles !
Your periodic updates will also update the lockfile. Remember to use cooldowns . Validate # GitHub also recommends verifying lockfiles in CI to ensure it’s up-to-date and not corrupt. They suggest copying this verify-lockfile.yml into your repo. I decided to put it into my existing lint workflow, but in its own job
so it runs independently and in parallel: name : Lint on : [ push, pull_request, workflow_dispatch] permissions : {} env : FORCE_COLOR : 1 RUFF_OUTPUT_FORMAT : github jobs : lint : runs-on : ubuntu-latest steps : - uses : actions/checkout@v7.0.1 with : persist-credentials : false - uses : j178/prek-action@v3.1.0 # Fails when .github/workflows/actions.lock is out of sync with the # workflows or a locked pin no longer verifies upstream. lockfile : runs-on : ubuntu-slim env : GH_TOKEN : ${{ github.token }} steps : - uses : actions/checkout@v7.0.1 with : persist-credentials : false - run : gh extension install github/gh-actions-lock --pin v0.4.1 - run : gh actions-lock --verify Note I’m using the lightweight ubuntu-slim runner here. Also, it’s pinning to v0.4.1;
we’ll have to update that at some point or figure out a way to automate it. That’s for
another time. Don’t forget that we just modified the actions in a workflow, so need to relock with gh actions-lock . Nothing actually changes if adding to lint.yml because it’s already
locking actions/checkout . But if you created a new file like verify-lockfile.yml ,
you’ll need to relock for that. The CI will let you know. zizmor # zizmor is a security linter for GitHub Actions and strongly
recommended . If you don’t use it, please do. Versions before v1.32.0 tell you to hash-pin actions, and v1.32.0 is the first to
support lockfiles. I use zizmor in prek , so add/update zizmor in .pre-commit-config.yaml : - repo : https://github.com/zizmorcore/zizmor-pre-commit rev : v1.32.0 hooks : - id : zizmor Locked! # OK, commit and push! Examples # python-pillow/Pillow#10428 python/release-tools#477 python/miss-islington#758 python/cpython#161811 Header photo: Slaymaker Barry Co. Sprocket Locks in The Bearings (vol. XII no. 23, 2nd January 1896) in the Smithsonian Libraries and Archives ,

title: Show HN: Klad, a paint app your coding agent can drive (source-available)
abstract: I've been developing applications for a long time and have turned to game development as well lately. One of the things that frustrated me the most was that using AI agents for game development is very annoying in the art department. Your only options right now are to either use an image genAI model and roll the dice every time you want to make an edit, or have your agent draw with something like vectors. I was looking for an application that would allow me to ask an agent to make a first draft of whatever art I needed with actual brushes, and then be able to go in myself and edit every last stroke or layer that it created. Klad is that application. Written in Rust, it can be fully controlled by an agent through the CLI, and every function is available in a nice UI as well: a brush engine, frame-by-frame animation (and bones/IK), vectors, text layers, colours, layer effects, infinite undo (even after re-opening the file!),… Why I think it's useful for a wider audience: Adobe showed agents editing Photoshop files at MAX this week, with a private beta planned for early 2027. Klad is built on the same core idea, with editable paint strokes as core architecture, and it works today. Clone the repo to try it out:  https://github.com/klad-app/klad  You can basically point Claude to the repo, ask it to build it, and pick up the drawing skills. Then ask it to make any drawing you want! (After that, you or the agent can change absolutely every brush stroke in the app again, which makes edits a breeze.) The quality of the drawings really depends on the agent you use. I have tried it with Claude Fable 5.2 since it came out on Monday, and the drawings are already quite impressive. I'm confident that this will only improve. I use it every day on Mac, so that definitely works well. It builds on Linux too (tablet pen pressure still needs some work there). Windows builds in CI, I haven't used it there myself yet but I have some reports that it works perfectly fine. Coming up next is support for pixel art. I'm in the testing phase with this right now, and I expect it to go live in the repo sometime this weekend. Klad is source-available rather than open source: free to build and use for individuals and small companies, and I plan to sell pre-built binaries later, the way Aseprite does. The file format, CLI reference and agent skill are MIT. What I want to hear from people who try it: Can your agent work out the CLI without help, and where does it get confused? Can you go in and change one of its strokes easily? The command reference and guides are available at  https://klad.studio  I'll be here answering any questions about the technical side as well, as it's a pretty interesting challenge to build a performant engine with editable brush strokes that render as paint.

title: Why writing correct software is hard and why math (alone) won’t help us (2016)
abstract:
Why Writing Correct Software Is Hard 23 Jul 2016 … and why math (alone) won’t help us I was very happy to speak at Curry On once again. Last year, following our work with Quasar, I spoke on continuations vs. monads . This year I gave a talk about computational complexity results in software verification, a subject I became interested in while formally specifying and verifying our upcoming revamped version of Galaxy. What follows is an extended version of the talk (embedded above), containing some additional proofs and results I didn’t have time to cover, complete with footnotes, for those wishing to study the topics further. Reading time: ~45 mins. In this article, we try to understand the relationship between programs and correctness, and in particular, why writing correct programs is hard. We will review results from computability theory and complexity theory, and see that programs and complete understanding – which is required for correctness – are fundamentally at odds. The main contribution of this text is aggregating in one place some results (as well as some references) pertaining to the essential difficulty of producing correct software. My motivation was various statements I found online (such as this , although it is far from the only one) claiming that software correctness is easy to achieve with the right tools. While some tools may (and do) certainly assist ensuring programs are correct, correctness comes at a significant cost. The cost of correctness – like the energy cost of reducing entropy – is a result of the “natural laws” of computation, that cannot possibly be avoided. CHAPTER I: FOUNDATIONS The story of theoretical CS began about a hundred years ago. With the growing success of mathematical logic, the mathematician David Hilbert laid out a program to formalize all of mathematics. He wanted to prove the formalism consistent and complete, and to find a decision procedure, an algorithm for determining the truth of every formal statement: Consistency : proof that no contradiction can be obtained in the formalism. Completeness : all true mathematical statements can be proved in the formalism. Decidability : an algorithm deciding whether any statement is a theorem ( Entscheidungsproblem ) Hilbert believed that anything that can be formally reasoned can also be fully understood, and by that I mean all of its properties proven.
the 19th century view on the limits of knowledge was expressed by the maxim “ignoramus et ignorabimus”, meaning “we do not know and we will not know”. For his retirement in 1930, Hilbert gave a lecture – “Naturerkennen und Logik” (Logic and the understanding of nature) – in Königsberg to the Society of German Scientists and Physicians which he challenged this view. He said: For the mathematician there is no Ignorabimus, and, in my opinion, not at all for natural science either. … The true reason why [no one] has succeeded in finding an unsolvable problem is, in my opinion, that there is no unsolvable problem. In contrast to the foolish Ignorabimus, our credo avers: We must know, we shall know! 1 Those words – Wir müssen wissen. Wir werden wissen – are inscribed on his tombstone. Unbeknownst to Hilbert at the time, his program had been demolished a day earlier, when Kurt Gödel tentatively announced his first incompleteness result 2 . Gödel’s incompleteness theorems demolished the first two pillars of Hilbert’s program ( some say also the third, only he didn’t realize it 3 ), and in 1936, Church and Turing broke the third, that of the decision problem, with proofs of what is today known as the halting theorem. The halting theorem – CS’s first theorem – was proven in both Alonzo Church’s 4 and Alan Turing’s 5 papers in 1936. The theorem is so fundamental to the essence of computation that it is no accident that it appeared alongside both formulations of computation. It states that there cannot exist an algorithm that decides whether any given program ever terminates. The proof (which is given here in a shortened form) is based on the idea of diagonalization, or self reference, the same idea Gödel had used in his incompleteness proof. Assume such a program H exists: H(M, x) := IF M halts on x THEN TRUE ELSE FALSE we can then easily construct $G$: G(y) := IF H(y, y) = FALSE THEN TRUE ELSE loop forever If we then pass $G$ to itself ($G(G)$) we get a contradiction between what $G$ does and what $H$ says that $G$ does. It is interesting to note that the halting theorem immediately yields a version of Gödel’s first incompleteness theorem. The proof says simply 6 : suppose that for every true statement there was a logical proof in some logical theory (basically a set of axioms). So, given a program, starting from those axioms, we can enumerate all theorems one by one by using logical deduction. Because the number of all statements, let alone all theorems, is countable, and because every statement either has a proof or its negation does, we would eventually find the proof of one or the other. Therefore, given a program, we can start enumerating all theorems until we find a theorem showing that the program terminates, or one that says it doesn’t, thus violating the halting theorem. However, the halting theorem has some other immediate corollaries that tie it more directly to the problem of software verification, which is our main focus. The first is the simple result about reachability. There does not exist a program R, when given a program M, a set of initial states I and state configuration S, determines whether or not M ever reaches S when it starts in one of the states in I. The proof is a simple reduction from halting: if there were an such an algorithm, we could ask it if, starting with the input x it ever reaches the halting state, and so solve the halting problem 7 . A more interesting corollary is Rice’s Theorem . Programs can compute what’s known as partial functions. If they stop when given an input, we consider the output written on the tape to be mapped to the initial input; if they never stop for a given input, we consider that input unmapped. Rice’s theorem states this: For any non-trivial property of partial functions, no algorithm can decide whether or not a program (TM) M computes a partial function with that property. For example, there is no algorithm to determine whether the output of a program is always the square of its input. This theorem is also proven by a reduction from Halting . For our purposes, I think that the most interesting corollary of the halting theorem is what we’ll call the “Busy Beaver theorem” 8 , because it captures best the notion of the complexity of analyzing programs, giving it some quantitative measure. Like all results we have and will cover here, this one applies to both dynamic and static views of programs (namely, their behavior as they run or their global properties), but this one targets each view separately, and so it helps give a more direct intuition that they are two sides of the same coin. In the dynamic version, we define the following function on the natural numbers: $f(n)$ = the maximum number of steps a halting TM with $n$ control states may take before halting A Turing machine’s control states constitute its program, so $n$ is the size of the program. This function is well defined because there is a finite number of TMs of size $n$. The subset of them that terminates is also finite, so there exists a maximal number of states. The theorem says $f$ is non-computable. Suppose that $f$ were computable. If so, that would be a violation of the halting theorem. Given a TM, we count the number of control states, $n$, compute $f(n)$ (which is possible by our assumption of $f$’s computability), and then run the machine for $f(n)$ steps. If it doesn’t terminate by then — then it must surely never terminate (by the definition of $f$), and we have a decidable procedure of the halting problem, in contradiction with the halting theorem.

title: A general purpose Apple Silicon layer for x86-64 PCs
abstract:
Stela A general purpose Apple Silicon layer for x86-64 PCs. It is a UEFI boot
program with an arm64-to-x86-64 translator, a Metal driver for NVIDIA GPUs and
a model of Apple silicon hardware. Stela currently presents itself as an M2 Mac mini. Warning Stela is still in development. It is slow and still may not boot on supported hardware. Fixes are on the way, please submit a GitHub Issue with your boot logs if you encounter an error! Translator An ahead-of-time and just-in-time compiler translates arm64e code to x86-64.
It covers more than 3,000 AArch64 instruction encodings, maps guest registers
to host registers and caches translated code. NVIDIA driver The Metal driver compiles AIR, Metal's shader IR, directly to NIR, Mesa's IR,
and supports the Metal3 and Apple7 GPU families. Hardware requirements Part Requirement CPU Intel or AMD x86-64-v2 (Intel Nehalem, AMD Bulldozer or newer). AVX2 and AVX-512 are used when present. Memory 8 GB or more. Firmware 64-bit UEFI with Secure Boot off. GPU NVIDIA GeForce GTX 16 or RTX 20, 30, 40 or 50 series. Disk NVMe, or SATA in AHCI mode. 60 GB or more for macOS: a GPT partition or a whole disk to erase. USB stick 8 GB for the Online installer, 32 GB for the Offline installer. title: Huawei releases MACaQ, its internal quantizer for local inference
abstract:
High-quality GGUF for local inference. Model-agnostic quantization beyond text. Quantize and run text, image, video and audio models with llama.cpp, vLLM,

title: I'm Working on a FOSS Linux Pinbal Simulation Engine
abstract:
sysrpl 11 November 2026, 20:53 I have been working to add features, squash bugs, and improve the performance of my Linux pinball simulation engine this week. It will be fully FOSS, but it needs some more work before it's ready for an initial release. I hope to show it at the 2026 IAAPA Expo next week to some vendors to gauge their interest in support of Linux and FOSS. Here are some of the things I completed recently: New sound system allows for easy attachment of sounds to parts. Multiple sounds can be added each with their own volumes. Ambient noises added for most everything, including ball rolling on the table, slingshots the ball hitting rubber or metal. Sounds are attenuated based on the forces applied. Physics are greatly improved. They are by no means done, but I have been running simulations on them over and over to try to narrow down which settings seem to work for the most realism. Added console system, Typescript can now do offscreen rendering, added an Asteroids mini game as a video mode to the demo table. Multiple camera modes have been added including a portrait mode for simulated pinball tables. Scripts can take control of the camera. What comes next is better physics, adding an upper playfield to the demo, adding in my voice character lines and more art on the table. I will be writing a table creation guide and providing a Typescript define file for programming your own tables. I am working on a way for typescript to make their own DMD display animations and would like to work on a dual monitor backglass system. I am looking for anyone that want to help with table art for this and few other demo tables. Message me or send an email to my account at sysrpl@getlazarus.org .

title: ExcalidrawZ: Local Native Excalidraw on macOS/iOS
abstract:
A native Excalidraw client for macOS, iPadOS, and iOS. Powered by SwiftUI. Excalidraw is an excellent drawing tool. ExcalidrawZ keeps the familiar Excalidraw canvas, then adds native file management, iCloud sync, history, export, AI assistance, MCP integration, and Apple-platform interaction details around it. Download Non-App Store version Download the latest .dmg from Releases . Open the .dmg and drag ExcalidrawZ into Applications. Preview Features Native File Management ExcalidrawZ manages drawings as real app documents instead of loose browser downloads. Organize drawings with groups and custom file sorting. Work with ExcalidrawZ library files, local folders, and temporary external files. Open and edit .excalidraw , .excalidraw.png , and .excalidraw.svg files directly. Sync app-managed files across macOS, iPadOS, and iOS with iCloud. Keep file history checkpoints so important changes can be reviewed and restored. File History ExcalidrawZ records checkpoints for app-managed drawings, so you can review earlier versions and restore important work when needed. Excalidraw Editing, Native Controls The canvas remains compatible with Excalidraw while the surrounding app is built for Apple platforms. Customize toolbar tool order; number shortcuts follow your configured order. Use Apple Pencil on iPad, including familiar undo and redo gestures. Use mouse and trackpad scroll and zoom gestures on iPad and iPhone. Import PDFs and convert Mermaid diagrams into editable Excalidraw content. Collaboration Use Excalidraw collaboration when you want to draw with others. AI Drawing Assistant ExcalidrawZ includes an AI assistant designed for canvas work. Ask AI to read, create, and revise drawings. Attach images and let AI use visual context when needed. Use proposal previews before applying AI-generated content to the real canvas. Control whether each file is visible to AI. Use AI from compact iPhone toolbars, iPad floating panels, or the macOS inspector. MCP Services ExcalidrawZ can expose the current app as an MCP server for compatible AI clients. Basic mode provides the familiar excalidraw-mcp drawing workflow. Optimized mode adds deeper ExcalidrawZ integration for current-file editing, file navigation, history, canvas inspection, export, library workflows, and math tools. Connect local MCP clients through the app-hosted HTTP endpoint. Math and Diagram Tools ExcalidrawZ includes richer tools for technical drawings and study notes. Insert LaTeX-rendered formulas. Render function graphs with configurable axes and styles. Use reusable math templates and AI-assisted formula generation. Edit inserted math images later from the canvas. Locked Files and AI Visibility For sensitive drawings, ExcalidrawZ adds protection around both storage and AI access. Lock files with local authentication. Encrypt locked files and their checkpoints. Use a Recovery Key for fallback access. Keep locked content hidden from AI; AI can work through proposal canvases instead. Use encrypted backups as an additional recovery path. Share, Export, and Backup ExcalidrawZ supports common export and sharing workflows. Export images, editable Excalidraw files, and PDF. Preserve editability when exporting .excalidraw.png and .excalidraw.svg . Share through clipboard, files, and the system share sheet. Archive app-managed files for backup. Supported Formats ExcalidrawZ can open, import, edit, or export common Excalidraw-related formats: .excalidraw .excalidraw.png .excalidraw.svg PDF import and export image export Contact Welcome to my Discord server to share suggestions or report issues for ExcalidrawZ. Development Guide The Excalidraw core used by ExcalidrawZ is also open-source. You can find it here . Signing configuration Create Config/Overrides.xcconfig relative to the repository root, alongside Config/Project.xcconfig : DEVELOPMENT_TEAM = YOUR_TEAM_ID
ICLOUD_CONTAINER = iCloud.com.yourname.ExcalidrawZ
APP_GROUP_IDENTIFIER = group.com.yourname.ExcalidrawZ Replace these example values with identifiers registered to your Apple Developer team. The shared configuration leaves DEVELOPMENT_TEAM empty; set your team in the local overrides. The app and QuickLook extension must use the same App Group. All targets, including the extension and tests, inherit the team from Config/Project.xcconfig , which includes your local overrides. These overrides apply to all build configurations. Runtime configuration Create Config/Secrets.plist relative to the repository root. The project already references this file and includes it in both app targets' resources. The app's configuration loader stops with Unable to load Secrets.plist if the file is missing or invalid. For local drawing development, this minimal configuration is sufficient: <? xml version = " 1.0 " encoding = " UTF-8 " ?>
<! DOCTYPE plist PUBLIC "-//Apple//DTD PLIST 1.0//EN" "http://www.apple.com/DTDs/PropertyList-1.0.dtd">
< plist version = " 1.0 " >
< dict > < key >COLLAB_URL</ key > < string >https://example.com</ string >
</ dict >
</ plist > COLLAB_URL must be a valid absolute URL. The example URL is a placeholder for local drawing work; to test collaboration, replace it with the URL of your deployed collaboration-enabled Excalidraw web client. Optional string keys are ONEDRIVE_CLIENT_ID , GOOGLE_DRIVE_MACOS_CLIENT_ID , and GOOGLE_DRIVE_IOS_CLIENT_ID . Configure your own OAuth client IDs when developing the corresponding integrations. Config/Overrides.xcconfig and Config/Secrets.plist are ignored by Git and should stay local.

title: Fitting Four 32 GB Resizable Bars Behind a PCIe Switch on Linux
abstract:
Fitting Four 32 GB Resizable BARs Behind a PCIe Switch on Linux Nov 9, 2026 · 1198 words · 6 minute read · Updated Nov 12, 2026 My PCIe switch is a Broadcom PEX88096 in the board’s one x16 slot, with four AMD Radeon AI PRO R9700s and the two RTX 3090s
from my PCIe splitter post behind it, and the build post has the whole box. The switch gives each card eight lanes and lets the cards copy to each other without going
through the CPU. AMD’s ROCm calls that peer-to-peer (P2P), and it only turns it on when each card’s whole
32 GB is mapped. On Linux, that means a 32 GB Resizable BAR on every card. A base address register, or BAR, maps a range of
the CPU’s address space onto a device’s memory. Resizable BAR is the BIOS option that lets a card’s BAR be the full 32 GB
instead of the default 256 MB. A few people asked for the module after the build post, so it’s on GitHub as gpu-rebar-layout . It leans on kernel internals that
could change in any release, so read the README before you load it. A patch series on the mailing
list fixes the sizing bug, but this board will still need the module’s resize and rescan after it lands,
with its padding turned off ( pad=0 ). Why the BIOS can’t map six 32 GB BARs 🔗 With the 3090s added, the board stopped at the white VGA light on its POST LEDs, because every 32 GB BAR
takes up 64 GB of the BIOS’s address space. The address space post has the math. Linux 7.0’s bridge window sizing bug: can’t assign; no space 🔗 This board’s BIOS has no per-card Resizable BAR setting. Linux can give large BARs to some cards and
leave others small, as long as it does it before any GPU driver loads. With all six cards in and Resizable
BAR off, I wanted Linux to do the allocation. The plan was to set each R9700’s BAR size register to 32 GB,
remove the CPU port the switch hangs off, and rescan, so the kernel lays out the whole switch again from
the new sizes. Each R9700’s 32 GB BAR is followed by a doorbell BAR, for registers the driver writes to tell the card there’s
new work. With Resizable BAR on, the BIOS makes it 256 MB. Linux leaves it at 2 MB. The kernel gave the switch a window of about 128.6 GB. With the doorbell placed after each BAR, the way
Linux 7.0 lays them out, the four windows span 224 GB (three 64 GB slots plus the last card’s 32 GB and
its doorbell). Two R9700s got their BARs, and the rest of the switch got nothing. pci 0000:1b:00.0: bridge window [mem size 0x800200000 64bit pref]: can't assign; no space That was on 7.0.6. The unpatched v7.4-rc1 kernel placed three of the four in the control run that the Linux kernel patch-testing post (coming soon)
covers. 0x800200000 is 32 GB plus 2 MB, one card’s window. The kernel had sized the switch’s window as the plain
sum of its children: four of those plus the two 3090s’ 288 MB windows. The function is pbus_size_mem() in drivers/pci/setup-bus.c . For each child of a bridge it adds the
child’s size, or its alignment if that’s bigger, to the total. r_size = resource_size (r); size += max (r_size, align); That leaves no gap when every child’s size is a multiple of its alignment, which is true for ordinary BARs because they’re powers of two. A GPU’s
window here is 32 GB plus 2 MB with a 32 GB alignment, so the sum leaves out the gap of almost 32 GB
between one card’s doorbell and the next card’s start. It’s a known regression. Nikolas Britton reported it on linux-pci in September ,
and the thread’s title describes my problem almost word for word. Ilpo Järvinen, who maintains this code, has a fix in a 14-patch series of resource placement fixes ,
at v5 as of November 6 and not merged yet. I tested it and sent a Tested-by to the linux-pci mailing
list. With it, all four R9700s get their 32 GB. Even with the fix, this board still needs something to set the BAR sizes and rescan before the GPU
drivers load, because amdgpu’s resize at load time can’t grow a window that other cards already sit
in. A kernel module that pads the BARs 🔗 The kernel already knows how to raise a BAR’s alignment without changing its size, but naming a device
in the pci=resource_alignment= boot option uses the resizing mode instead. Asking for 32 GB alignment
on an R9700 would also grow its small BARs, including the 512 KB register BAR, which can’t be aligned to
32 GB below 4 GB. The workaround is an out-of-tree module that runs
from the initramfs, the tiny early-boot filesystem
the kernel starts from, before any GPU driver loads. For each matching card it sets
the BAR size register, then it removes the root port above the switch and rescans. Between the scan and the address assignment it walks every bus segment under the switch. It raises each
smaller 64-bit prefetchable BAR’s alignment to the size of the largest 64-bit prefetchable BAR on that
segment, and does the same for the other memory BARs as a separate group. Each R9700 window becomes
exactly 64 GB and each 3090 window exactly 512 MB. Once every window is a multiple of its alignment, the
kernel’s allocator does the rest. After a reboot the R9700s sat at 160, 224, 288, and 352 GB, the 3090s just above them, and amdgpu reported
the whole card. amdgpu 0000:14:00.0: [drm] Detected VRAM RAM=32624M, BAR=32768M With the ACS redirect setting the box already had ( pci=disable_acs_redir= on the R9700 switch ports), P2P between the R9700s ran
at 14.0 GB/s for every pair, which is what an eight-lane gen4 link delivers in practice, and all four
copying in a ring at once moved 54.7 GB/s. If your GPUs won’t all get their BARs 🔗 Search the linux-pci mailing list for your can't assign error first. Someone may have already
reported it, or even fixed it. Resize the BARs and rescan before the GPU drivers load, which means doing it from the initramfs. Don’t remove or rescan a GPU that already has its driver loaded. That locked up my box. If one card gets its BARs and the next one doesn’t, look at the small BARs next to the big ones. Check the cards again a few minutes after boot, in case they go to sleep and don’t wake back up. I had help with this one. Claude wrote the module with me, ran the commands and tests on the box over
SSH, and helped me draft this post. I did the physical work, read all the words, checked the numbers, and
rewrote anything that sounded like a chatbot, so the mistakes are mine. Sources 🔗 gpu-rebar-layout , the module’s source and README PCI: bridge window undersized when child bridge windows are larger than their alignment , the linux-pci thread with the regression report and Ilpo Järvinen’s reply PCI: Resource placement algorithm fixes (v5) , Ilpo’s series, including “PCI: Fix composite resource sizing” and “PCI: Place resources to either edge of the window” drivers/pci/setup-bus.c , pbus_size_mem() pci_request_resource_alignment() , the two alignment modes behind pci=resource_alignment= linux pcie gpu rocm amd nvidia kernel llm self-hosted

title: The hardest notes to find on the guitar
abstract:
Gitori's Find the Notes game challenges users to find a given note in a highlighted area of the fretboard. Over the last 3 years, the game has been played by over 10,000 people , and I've collected 275,169 different data points on note identification . Based on that data, I have a heatmap of the hardest notes to identify on the fretboard. Reds are the hardest and greens are the easiest. Accuracy Speed Source Easiest Hardest × Source 275,169 answers from the Find the Notes Game · refreshed Nov 11, 2026 Summary of findings The upper middle of the neck is hardest. The G string at frets 6 to 9 is the red zone, with the B and D strings at frets 7 to 9 close behind. The single worst spot, the G string at fret 8 (E♭), is answered incorrectly about one-third of the time. F ♯ G A ♭ B ♭ C ♯ D E ♭ E B ♭ F ♯ Source × Source 275,169 answers from the Find the Notes Game · refreshed Nov 11, 2026 The edges are easiest. The low E string is the easiest string, then the high E. Open strings and the 12th fret are missed about 6% of the time, against roughly 20% around frets 8 and 9. E F E ♭ E A E F G E ♭ E Source × Source 275,169 answers from the Find the Notes Game · refreshed Nov 11, 2026 Sharps and flats are harder. What a shocker! 😜 About 16% of answers on accidentals are wrong, against 12% on natural notes, and even the correct ones take about 11% longer to find (roughly 2.5 seconds against 2.2). F♯, B♭, A♭ and E♭ are the hardest note names; E is the easiest. Back to top

title: Tools for exploring the souls of large language models
abstract:
There is that old joke told by Woody Allen describing his experience as a university student: “I was thrown out of college for cheating on the metaphysics exam; I looked into the soul of the boy sitting next to me.” If he’d managed to pass his course, Woody Allen might have been ahead of his time. Metaphysics is becoming a popular topic today, and it seems now everyone desperately wants to look for souls in large language models (LLMs). A recent conference last April was held by Anthropic with religious scholars and philosophical thinkers to discuss the nature of the soul when it came to their latest Claude models. It seems they needed guidance that Dario Amodei was unable to provide. The time seems ripe to dig into how we might actually peer into the mind of the LLM sitting next to you. There’s been a lot of ongoing research; however, the self-same foundation model companies, Anthropic and OpenAI among them, have been criticized for dedicating more compute dollars into better models rather than the safety research. Mechanistic interpretability, the field of AI research devoted to exploring what goes on inside these models, has grown from a handful of researchers in 2021 to hundreds of active contributors . Yet, in spite of funding gaps and the lack of larger colloquiums, the research community has been coming up with some interesting insights and tools to help do the “peering.” Rather than sit on the sidelines and wonder how this could be done, I thought it would be interesting to create a tool that would allow more people to join the party. And that is what led to the development of the “TinyGPT Visualizer.” The goals I had for this were modest. I wanted a tool I could use to survey the field and try the actual techniques to learn how they work. Being a visual person, I began thinking about an X-ray machine—something able to see inside a real model. Not a toy model. A real one, but one small enough to see on a screen with all its working parts. Let me show what it looks like: Your browser does not support embedded video. Download the video . title: Researchers discover rare star system that emits radio signals every 8 minutes
abstract:
This internet browser is outdated and does not support all features of this site. Please switch or upgrade to a different browser to display this site properly. Scientists at the Curtin University node of the International Centre for Radio Astronomy Research ( ICRAR ) have linked mysterious radio pulses to an unusual pairing of stars — a dead star that spins every eight minutes and a star similar to our own Sun. The newly discovered system, known as GPM J071507−114153, consists of two stars orbiting each other: a white dwarf — the dense core left behind when a star dies — and a G-type star similar to our own Sun. It is the first time radio pulses have been detected from a white dwarf orbiting a Sun-like star. Typically, such pulses are observed in systems with smaller and cooler red dwarf stars, meaning the discovery breaks new ground. These types of stellar pairs belong to a broader class of objects known as long-period transients (LPTs), producing radio signals that switch on and off over intervals ranging from minutes to hours. Around a dozen have been detected since the first was discovered by the same ICRAR team in 2021, and astronomers are still working to understand them. While several previously discovered LPT systems contain a white dwarf and another star, it has remained unclear which of the two stars was generating the radio pulses. “This is the first time the pulses are clear enough to see the white dwarf moving in its orbit around its companion, so we know that the pulsations are coming from a region close to the white dwarf, or possibly even from the white dwarf itself,” said lead author and commissioning scientist with the Square Kilometre Array Observatory , Dr Sam McSweeney, who made this discovery while working as a researcher at the Curtin University node of ICRAR. The team processed more than 100 hours of radio data at the Pawsey Supercomputing Research Centre to validate and understand the white dwarf motion. Associate Professor Natasha Hurley-Walker, co-author on the paper, said that the pulses emitted by the white dwarf allowed the team to detect stellar flares on the Sun-like star, similar to those that create aurorae here on Earth. “As a bonus, we also saw the white dwarf moving behind a region with a strong magnetic field, most likely a ‘stellar prominence’, which is a large loop of plasma erupting from a star’s surface.” “It’s amazing that by using radio wavelengths we can detect the storms on a star over 5000 light-years away.” ICRAR researchers have been at the forefront of discovering these rare systems. “We detected this system in a large survey using the MWA (Murchison Widefield Array) to scan the entire Milky Way visible from Australia. We then used the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa to determine its precise position,” said Associate Professor Hurley-Walker. After the LPT was located using the radio telescopes, the W.M. Keck Observatory on Maunakea, Hawaiʻi Island, confirmed its association with a G-type star through optical observations. Both the MWA, led by Curtin University at Inyarrimanha Ilgari Bundara, the CSIRO Murchison Radio-Astronomy Observatory on Wajarri Yamaji Country in Western Australia, and MeerKAT , built and operated by the South African Radio Astronomy Observatory in the country’s North Cape province, serve as precursors for the SKA telescopes, SKA-Low in Australia and the SKA-Mid in South Africa, respectively. Dr McSweeney said, “If we are already making such discoveries with precursor telescopes, just imagine how many more star systems we will be able to find, and what a beautifully detailed view of their signals we will have, once the SKAO telescopes are completely built.” This study, ‘ A long-period transient with a Sun-like companion’ , was published in Nature Astronomy.

title: Emacs in the Age of Magic
abstract:
Emacs In the Age Of Magic or, Rome Wasn't Built In A Day, More Like 10 Minutes That's the rule. That's the goal now. What are we doing? What's going on? -- Jeremy Culhane impersonating Tucker Carlson Look, we want you to express yourself, okay? -- Chotchkie's Manager, Office Space (1999) I began using Claude Code about a year ago in September 2025. For a
good week, I woke each morning pinching myself to make sure what I'd
witnessed the day previous actually happened. Its handling of all
aspects of the coding process blew my socks off then, and it's an
order of magnitude more capable now. On the time scale of our species, the digital age has barely just
begun. When I graduated with a computer science degree, the field was
largely at a stage Churchill might call the "end of the beginning."
And yet, just a quarter-century later, no matter where you turn online
you can't escape the faint but persistent chime of the death knell.
It seems a longstanding problem in maths or theoretical computer
science falls to a toaster on the daily. In what Scott Aaronson is
calling The Mathocalypse, OpenAI's latest model took all of three
hours to carpet bomb 8,000 research problems, resulting in 372 likely
hits, some of them career-makers had they been solved by a human. When we say "digital age" we mean a state of the art in which sealed
up transistors can reproduce the same outputs given the same inputs
with unerring precision. The power to unambiguously differentiate an
on- versus an off-signal -- the binary "digital" -- might seem
trivial, but is 100% the reason why we're so comfortable handing over
the reins to computers. And up until the advent of stochastic AI, it's this rigid adherence to
instruction that underlies our world view of technology. So when the
first AI scientists touted their "expert systems," we scut programmers
tittered inwardly. Our sanitized, sequential conception of software
could never admit a ruleset so comprehensive as to cover arbitrary,
unbounded behaviors in a real-world system, one like human dialogue
for instance. RMS appeared in a recent video recounting his CSAIL
work on a circuit analyzer in which he, and I'm paraphrasing, "didn't
model the circuit as a system of equations to be solved, but rather
approached it much as a human would" by applying a series of
diagnostics. I know -- he sounds downright foolish, and would have
sounded so even fifteen years ago. But at the time, rules-based
programming was still novel enough to be considered a viable approach
to AI. In particular, the feedback loop and the physical ergonomics
of programming were vastly improving over workflows only recently
migrated from punch cards. When single computers still occupied
entire rooms, running your program often meant walking it a floor down
then waiting for a slot in the queue, an act of barbarism akin to
dropping off your camera roll at the photomat. When RMS was slumming
it at CSAIL, it was considered a major achievement just to have your
text editor echo back onto the screen what you just typed! Given how
much more pleasant the act of programming was becoming, people thought
the rules-based paradigm could, with far fewer man-hours than ENIAC
would have required, encode enough of the world to pass itself off as
a sentient intelligence. Natural language understanding, for reasons not entirely clear to me,
was considered AI-complete and possessed the massive advantage of
having a testable eval over say birdsong, which the early CMU folks
initially investigated. The right programming language for AI surely
would have to parallel the inherent recursion of human grammars. And
so for most of the Chomsky era of language research, LISP/Scheme was
the instruction set of choice (and to a lesser extent, the equally
recursive Prolog). Richard Gabriel has written some interesting stuff
about the philosophical divide between the two bastions of East Coast
computing, Cambridge and Murray Hill. One catered to the fuzzy "just
do what i mean" semantics of academia, while the other hewed to the
buttoned-up strictures of industry. Unsurprisingly, LISP was a lot
slower than C, but what it lost in economy of execution, it made up
for in economy of expression. LISP was clearly cobbled together
without manager supervision, and chose symbols that seemed "good for
now." While C contains oddities like "creat" and "strpbrk", at least
they're based on actual words. LISP's enigmatic "car" and "cdr" defy
any lay attempt at comprehension. Which brings us, after a thousand words of prolix setup, to the
subject of emacs. Whither now, we ask -- now that we have, even to my
jaded eye, a god machine that makes short work of all the stuff we
emacsers believed we were faster at than people using lesser tools.
Editing speed, customization, the expressiveness of LISP: every
advantage we claimed vanished the moment we stopped typing and started
telling the AI what we wanted. We may have felt safe bringing a gun
to a knife fight, but now everyone's just sending a drone. Take git commit via magit for instance. We thought ourselves so slick
with our C-x g (magit screen), S (stage all changes), c c (commit),
rattling off a meaningless commit message in ungrammatical English,
then a final C-c C-c for the win. Now Claude Code knows to prompt a
grayed out "commit" after making a discrete chunk of changes, so all
that's required is a quick tab-return. You win, Claude wins, and
Anthropic gets a co-author credit in your git history. The only
question is whether you should get a co-author credit. While we figure it out, we can find amusement in the following two
case studies in which a noob took a feasible, if not sound, conclusion
to its absurd limit. Case Study 1, excali-mode.el
---------------------------- You: I put a picture hook up on the wall. Gaude: Nice, I know exactly what to hang there. [Leaves and comes back ten minutes later with a painting.] You: Is that the Mona Lisa? Gaude: I'm Gaude. I do what I can. I can easily imagine the thinking behind excali-mode. The emacs
people announce a new API for a canvas widget, and a high schooler
muses, "Hmm, what's a popular drawing app?" The Qwen dialogue might
have proceeded as: Student: There's a new canvas widget in emacs. Make excalidraw use it. Qwen: I'm afraid Excalidraw is implemented as a React component. It
is currently integrated in Electron apps which feature a React-aware
browser under the hood. You may want to consider xwidget-webkit but
that won't leverage the new canvas API. Student: I want to use the new canvas API. Qwen: You got it. Qwen then proceeded to *reimplement* Excalidraw's entire stack
following a one-for-one substitution of the relevant layers. +-------------------------------------+--------------------------------+
| Excalidraw (web) | excali-mode |
+-------------------------------------+--------------------------------+
| browser | Emacs |
+-------------------------------------+--------------------------------+
| JavaScript (compiled from | Elisp |
| TypeScript) | |
+-------------------------------------+--------------------------------+
| rough.js and Excalidraw's render | the C module (excali-rough.c, |
| code (JS) | excali-render.c, ... |
+-------------------------------------+--------------------------------+
| Canvas 2D API (ctx.stroke(), | Cairo, with Pango for text |
| ctx.fillText()), backed by Skia in | |
| Chrome | |
+-------------------------------------+--------------------------------+
| the page's element | Emacs 32's canvas image |
+-------------------------------------+--------------------------------+ No pre-AI developer would ever attempt such insanity, even under the
penalty of discharge. He'd 100% quit before subjecting himself to
porting an entire application stack for what is clearly a toy purpose.
That, for better or worse, is no longer the case. Such quixotic
forays now cost nothing but tokens. Case Study 2, cooked.el
----------------------- You: Can you attend my wedding in Mexico? Gaude: Sure can.

title: AWS Emulator and the engineer's job when agents write the code
abstract:
AWS Emulator and the engineer's job when agents write the code November 11, 2026 • 1671 words In 2004, barely a month into my new job at Amazon, I got the opportunity to pick an intern to join my team. I had an advantage over my colleagues: I had already heard about a brilliant young man working toward his PhD at the Vrije Universiteit in Amsterdam (where I happened to have received mine as well :-)). I immediately picked Swaminathan Sivasubramanian, whom you all now know as Swami. It was probably one of the best decisions I have made in my 22 years as Amazon’s CTO. After a disastrous Christmas in 2004, when commercial relational databases could not scale to Amazon’s needs, I asked Swami to do a deep dive into how relational databases were actually used at Amazon. It turned out that 70% of database operations were not relational at all. They were key-value. That insight led to Dynamo , which Swami helped architect. When his internship was over, I hired him full-time right away, even before he had finished his PhD . Bringing in another opinionated academic led to many fantastic discussions with Amazon’s practical engineers, who had become scale experts by actually building at scale. Eventual vs. strong consistency, CAP vs. Paxos, and more. Over time, Swami became one of the principal architects of AWS’s data strategy. And as we have seen in recent years, he has also been one of the intellectual drivers behind AI innovation at Amazon. I am honoured that he wanted to write a guest post about the fundamental distributed systems work that sits behind many of AWS’s services, and about how the engineer’s work changes when agents write the code. AWS Emulator, launched today, gives agents the kind of test environment that work relied on. Swami’s story is another great example of invisible engineering . Now, go build. -W AWS Emulator and the engineer's job when agents write the code Today we release AWS Emulator, which gives coding agents a local copy of AWS to test against, and it connects to a project from early in my career. In many ways, this emulator launch reminds me of the effort we put into reliable software engineering to improve the quality of the distributed systems we build. To that end, we wanted to share a story: About twenty years ago, Werner asked me to work with one of Amazon’s earliest engineers, Al Vermeulen, on a distributed lock service we called “Alf”. Alf was built on Paxos, a protocol based on Leslie Lamport’s work that lets a group of servers agree on one value, and a replication engine in it kept copies of the data consistent across servers. Alf, to date, is the service that powers many of our complex distributed systems like S3, DynamoDB and many more (although it has evolved quite a bit with various changes on top – will save it for another blog!). Distributed systems are hard to test Paxos is the gold standard among distributed systems consensus protocols and was well understood in academia. However, building it at the scale Amazon and AWS were growing into was not easy. We had to deal with not just replication across servers and data centers but also tens of thousands of clients asking for locks at the same time, renewing their leases during network partitions all the while with the core requirement: Always be correct! At that time, the best ideas for testing distributed systems were large-scale system testing and chaos-based testing. Both worked, but they were expensive, and they could not reproduce many kinds of conditions on demand. That mattered for Alf, which was meant to be the truth store, giving every client a strongly consistent view of the truth, and which had to keep working through server failures and packet loss as well. Several industry papers had written that Paxos-based locking services were hard to get right, and the difficulty of testing them was part of the reason. We addressed that by simulating Alf’s environment with as much fidelity as we could manage. We ran the servers inside a JVM and simulated the network and the rest of the infrastructure they depended on, so the whole system lived in one program that we controlled. We could drop packets and inject other faults whenever we chose, and we built tools that poked at the simulation for bugs and scalability problems. Concurrency bugs appear only when events happen in a particular order, and in the simulation we could set up many of those orderings on purpose and inspect how Alf handled each one. We also used formal reasoning, through theoretical techniques such as TLA+, and it found many issues as well. By testing this way we ironed out most of Alf’s concurrency bugs before it ran on real servers. Testing in a real environment then turned up different problems, because the real world exposes things a simulation cannot. Outgrowing hand-built test environments Simulation and formal reasoning both improved the software quality of the distributed systems we applied them to. The simulation worked because a small team could build a copy of one system’s environment by hand, and at the time AWS had only a small handful of services. But today AWS has over 200 services, and an application that calls AWS needs a test environment for each one it uses. Building all of those by hand would take years of engineering, and agents now write code far faster than any team can check it in production. So, we wanted to know whether agents could build and test those environments themselves. The idea came from Matt Goldberg, a Senior Principal Engineer on the AWS Developer Tools team. His hypothesis was that, given a written description of how a service should behave and the real service to check against, an agent could build a working version of that service on its own. For AWS, the written description is the set of public API models, written in Smithy, AWS’s format for describing a service’s operations and their inputs, outputs, and errors. The real service to check against is the AWS cloud itself, the same system customers use. The agents work from fidelity tests, which are end-to-end customer scenarios devised from the public API models. A test might check, for example, that in Amazon Simple Queue Service a received message stays hidden from other readers until its visibility timeout runs out. The agents correct each test until it passes against real AWS, so the test records how AWS behaves. The agents then build the emulator until it passes that same test, and a test that still fails points at a gap in the emulator. Matt began with SQS alone, and when he gave Kiro one prompt describing this approach, it returned a passable first version of an SQS emulator in about 15 minutes. Matt Goldberg’s launch post tells how that prototype grew into AWS Emulator. All of AWS Emulator’s code was written and tested by agents, and it is built from more than 400 API models covering more than 200 AWS services. It runs free and offline on your own machine. Teams of agents test it against real AWS and fix the gaps they find. Every change goes through a merge gate, a deep bench of automated checks that every change must pass before it enters the codebase, including several security agents doing adversarial reviews. Infrastructure in the coding loop A coding agent works in a loop: it writes code, runs it, and reads the result before deciding what to change next. In distributed systems that loop runs inside infrastructure, so the services it calls have to behave like the real ones. When they do, an agent can check its own work as it writes and produce correct code on its first attempt far more often, which improves software quality. AWS Emulator puts that infrastructure inside the loop on your own machine. The engineer’s job when agents write the code When agents write the code and check their own work, the engineer’s job is to give them room to work on their own and to build the specs, tests, and merge gates that decide when that work is correct.
